docs.text: Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see the truth: two products almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . Later sessions return to each one with real data. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause Correlation and regression Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part Metrics and KPIs Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Visualisation principles Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Time series and trends Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories Descriptive statistics Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Marketing case Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Business cases A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn?
docs.title: Part 6: A preview of how numbers mislead

docs.text: Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened, why, what next and what to do. Good analysis starts from a decision , and a good question names a decision, population, period and measure. The seven-step workflow keeps evidence at each step so someone else can check your work. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixing groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors.

docs.text: Session 2 lab: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Turn a vague request into a clear question, take the retail table apart, and prove you can count its orders correctly before anyone draws a chart. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first. But before you show me any chart: can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" This is not yet a question you can answer with data, and a wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today you turn the request into a question and build trust in the data. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company, not a real one. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the file does not state a currency, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G7 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I6 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Write a business question that names a decision, a population, a period and a measure. Explain what the setup cell's load_orders() does, step by step. State the grain of the table and count orders correctly with nunique() . Write a data dictionary and run a quality checklist across five dimensions. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check one order by hand and keep a preparation log . Evidence you keep: your question, grain statement, data dictionary, quality checklist, preparation log, one hand-checked order and a first chart with its filters written down. Before you start, work through the Session 2 lecture and the Session 1 lab , and have your evidence log open. Guided practice ¶ G1 (Core): From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course data Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn Rewrite the head's request as your own one-sentence question, using the four parts. Write it in your evidence log. G2 (Core): Load the data ¶ Run the setup cell first. It downloads the sample from Tableau's website, checks it is exactly the version this course was written for, and prepares the table. In G4 you will open it up and see what each step does. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Now load the table into a variable called df and look at the first rows. df = load_orders () df . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } row_id order_id order_date ship_date ship_mode customer_id segment country_region region category ... product_name sales quantity discount profit returned_order_flag customer_analysis_eligible customer_order_conflict order_to_ship_days order_month 0 1 US-2023-103800 2023-01-03 2023-01-07 Standard Class DP-13000 Consumer United States Central Office Supplies ... Message Book, Wirebound, Four 5 1/2" X 4" Form... 16.45 2 0.20 5.55 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 1 2 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 Standard Class PO-19195 Home Office United States Central Office Supplies ... GBC Standard Plastic Binding Systems Combs 3.54 2 0.80 -5.49 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 2 3 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 Standard Class PO-19195 Home Office United States Central Office Supplies ... Avery 508 11.78 3 0.20 4.27 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 3 4 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 Standard Class PO-19195 Home Office United States Central Office Supplies ... SAFCO Boltless Steel Shelving 272.74 3 0.20 -64.77 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 4 5 US-2023-141817 2023-01-05 2023-01-12 Standard Class MB-18085 Consumer United States East Office Supplies ... Avery Hi-Liter EverBold Pen Style Fluorescent ... 19.54 3 0.20 4.88 0 1 0 7 2023-01-01 5 rows × 22 columns G3 (Core): Size, column types and dates ¶ print ( "Rows, columns:" , df . shape ) df . dtypes Rows, columns: (6815, 22) row_id int64 order_id object order_date datetime64[ns] ship_date datetime64[ns] ship_mode object customer_id object segment object country_region object region object category object sub_category object product_id object product_name object sales float64 quantity int64 discount float64 profit float64 returned_order_flag int64 customer_analysis_eligible int64 customer_order_conflict int64 order_to_ship_days int64 order_month datetime64[ns] dtype: object Check the types make sense: order_id , segment , region are text ( object ). sales , profit , discount are decimals ( float64 ); quantity is a whole number. order_date , ship_date , order_month are dates ( datetime64 ). IDs are not amounts row_id is stored as a number, but adding it up means nothing. It is an identifier: a nominal variable, whatever its storage type. Which dates are included? print ( "First order date:" , df [ "order_date" ] . min () . date ()) print ( "Last order date: " , df [ "order_date" ] . max () . date ()) First order date: 2023-01-03 Last order date: 2025-12-31 G4 (Core): What load_orders() does ¶ So far you used load_orders() without looking inside. Now we open it up. You do not need to memorise this code; you need to know what was changed between the original file and df , so you can explain your numbers. The function does seven things: Step What happens Why 1 Reads the Orders and Returns sheets from the Excel file These are the raw tables 2 Finds orders that have more than one Customer ID A known data issue, flagged before filtering 3 Keeps orders placed from 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31 Gives the course a fixed, complete period 4 Renames columns to short lowercase names Easier to type: order_id instead of "Order ID" 5 Adds returned_order_flag Marks orders on the returns list 6 Adds customer_order_conflict and customer_analysis_eligible Marks the customer-ID issue from step 2 7 Adds order_to_ship_days and order_month , then keeps 22 columns sorted by row_id Handy derived columns The cells below repeat each step on its own so you can see the effect. Step 1: Read the raw sheets ¶ SOURCE_FILE is the Excel file the setup cell downloaded. pd.read_excel reads one sheet into a DataFrame. raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) print ( "Raw Orders sheet, rows and columns:" , raw . shape ) print ( "Returns sheet, rows and columns: " , returns . shape ) print ( "Order dates in the raw file:" , raw [ "Order Date" ] . min () . date (), "to" , raw [ "Order Date" ] . max () . date ()) Raw Orders sheet, rows and columns: (10194, 21) Returns sheet, rows and columns: (296, 2) Order dates in the raw file: 2023-01-03 to 2026-12-30 The raw file has more rows than df , and its dates run further. The Returns sheet is just a list of order IDs: returns . head ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Order ID Returned 0 US-2023-100762 Yes 1 US-2023-100867 Yes 2 US-2023-102652 Yes Step 2: Find orders with more than one customer ¶ Every order should belong to one customer. The code counts the different Customer IDs inside each order and keeps the orders where that count is above 1. This is done on the whole raw file , before any filtering, so no conflict is hidden by the date filter. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) conflict_orders {'CA-2025-121465', 'CA-2026-130494'} Step 3: Keep orders placed 2023 to 2025 ¶ The filter keeps rows whose Order Date is on or after 1 January 2023 and before 1 January 2026. It looks at the order date only. in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) print ( "Rows kept: " , in_scope . sum ()) print ( "Rows dropped:" , ( ~ in_scope ) . sum ()) Rows kept: 6815 Rows dropped: 3379 The ship date is not filtered. An order placed late in 2025 may ship in early 2026, and it stays in, because the order date defines the period: print ( "Lines in df that shipped in 2026:" , ( df [ "ship_date" ] >= "2026-01-01" ) . sum ()) Lines in df that shipped in 2026: 34 Step 4: Rename columns ¶ rename swaps the original names (with spaces and capitals) for short names. Four raw columns are not kept at all, because the course does not need them: kept_raw = [ "Row ID" , "Order ID" , "Order Date" , "Ship Date" , "Ship Mode" , "Customer ID" , "Segment" , "Country/Region" , "Region" , "Category" , "Sub-Category" , "Product ID" , "Product Name" , "Sales" , "Quantity" , "Discount" , "Profit" ] [ col for col in raw . columns if col not in kept_raw ] ['Customer Name', 'City', 'State/Province', 'Postal Code'] Step 5: The returns flag ¶ isin asks, for each row, "is this order ID on the returns list?". The answer True / False is turned into 1 / 0 . A three-line order on the list gets a 1 on all three lines . Step 6: The customer-conflict flags ¶ The same isin trick marks every line of a conflicted order with customer_order_conflict = 1 . customer_analysis_eligible is the opposite ( 1 - conflict ). These lines stay in all Sales and order counts; they are left out only when we later analyse individual customers. df . groupby ( "customer_order_conflict" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () customer_order_conflict 0 3387 1 1 Name: order_id, dtype: int64 Compare this with the output of Step 2: not every conflicted order in the raw file was placed inside the course period, so fewer of them appear in df . Step 7: Two derived date columns ¶ order_to_ship_days = ship date minus order date, in whole days. order_month = the first day of the order's month, used to group by month. df [[ "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" ]] . head ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id order_date ship_date order_to_ship_days order_month 0 US-2023-103800 2023-01-03 2023-01-07 4 2023-01-01 1 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 4 2023-01-01 2 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 4 2023-01-01 Remember The original Excel file is never changed. load_orders() builds a fresh, prepared copy every time you run it, so anyone can repeat your work and get the same table. G5 (Core): Find the grain and count orders ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Use the second one whenever a question is about orders. docs.text: The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first. But before you show me any chart: can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" This is not yet a question you can answer with data, and a wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today you turn the request into a question and build trust in the data. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company, not a real one. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the file does not state a currency, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else.

Predict before you run the next cell: will the number of rows equal the number of orders? print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 Remember len(df) counts rows . df["order_id"].nunique() counts different orders . Use the second one whenever a question is about orders. How many lines do orders usually have? groupby("order_id").size() counts the lines in each order; value_counts() then counts how many orders have 1 line, 2 lines, and so on. lines_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . size () . value_counts () . sort_index () lines_per_order . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "How many lines each order has, orders placed 2023–2025" ) plt . xlabel ( "Lines in the order" ) plt . ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () Many orders have one line, but plenty have several. docs.text: returned_order_flag is 1 when an order is on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. The order you looked at in G5 is on the list. See how the flag repeats: df [ df [ "order_id" ] == "US-2023-100762" ][[ "row_id" , "order_id" , "returned_order_flag" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } row_id order_id returned_order_flag 1684 1685 US-2023-100762 1 1688 1689 US-2023-100762 1 1690 1691 US-2023-100762 1 1691 1692 US-2023-100762 1 Now compare two ways of counting: flagged = df [ df [ "returned_order_flag" ] == 1 ] print ( "Sum of the flag (counts LINES): " , df [ "returned_order_flag" ] . sum ()) print ( "Distinct orders on the returns list: " , flagged [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Sum of the flag (counts LINES): 511 Distinct orders on the returns list: 191 A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag counts lines of listed orders, not orders. To count orders on the returns list, filter to flag 1 and use nunique() on order_id , as in the second line of the output above. Say "orders on the returns list", not "returned orders" or "return rate": the list tells us membership only.

In this table every order has exactly one segment, so the segment counts add up to the overall total. One order can contain products from several categories . That order is counted once in each category it touches, so the category counts add up to more than the overall total. Distinct counts do not always add up Sales and Profit can be added across groups. Distinct order counts can only be added when every order belongs to exactly one group. Always recount distinct orders at the level you display. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Part 1: Levels of measurement ¶ Not every number is a quantity. A postcode, a shirt size and a temperature are all written with digits or ordered labels, yet you cannot treat them the same way. Statisticians sort variables into four levels of measurement . Each level allows everything the level above it allows, plus something new. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Segment, region, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5, ship class + median, percentiles, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps , but zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Sales, quantity, days to ship, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative). Predict, then reveal: is 20 °C twice as hot as 10 °C? ¶ Write down yes or no , then run the cell. It converts both temperatures to Fahrenheit and compares the ratios. celsius = pd . Series ([ 10 , 20 ], index = [ "cool day" , "warm day" ]) fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 print ( "Ratio in Celsius: " , celsius [ "warm day" ] / celsius [ "cool day" ]) print ( "Ratio in Fahrenheit:" , round ( fahrenheit [ "warm day" ] / fahrenheit [ "cool day" ], 2 )) print ( "Difference in Celsius:" , celsius [ "warm day" ] - celsius [ "cool day" ], "degrees" ) Ratio in Celsius: 2.0 Ratio in Fahrenheit: 1.36 Difference in Celsius: 10 degrees The ratio changes when the unit changes, because 0 °C is not "no temperature". So ratios on an interval scale mean nothing. The difference is meaningful in either unit. Sales is different: 0 really means no sales, so "Region A sold twice as much as Region B" stays true whatever the currency. That is a ratio scale. Predict, then reveal: numbers that are not quantities ¶ The table below is made up. pandas sees three numeric columns. Which of the three averages printed by the next cell actually mean something? survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" , "C4" , "C5" , "C6" ], "postcode" : [ 44600 , 44700 , 44600 , 33700 , 44600 , 44800 ], "satisfaction_1_to_5" : [ 5 , 4 , 5 , 1 , 4 , 2 ], "orders_last_year" : [ 3 , 1 , 6 , 2 , 0 , 4 ], }) print ( survey . dtypes , end = " 

 " ) survey [[ "postcode" , "satisfaction_1_to_5" , "orders_last_year" ]] . mean () customer object postcode int64 satisfaction_1_to_5 int64 orders_last_year int64 dtype: object postcode 42,833.33 satisfaction_1_to_5 3.50 orders_last_year 2.67 dtype: float64 Postcode is nominal. The average postcode is not a place. Satisfaction is ordinal. The gap between 1 and 2 need not equal the gap between 4 and 5, so the mean is risky. The median and the share of 4s and 5s are safer. Orders last year is ratio. Its mean is meaningful. The right summaries for the first two: print ( "Most common postcode:" , survey [ "postcode" ] . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "Median satisfaction: " , survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] . median ()) print ( "Share scoring 4 or 5:" , ( survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] >= 4 ) . mean ()) Most common postcode: 44600 Median satisfaction: 4.0 Share scoring 4 or 5: 0.6666666666666666 Telling pandas about order ¶ An ordinal column stored as text sorts alphabetically, which is wrong. An ordered categorical keeps the real order. sizes = pd . Series ([ "M" , "S" , "XL" , "L" , "S" , "M" ]) print ( "Alphabetical:" , sorted ( sizes . unique ())) sizes = pd . Categorical ( sizes , categories = [ "S" , "M" , "L" , "XL" ], ordered = True ) print ( "Real order: " , list ( sizes . categories )) print ( "Largest size:" , sizes . max ()) Alphabetical: ['L', 'M', 'S', 'XL'] Real order: ['S', 'M', 'L', 'XL'] Largest size: XL Check your understanding 1 Classify each Superstore column as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio: segment , ship_mode , order_date , sales , quantity , order_to_ship_days , row_id . For one of them, explain why someone could reasonably argue for two levels. Remember The data type pandas shows ( int64 , object ) is about storage . The level of measurement is about meaning . An ID stored as a number is still nominal. Part 2: Tidy data ¶ A table is tidy when: Each variable is a column. Each observation is a row. Each value is a single cell. Spreadsheets for people are often not tidy: months spread across columns look good on a page but are awkward to filter, group and chart. wide = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "East" ], "Jan" : [ 120 , 95 , 80 ], "Feb" : [ 130 , 90 , 85 ], "Mar" : [ 150 , 110 , 70 ], }) wide .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region Jan Feb Mar 0 North 120 130 150 1 South 95 90 110 2 East 80 85 70 Predict, then reveal ¶ The table has 3 rows and 3 month columns. After reshaping to one row per region and month , how many rows will there be? melt turns column names into values of a new column. tidy = wide . melt ( id_vars = "region" , var_name = "month" , value_name = "sales" ) print ( "Rows after melt:" , len ( tidy )) tidy Rows after melt: 9 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region month sales 0 North Jan 120 1 South Jan 95 2 East Jan 80 3 North Feb 130 4 South Feb 90 5 East Feb 85 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 Now "sales for March" is a filter and "sales by region" is a groupby , both one line of code: print ( tidy [ tidy [ "month" ] == "Mar" ]) print () print ( tidy . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum ()) region month sales 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 region East 235 North 400 South 295 Name: sales, dtype: int64 The opposite move, long to wide, is pivot . Use wide tables for reading , tidy tables for analysing . A second untidy pattern: two values in one cell. messy = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment_region" : [ "Consumer/West" , "Corporate/East" , "Consumer/East" ]}) messy [[ "segment" , "region" ]] = messy [ "segment_region" ] . str . split ( "/" , expand = True ) messy .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer segment_region segment region 0 C1 Consumer/West Consumer West 1 C2 Corporate/East Corporate East 2 C3 Consumer/East Consumer East Check your understanding 2 A finance file has one row per department and a column for each of the 12 months' budgets, plus 12 columns for actual spend. Which tidy rule does it break? Sketch the column names of a tidy version. Part 3: Grain and keys ¶ The grain of a table is what one row represents: one order, one product within an order, one customer per month, one employee per day. Grain decides what simple counting means. If a row is a product within an order, then counting rows counts order lines , not orders. Two kinds of key make grain explicit: Key Meaning Check Primary key Column(s) that identify each row uniquely; never missing No duplicates, no blanks Foreign key Column that points to the primary key of another table Every value exists in that other table Here is a tiny made-up shop with three tables at three different grains. customers = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment" : [ "Consumer" , "Corporate" , "Consumer" ]}) orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O4" ], "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "shipping_fee" : [ 5 , 5 , 10 , 5 ]}) order_lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ], "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O3" , "O3" , "O4" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Desk" , "Chair" , "Pen" , "Lamp" , "Paper" , "Desk" ], "sales" : [ 4 , 200 , 150 , 4 , 30 , 8 , 220 ]}) order_lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product sales 0 1 O1 Pen 4 1 2 O1 Desk 200 2 3 O2 Chair 150 3 4 O3 Pen 4 4 5 O3 Lamp 30 5 6 O3 Paper 8 6 7 O4 Desk 220 Grain of each table: customers : one customer, primary key customer_id . orders : one order, primary key order_id ; customer_id is a foreign key. order_lines : one product within an order, primary key line_id ; order_id is a foreign key. Check the keys with code: print ( "line_id unique in order_lines? " , order_lines [ "line_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in order_lines?" , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in orders? " , orders [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Every line's order exists? " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . isin ( orders [ "order_id" ]) . all ()) print () print ( "Rows in order_lines:" , len ( order_lines )) print ( "Different orders: " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) line_id unique in order_lines? True order_id unique in order_lines? False order_id unique in orders? True Every line's order exists? True Rows in order_lines: 7 Different orders: 4 Predict, then reveal: the shipping fee trap ¶ We want total shipping fees. The fee lives in orders (one per order). A colleague joins it onto the order lines and adds it up. Look at the orders table above and work out the true total fee by hand. Will the colleague's number be the same? joined = order_lines . merge ( orders , on = "order_id" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) print ( "True total fee (orders table): " , orders [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) print ( "Colleague's total (after the join):" , joined [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) joined [[ "line_id" , "order_id" , "product" , "shipping_fee" ]] True total fee (orders table): 25 Colleague's total (after the join): 50 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product shipping_fee 0 1 O1 Pen 5 1 2 O1 Desk 5 2 3 O2 Chair 5 3 4 O3 Pen 10 4 5 O3 Lamp 10 5 6 O3 Paper 10 6 7 O4 Desk 5 After the join, each order's fee appears on every line of that order, so summing it counts the fee once per line. The join changed the grain of the fee. Two habits prevent this: Before adding up a column, ask: at what grain is this value recorded? Use validate= in merge to state the relationship you expect ( "one_to_one" , "many_to_one" , "one_to_many" ). pandas raises an error if the keys break it. The correct total, taken back at the order grain: print ( "Fee, one per order:" , joined . drop_duplicates ( "order_id" )[ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) Fee, one per order: 25 Check your understanding 3 A table has one row per employee per month. What is its primary key? If you sum headcount = 1 over the whole year, what have you counted? Part 4: Data dictionaries ¶ A data dictionary describes every column so that anyone can use the table correctly without asking you. Field Example for sales Name sales Meaning Sales reported for the order line Type (storage) float64 Level of measurement Ratio Unit Source monetary units; currency not stated Allowed values Zero or more Can you add it up? Yes, across lines and groups Source and changes Orders sheet, column "Sales"; not changed pandas can fill in the mechanical fields for you. The human fields (meaning, unit, "can you add it up?") need your judgement. def profile_columns ( data ): """One row per column: storage type, missing values, distinct values and an example.""" return pd . DataFrame ({ "dtype" : data . dtypes . astype ( str ), "missing" : data . isna () . sum (), "distinct" : data . nunique (), "example" : data . iloc [ 0 ], }) profile_columns ( order_lines ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example line_id int64 0 7 1 order_id object 0 4 O1 product object 0 5 Pen sales int64 0 6 4 Check your understanding 4 profile_columns says line_id is int64 with as many distinct values as rows. Which human fields of the dictionary would you add for it, and what would you write under "Can you add it up?" Part 5: Data-quality dimensions ¶ "Is the data good?" is too vague to check. Break it into dimensions , each with a test you can run. Dimension Question Example pandas check Completeness Are values missing that should be present? df.isna().sum() Validity Do values follow the rules (type, range, allowed list)? (df["quantity"] > 0).all() Consistency Do related values agree, within and across tables? Ship date not before order date Uniqueness Is each real-world thing recorded once? df["id"].is_unique , df.duplicated() Timeliness Is the data recent enough, and is the period complete? df["date"].max() versus the reporting date Here is a small made-up extract with a problem planted in each dimension. Read it first and try to spot them. extract = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A3" , "A5" , "A6" ], "region" : [ "West" , "west" , "East" , "East" , None , "South" ], "order_date" : pd . to_datetime ([ "2025-03-01" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-04" , "2025-03-05" ]), "ship_date" : pd . to_datetime ([ "2025-03-03" , "2025-03-01" , "2025-03-05" , "2025-03-05" , "2025-03-06" , "2025-03-07" ]), "quantity" : [ 2 , 1 , 3 , 3 , - 4 , 1 ], }) extract .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 0 A1 West 2025-03-01 2025-03-03 2 1 A2 west 2025-03-02 2025-03-01 1 2 A3 East 2025-03-02 2025-03-05 3 3 A3 East 2025-03-02 2025-03-05 3 4 A5 None 2025-03-04 2025-03-06 -4 5 A6 South 2025-03-05 2025-03-07 1 print ( "Completeness: missing values per column" ) print ( extract . isna () . sum (), end = " 

 " ) print ( "Validity: rows with quantity not above zero" ) print ( extract [ extract [ "quantity" ] <= 0 ], end = " 

 " ) print ( "Consistency (labels): region spellings ->" , sorted ( extract [ "region" ] . dropna () . unique ())) print ( "Consistency (dates): rows shipped before they were ordered" ) print ( extract [ extract [ "ship_date" ] < extract [ "order_date" ]], end = " 

 " ) print ( "Uniqueness: is order_id unique?" , extract [ "order_id" ] . is_unique , "| fully duplicated rows:" , extract . duplicated () . sum (), end = " 

 " ) reporting_date = pd . Timestamp ( "2025-03-31" ) print ( "Timeliness: last order" , extract [ "order_date" ] . max () . date (), "| days before the reporting date:" , ( reporting_date - extract [ "order_date" ] . max ()) . days ) Completeness: missing values per column order_id 0 region 1 order_date 0 ship_date 0 quantity 0 dtype: int64 Validity: rows with quantity not above zero order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 4 A5 None 2025-03-04 2025-03-06 -4 Consistency (labels): region spellings -> ['East', 'South', 'West', 'west'] Consistency (dates): rows shipped before they were ordered order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 1 A2 west 2025-03-02 2025-03-01 1 Uniqueness: is order_id unique? False | fully duplicated rows: 1 Timeliness: last order 2025-03-05 | days before the reporting date: 26 Finding a problem does not mean deleting it. For each one, decide and record whether to fix, flag, exclude or keep, and why. Session 3 is about those decisions. Check your understanding 5 For each planted problem above, name the dimension and say what you would do. Which one could be a genuine business event rather than an error? Part 6: Worked case — the Superstore order lines ¶ Now apply every idea to the course data. The question from the business: "How many orders did we have, and can I trust the number?" Step 1: Load and profile ¶ df = load_orders () print ( "Rows, columns:" , df . shape ) profile_columns ( df ) Rows, columns: (6815, 22) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example row_id int64 0 6815 1 order_id object 0 3388 US-2023-103800 order_date datetime64[ns] 0 918 2023-01-03 00:00:00 ship_date datetime64[ns] 0 989 2023-01-07 00:00:00 ship_mode object 0 4 Standard Class customer_id object 0 793 DP-13000 segment object 0 3 Consumer country_region object 0 2 United States region object 0 4 Central category object 0 3 Office Supplies sub_category object 0 17 Paper product_id object 0 1803 OFF-PA-10000174 product_name object 0 1794 Message Book, Wirebound, Four 5 1/2" X 4" Form... sales float64 0 4640 16.45 quantity int64 0 14 2 discount float64 0 12 0.20 profit float64 0 5471 5.55 returned_order_flag int64 0 2 0 customer_analysis_eligible int64 0 2 1 customer_order_conflict int64 0 2 0 order_to_ship_days int64 0 9 4 order_month datetime64[ns] 0 36 2023-01-01 00:00:00 Step 2: Predict, then reveal — what is the grain? ¶ Is the primary key order_id or row_id ? Predict, then check both. print ( "row_id unique? " , df [ "row_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique?" , df [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print () print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) row_id unique? True order_id unique? False Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 row_id is unique and order_id repeats: one row is one product line within an order , identified by row_id . order_id behaves like a foreign key to an (invisible) orders table. So the answer to "how many orders?" is nunique() on order_id , never len(df) . Step 3: Which attributes belong to the order, and which to the line? ¶ If a column is an attribute of the order , it should take exactly one value within each order. The next cell counts, for each column, the largest number of different values found inside one order. columns_to_test = [ "order_date" , "ship_mode" , "segment" , "region" , "category" , "product_id" , "sales" ] values_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ columns_to_test ] . nunique () . max () values_per_order . rename ( "max distinct values within one order" ) order_date 1 ship_mode 1 segment 1 region 1 category 3 product_id 11 sales 11 Name: max distinct values within one order, dtype: int64 Where the maximum is 1, the column is recorded at order grain (repeated on every line). Where it is above 1, it is recorded at line grain . This matters for counting. Distinct orders add up across groups of an order-grain column, but not across groups of a line-grain column: for column in [ "segment" , "category" ]: orders_per_group = df . groupby ( column )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( f " { column : 9s } : group order counts add up to { orders_per_group . sum () } " f " | overall distinct orders { df [ 'order_id' ] . nunique () } " ) segment : group order counts add up to 3388 | overall distinct orders 3388 category : group order counts add up to 4779 | overall distinct orders 3388 Step 4: Five quality dimensions in one cell ¶ print ( "Completeness | missing values:" , df . isna () . sum () . sum ()) print ( "Validity | quantity always above zero:" , ( df [ "quantity" ] > 0 ) . all (), "| sales never negative:" , ( df [ "sales" ] >= 0 ) . all ()) print ( "Consistency | ship date never before order date:" , ( df [ "ship_date" ] >= df [ "order_date" ]) . all ()) print ( "Uniqueness | row_id unique:" , df [ "row_id" ] . is_unique , "| fully duplicated rows:" , df . duplicated () . sum ()) print ( "Timeliness | order dates from" , df [ "order_date" ] . min () . date (), "to" , df [ "order_date" ] . max () . date (), "| months present:" , df [ "order_month" ] . nunique ()) Completeness | missing values: 0 Validity | quantity always above zero: True | sales never negative: True Consistency | ship date never before order date: True Uniqueness | row_id unique: True | fully duplicated rows: 0 Timeliness | order dates from 2023-01-03 to 2025-12-31 | months present: 36 Read the output line by line. Each line is one entry for a quality checklist, with its evidence. One known consistency issue A few orders in the raw file carry more than one customer ID. The setup cell flags them in customer_order_conflict . They stay in all order and Sales counts; they are excluded only when analysing individual customers. You will explore this in the lab. Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Levels of measurement Nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio; only ratio data supports "twice as much" Tidy data One variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell Grain Say what one row is before you count anything Keys Primary key unique and complete; foreign keys point to another table; validate= guards joins Data dictionary Meaning, type, level, unit, rules, additivity and source for each column Quality dimensions Completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness, timeliness, each with a check and a decision Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Give one example each of a nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio variable from a business you know. Why is "the average satisfaction score rose from 3.9 to 4.1" weaker evidence than "the share of customers scoring 4 or 5 rose from 62% to 70%"? A table lists one row per store with columns sales_2024 and sales_2025 . Is it tidy? What would the tidy version look like? In the Superstore table, why does len(df) not answer "how many orders?" What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key? A delivery fee recorded once per order is joined onto order lines and summed. What goes wrong, and how do you avoid it? Name the quality dimension each check belongs to: (a) no ship date before its order date, (b) row_id has no duplicates, (c) no blank region , (d) last order date is close to today. Why are distinct order counts by category not additive, while those by segment are? Lab briefing ¶ In the Session 2 lab you will turn a vague request into a question, take the Superstore table apart, write its grain statement and data dictionary, run a five-dimension quality checklist, hand-check one order and fix a colleague's counting mistakes. Evidence to keep: your question, grain statement, data dictionary, quality checklist, preparation log and one hand-checked order.

docs.title: What you will be able to explain

docs.text: Not every number is a quantity. A postcode, a shirt size and a temperature are all written with digits or ordered labels, yet you cannot treat them the same way. Statisticians sort variables into four levels of measurement . Each level allows everything the level above it allows, plus something new. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Segment, region, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5, ship class + median, percentiles, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps , but zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Sales, quantity, days to ship, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative).
docs.title: Part 1: Levels of measurement

docs.text: Write down yes or no , then run the cell. It converts both temperatures to Fahrenheit and compares the ratios. celsius = pd . Series ([ 10 , 20 ], index = [ "cool day" , "warm day" ]) fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 print ( "Ratio in Celsius: " , celsius [ "warm day" ] / celsius [ "cool day" ]) print ( "Ratio in Fahrenheit:" , round ( fahrenheit [ "warm day" ] / fahrenheit [ "cool day" ], 2 )) print ( "Difference in Celsius:" , celsius [ "warm day" ] - celsius [ "cool day" ], "degrees" ) Ratio in Celsius: 2.0 Ratio in Fahrenheit: 1.36 Difference in Celsius: 10 degrees The ratio changes when the unit changes, because 0 °C is not "no temperature". So ratios on an interval scale mean nothing. The difference is meaningful in either unit. Sales is different: 0 really means no sales, so "Region A sold twice as much as Region B" stays true whatever the currency. That is a ratio scale.

docs.text: The table below is made up. pandas sees three numeric columns. Which of the three averages printed by the next cell actually mean something? survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" , "C4" , "C5" , "C6" ], "postcode" : [ 44600 , 44700 , 44600 , 33700 , 44600 , 44800 ], "satisfaction_1_to_5" : [ 5 , 4 , 5 , 1 , 4 , 2 ], "orders_last_year" : [ 3 , 1 , 6 , 2 , 0 , 4 ], }) print ( survey . dtypes , end = " \n\n " ) survey [[ "postcode" , "satisfaction_1_to_5" , "orders_last_year" ]] . mean () customer object postcode int64 satisfaction_1_to_5 int64 orders_last_year int64 dtype: object postcode 42,833.33 satisfaction_1_to_5 3.50 orders_last_year 2.67 dtype: float64 Postcode is nominal. The average postcode is not a place. Satisfaction is ordinal. The gap between 1 and 2 need not equal the gap between 4 and 5, so the mean is risky. The median and the share of 4s and 5s are safer. Orders last year is ratio. Its mean is meaningful. The right summaries for the first two: print ( "Most common postcode:" , survey [ "postcode" ] . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "Median satisfaction: " , survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] . median ()) print ( "Share scoring 4 or 5:" , ( survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] >= 4 ) . mean ()) Most common postcode: 44600 Median satisfaction: 4.0 Share scoring 4 or 5: 0.6666666666666666

docs.text: A table is tidy when: Each variable is a column. Each observation is a row. Each value is a single cell. Spreadsheets for people are often not tidy: months spread across columns look good on a page but are awkward to filter, group and chart. wide = pd . docs.text: The grain of a table is what one row represents: one order, one product within an order, one customer per month, one employee per day. Grain decides what simple counting means. If a row is a product within an order, then counting rows counts order lines , not orders. Two kinds of key make grain explicit: Key Meaning Check Primary key Column(s) that identify each row uniquely; never missing No duplicates, no blanks Foreign key Column that points to the primary key of another table Every value exists in that other table Here is a tiny made-up shop with three tables at three different grains. customers = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment" : [ "Consumer" , "Corporate" , "Consumer" ]}) orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O4" ], "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "shipping_fee" : [ 5 , 5 , 10 , 5 ]}) order_lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ], "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O3" , "O3" , "O4" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Desk" , "Chair" , "Pen" , "Lamp" , "Paper" , "Desk" ], "sales" : [ 4 , 200 , 150 , 4 , 30 , 8 , 220 ]}) order_lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product sales 0 1 O1 Pen 4 1 2 O1 Desk 200 2 3 O2 Chair 150 3 4 O3 Pen 4 4 5 O3 Lamp 30 5 6 O3 Paper 8 6 7 O4 Desk 220 Grain of each table: customers : one customer, primary key customer_id . orders : one order, primary key order_id ; customer_id is a foreign key. order_lines : one product within an order, primary key line_id ; order_id is a foreign key. Check the keys with code: print ( "line_id unique in order_lines? " , order_lines [ "line_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in order_lines?" , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in orders? " , orders [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Every line's order exists? " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . isin ( orders [ "order_id" ]) . all ()) print () print ( "Rows in order_lines:" , len ( order_lines )) print ( "Different orders: " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) line_id unique in order_lines? True order_id unique in order_lines? False order_id unique in orders? True Every line's order exists? True Rows in order_lines: 7 Different orders: 4

docs.text: We want total shipping fees. The fee lives in orders (one per order). A colleague joins it onto the order lines and adds it up. Look at the orders table above and work out the true total fee by hand. Will the colleague's number be the same? joined = order_lines . merge ( orders , on = "order_id" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) print ( "True total fee (orders table): " , orders [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) print ( "Colleague's total (after the join):" , joined [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) joined [[ "line_id" , "order_id" , "product" , "shipping_fee" ]] True total fee (orders table): 25 Colleague's total (after the join): 50 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product shipping_fee 0 1 O1 Pen 5 1 2 O1 Desk 5 2 3 O2 Chair 5 3 4 O3 Pen 10 4 5 O3 Lamp 10 5 6 O3 Paper 10 6 7 O4 Desk 5 After the join, each order's fee appears on every line of that order, so summing it counts the fee once per line. The join changed the grain of the fee. Two habits prevent this: Before adding up a column, ask: at what grain is this value recorded? Use validate= in merge to state the relationship you expect ( "one_to_one" , "many_to_one" , "one_to_many" ). pandas raises an error if the keys break it. The correct total, taken back at the order grain: print ( "Fee, one per order:" , joined . drop_duplicates ( "order_id" )[ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) Fee, one per order: 25 Check your understanding 3 A table has one row per employee per month. What is its primary key? If you sum headcount = 1 over the whole year, what have you counted?

docs.text: A data dictionary describes every column so that anyone can use the table correctly without asking you. Field Example for sales Name sales Meaning Sales reported for the order line Type (storage) float64 Level of measurement Ratio Unit Source monetary units; currency not stated Allowed values Zero or more Can you add it up? Yes, across lines and groups Source and changes Orders sheet, column "Sales"; not changed pandas can fill in the mechanical fields for you. The human fields (meaning, unit, "can you add it up?") need your judgement. def profile_columns ( data ): """One row per column: storage type, missing values, distinct values and an example.""" return pd . DataFrame ({ "dtype" : data . dtypes . astype ( str ), "missing" : data . isna () . sum (), "distinct" : data . nunique (), "example" : data . iloc [ 0 ], }) profile_columns ( order_lines ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example line_id int64 0 7 1 order_id object 0 4 O1 product object 0 5 Pen sales int64 0 6 4 Check your understanding 4 profile_columns says line_id is int64 with as many distinct values as rows. "Is the data good?" is too vague to check. Break it into dimensions , each with a test you can run. Dimension Question Example pandas check Completeness Are values missing that should be present? df.isna().sum() Validity Do values follow the rules (type, range, allowed list)? (df["quantity"] > 0).all() Consistency Do related values agree, within and across tables? Ship date not before order date Uniqueness Is each real-world thing recorded once? df["id"].is_unique , df.duplicated() Timeliness Is the data recent enough, and is the period complete? df["date"].max() versus the reporting date Here is a small made-up extract with a problem planted in each dimension. docs.text: If a column is an attribute of the order , it should take exactly one value within each order. The next cell counts, for each column, the largest number of different values found inside one order. columns_to_test = [ "order_date" , "ship_mode" , "segment" , "region" , "category" , "product_id" , "sales" ] values_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ columns_to_test ] . nunique () . max () values_per_order . rename ( "max distinct values within one order" ) order_date 1 ship_mode 1 segment 1 region 1 category 3 product_id 11 sales 11 Name: max distinct values within one order, dtype: int64 Where the maximum is 1, the column is recorded at order grain (repeated on every line). Where it is above 1, it is recorded at line grain . This matters for counting. Distinct orders add up across groups of an order-grain column, but not across groups of a line-grain column: for column in [ "segment" , "category" ]: orders_per_group = df . groupby ( column )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( f " { column : 9s } : group order counts add up to { orders_per_group . sum () } " f " | overall distinct orders { df [ 'order_id' ] . nunique () } " ) segment : group order counts add up to 3388 | overall distinct orders 3388 category : group order counts add up to 4779 | overall distinct orders 3388

docs.text: Session 3 lab: Clean it, check it, log it ¶ Three files from three sources, each with its own problems: repeated football matches, a usage file with most of its dates missing, and a retail workbook whose sheets must be joined without losing or doubling anything. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The head of analytics says: "We have been handed three files for next quarter's reports. Before anyone builds a chart on them: what is wrong with each one, what did you fix, and can I see the proof?" Your job today is not to find insights. It is to make each file fit for use , show the evidence, and say clearly what still cannot be trusted. docs.text: Three files from three sources, each with its own problems: repeated football matches, a usage file with most of its dates missing, and a retail workbook whose sheets must be joined without losing or doubling anything. docs.text: The head of analytics says: "We have been handed three files for next quarter's reports. Before anyone builds a chart on them: what is wrong with each one, what did you fix, and can I see the proof?" Your job today is not to find insights. It is to make each file fit for use , show the evidence, and say clearly what still cannot be trusted. About the data World Cup results : compiled for Sports Viz Sundays 2018 and published in Tableau's sample-data catalog. We download it from that source for learning; we do not redistribute it, and the course does not claim a licence for it. Mobile OS usage : from Statcounter Global Stats (licence CC BY-SA 3.0), via Tableau's sample-data catalog. Each percentage is a share of page views on the websites Statcounter tracks, not a share of devices sold or of people. Superstore : Tableau's sample for a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units; no currency is stated.

DataFrame ({ "match_rows" : matches_raw . groupby ( "Year" ) . size (), "official_matches" : cups . set_index ( "Year" )[ "MatchesPlayed" ], }) check [ "difference" ] = check [ "match_rows" ] - check [ "official_matches" ] check [ check [ "difference" ] != 0 ] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } match_rows official_matches difference Year 2014 80 64 16 Predict before you continue Only one tournament disagrees, and it has more rows than matches played. Each match is one real event, so these are true duplicates . Remove them from a copy, log the step, and run the independent check again. before = len ( matches_raw ) matches = matches_raw . drop_duplicates () . copy () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Removed exact duplicate rows" , "Same match recorded twice; match count exceeded the official total" , before , len ( matches )) check [ "match_rows_clean" ] = matches . groupby ( "Year" ) . size () print ( "Years where clean rows differ from the official count:" , ( check [ "match_rows_clean" ] != check [ "official_matches" ]) . sum ()) Years where clean rows differ from the official count: 0 Remember The fix is confirmed by a number that came from somewhere else (the official match count), not just by "the duplicates are gone". docs.text: Text columns hide problems that are invisible when you look at a few rows. Start with stray spaces. for column in [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ]: text = matches [ column ] . astype ( str ) print ( f " { column : 9 } values with leading or trailing spaces: { ( text != text . str . strip ()) . sum () } " ) City values with leading or trailing spaces: 836 Stadium values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 HomeTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 AwayTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 Every City value ends with a space. That is harmless until you join on city or type "Paris" in a filter. Strip it and log it (a text fix does not change the row count, so before and after are the same). matches [ "City" ] = matches [ "City" ] . str . strip () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Stripped spaces from City" , "Every City value ended in a space" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) print ( "Cities with spaces left:" , ( matches [ "City" ] != matches [ "City" ] . str . strip ()) . sum ()) Cities with spaces left: 0 Next, broken characters . The symbols ï¿½ are what is left of letters such as ô or é after the file passed through the wrong encoding. The original letter is gone. text_columns = [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ] broken = matches [ text_columns ] . apply ( lambda column : column . astype ( str ) . str . contains ( "ï¿½" )) print ( "Rows with a broken character:" , broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . sum ()) pd . Series ( pd . unique ( matches [ text_columns ] . where ( broken ) . stack ())) . head ( 12 ) Rows with a broken character: 73 0 Stade Vï¿½lodrome 1 Maracanï¿½ - Estï¿½dio Jornalista Mï¿½rio Filho 2 Malmï¿½ 3 Norrkï¿½Ping 4 Nou Camp - Estadio Leï¿½n 5 Dï¿½Sseldorf 6 Estadio Josï¿½ Marï¿½a Minella 7 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Chateau Carreras 8 Estadio Municipal de Balaï¿½dos 9 La Coruï¿½A 10 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Universitario 11 Cï¿½te d'Ivoire dtype: object Some of these are easy to read ( Cï¿½te d'Ivoire is Côte d'Ivoire), others are not. We flag the affected rows rather than guessing; correcting them needs a trusted reference list. matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] = broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . astype ( int ) log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Flagged rows with broken characters (not corrected)" , "Encoding damage; original letters cannot be recovered from the file" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] . value_counts () text_broken_flag 0 763 1 73 Name: count, dtype: int64 Finally, names . Look for teams that might be the same country under two names. teams = pd . concat ([ matches [ "HomeTeam" ], matches [ "AwayTeam" ]]) teams [ teams . str . contains ( "Iran|Germany" )] . value_counts () Germany FR 62 Germany 44 Iran 6 IR Iran 6 Name: count, dtype: int64 Not every difference is an error Iran and IR Iran are the same team written two ways: a candidate for a documented mapping.
