docs.text: A colleague wants to show "which sub-categories are in the most orders". Their chart: orders_by_sub = df . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () orders_by_sub . plot ( kind = "pie" , figsize = ( 7 , 7 ), title = "Orders by sub-category" , textprops = { "fontsize" : 8 }) plt . ylabel ( "" ) plt . show () print ( "Slices add up to:" , orders_by_sub . sum (), "| distinct orders:" , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Slices add up to: 6232 | distinct orders: 3388 Read the printed line. The slices add up to more than the number of orders, because one order can contain several sub-categories (you met this overlap in Session 2). A pie says "these parts make one whole", so here it is not just hard to read; it is wrong . Problems: Seventeen slices: angles of similar size cannot be compared. Alphabetical order around the circle: the ranking is hidden. The parts overlap, so a part-of-a-whole chart misstates the data. The redesign: the share of orders that contain each sub-category, as sorted bars, with the largest highlighted. The subtitle warns that shares add up to more than 100%. share = ( orders_by_sub / df [ "order_id" ] . nunique () * 100 ) . sort_values () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( share . index , share , color = highlight ( share . index , share . idxmax ())) for name , value in share . items (): ax . text ( value + 0.3 , name , f " { value : .0f } %" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , share . max () * 1.1 ) ax . grid ( False ) ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . spines [ "bottom" ] . set_visible ( False ) finish ( ax , f " { share . idxmax () } is in more orders than any other sub-category" , "Share of orders containing each sub-category, orders placed 2023–2025. \n " "An order can contain several sub-categories, so the shares add up to more than 100%." ) plt . show () Write your critique In your evidence log, write two or three sentences: what was wrong with the pie, which principle each change applies (task, encoding, highlight, honest framing), and what a reader can now see in seconds.

docs.text: How big is a typical order? First add up Sales per order (an order has several lines), then look at the distribution . order_value = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "sales" ] . sum () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 )) ax1 . hist ( order_value , bins = 40 , color = BLUE ) ax1 . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) finish ( ax1 , "A few very large orders stretch the axis" , "Sales per order, all orders" , xlabel = "Order value" ) bins = np . geomspace ( order_value . min (), order_value . max (), 40 ) ax2 . hist ( order_value , bins = bins , color = BLUE ) ax2 . set_xscale ( "log" ) ax2 . axvline ( order_value . median (), color = HIGHLIGHT , linewidth = 2 ) ax2 . text ( order_value . median () * 1.15 , ax2 . get_ylim ()[ 1 ] * 0.97 , f "median { order_value . median () : ,.0f } " , color = HIGHLIGHT , fontsize = 9 , va = "top" , bbox = { "facecolor" : "white" , "linewidth" : 0 , "pad" : 1 }) ax2 . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( " {x:,.0f} " ) ax2 . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) finish ( ax2 , "On a log scale the typical order is visible" , "Same data, logarithmic x-axis" , xlabel = "Order value (log scale)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( f "Median order value: { order_value . median () : ,.2f } | mean: { order_value . mean () : ,.2f } " ) Median order value: 151.46 | mean: 466.64 The left histogram is squeezed against the axis by a long right tail. On a log scale each step to the right multiplies the value, so the bulk of orders spreads out. The mean is pulled above the median by the large orders: Session 4 goes deeper into this. docs.text: Does discounting hurt profit? A first scatter plot of every order line: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( df [ "discount" ], df [ "profit" ], s = 10 ) finish ( ax , "Discount vs profit" , xlabel = "Discount" , ylabel = "Profit" ) plt . show () Thousands of points sit on top of each other in a few vertical stripes (the discount levels), and a handful of huge values set the scale. Three fixes: Use profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales) so a large and a small line are comparable. Add a little random jitter sideways and make points transparent , so overlapping points become visible as darker areas. Add the total profit ratio at each discount level (a ratio of sums, as in Session 5) and a zero line. line_ratio = df [ "profit" ] / df [ "sales" ] * 100 jitter = rng . normal ( 0 , 0.6 , len ( df )) by_discount = df . groupby ( "discount" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), lines = ( "row_id" , "count" )) by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] = by_discount [ "profit" ] / by_discount [ "sales" ] * 100 losing = by_discount . index [ by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] < 0 ] first_loss = losing . min () all_after_lose = ( by_discount . loc [ by_discount . index >= first_loss , "profit_ratio_pct" ] < 0 ) . all () if all_after_lose : title = f "From a { first_loss : .0% } discount upward, every discount level loses money overall" else : title = f "Some discount levels from { first_loss : .0% } upward lose money overall" fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( df [ "discount" ] * 100 + jitter , line_ratio , s = 8 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.25 , linewidth = 0 ) ax . scatter ( by_discount . index * 100 , by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ], s = 70 , color = HIGHLIGHT , zorder = 3 , label = "Total profit ratio at that discount" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" , fontsize = 9 ) finish ( ax , title , "Grey: each order line (jittered sideways). Orange: Profit ÷ Sales for all lines at that discount." , xlabel = "Discount (%)" , ylabel = "Profit ratio (%)" ) plt . show () by_discount . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales profit lines profit_ratio_pct discount 0.00 748,350.60 220,093.60 3296 29.40 0.10 35,773.80 5,796.90 67 16.20 0.15 18,795.70 881.50 36 4.70 0.20 521,404.90 57,800.10 2464 11.10 0.30 72,640.60 -6,593.20 161 -9.10 0.32 10,776.30 -1,898.90 16 -17.60 0.40 82,397.70 -15,253.20 138 -18.50 0.45 2,975.40 -1,264.70 7 -42.50 0.50 45,117.10 -13,642.00 47 -30.20 0.60 4,954.00 -4,143.40 107 -83.60 0.70 28,646.80 -28,111.60 283 -98.10 0.80 9,134.00 -17,294.60 193 -189.30 Correlation is not causation The chart shows that heavily discounted lines lose money. It does not prove the discount caused the loss: some products may be both hard to sell (so discounted) and low-margin. Session 8 returns to this. docs.text: Session 6 lecture: Visualisation principles ¶ A chart is an argument made with shapes and colours. This lecture shows how the eye reads a chart, which choices make a comparison easy or hard, and how to turn a default plot into one a manager understands in seconds. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Start by answering the Session 5 quiz. Write your answers down before the discussion. What you will be able to explain ¶ How to choose a chart from the task the reader has to do. Why some encodings (position, length) are read more accurately than others (angle, area, colour). Which pre-attentive attributes make one thing stand out, and how to use only one at a time. How to remove non-data ink without removing meaning. How the Gestalt principles decide what the reader compares. When to use categorical , sequential and diverging colour, and how to stay colour-blind safe. When an axis must start at zero, and why dual axes are dangerous. How to write a message title , add annotations and use small multiples . Part Topic 1 Choose the chart from the task 2 How accurately we read encodings 3 Pre-attentive attributes 4 Data-ink and decluttering 5 Gestalt: what belongs together 6 Colour with a job 7 Honest axes 8 Message titles and annotation 9 Small multiples This lecture goes deeper than the Foundations pages Designing clear visuals and How statistics can mislead . Read them first if you have not. How to use this notebook Every idea comes as a before and an after chart, both drawn by code. With the pie, you had to compare angles of slices that do not share a starting line. "Has the share of online sales grown over the last three years?" "Do customers who get bigger discounts buy more items?" "Which of our 12 warehouses had the highest return rate last quarter?" Part 2: How accurately we read encodings ¶ An encoding is how a number becomes something visible: a position, a length, an angle, an area, a colour. Experiments by William Cleveland and Robert McGill (1984), repeated many times since, found that people judge some encodings much more accurately than others. Rank Encoding Example 1 (most accurate) Position on a common scale Dots or bar ends against one axis 2 Length Bars that start at the same baseline 3 Angle and slope Pie slices, line steepness 4 Area Bubbles, treemaps 5 (least accurate) Colour intensity and hue Shaded maps, heatmaps So: put the most important comparison on position or length . Use colour and area for secondary information, or for highlighting. Predict, then reveal ¶ Five made-up values are shown as pie slices and as bubbles. Rank them from largest to smallest using only these two pictures, and write your ranking down. values = pd . Series ({ "A" : 20 , "B" : 23 , "C" : 17 , "D" : 21 , "E" : 19 }) fig , ( ax_pie , ax_bubble ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) ax_pie . pie ( values , labels = values . index , startangle = 90 , counterclock = False , colors = OKABE_ITO [: 5 ]) ax_pie . set_title ( "Angle and area" ) ax_bubble . scatter ( range ( len ( values )), [ 0 ] * len ( values ), s = values * 60 , color = BLUE ) for i , label in enumerate ( values . index ): ax_bubble . text ( i , - 0.35 , label , ha = "center" ) ax_bubble . set_xlim ( - 0.7 , 4.7 ) ax_bubble . set_ylim ( - 0.6 , 0.6 ) ax_bubble . axis ( "off" ) ax_bubble . set_title ( "Area only" ) plt . show () Now the same five values as bars on a common baseline. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.5 )) ax . bar ( values . index , values , color = BLUE ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Position and length: the ranking is easy" ) plt . show () print ( "True ranking:" , ", " . join ( values . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . index )) True ranking: B, D, A, E, C Most people get the bubbles and slices partly wrong when the values are close, and nearly everyone gets the bars right. This is the main reason analysts prefer bars and dots. Check your understanding 2 A colleague shows a map where each region's profit is shown only by its shade of green. Name one question about the regions this map answers badly, and suggest a chart that answers it better. Part 3: Pre-attentive attributes ¶ Some differences are seen in a fraction of a second, before you consciously search: colour , size , position , orientation , shape , enclosure . They are called pre-attentive attributes. Predict, then reveal ¶ The next cell draws two panels. In each, find the odd one out. Which panel is faster, and why? fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 4.2 )) xy = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 1 :, 0 ], xy [ 1 :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = GREY ) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 0 , 0 ], xy [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE ) ax1 . set_title ( "Find the odd one out (colour only)" ) xy2 = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) half = len ( xy2 ) // 2 ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 1 : half , 0 ], xy2 [ 1 : half , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "s" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ half :, 0 ], xy2 [ half :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = BLUE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 0 , 0 ], xy2 [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . set_title ( "Find the orange circle (colour AND shape)" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) plt . show () In the left panel the orange dot "pops out" at once. In the right panel you must scan, because the target differs only by a combination of colour and shape, and combinations are not pre-attentive. Lesson for charts: Use one pre-attentive attribute to mark what matters, usually a single strong colour against grey. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Five bright colours give the eye five places to look. Do not ask the reader to decode combinations ("orange squares are 2024 West"). Part 4: Data-ink and decluttering ¶ Edward Tufte's data-ink ratio asks: how much of the ink shows data? Everything else (heavy grids, borders, colours with no meaning, rotated labels) costs the reader attention. Here is matplotlib's default style with Profit by sub-category. The plt.style.context("default") line switches off the course style for this one chart. profit_sub = df . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () with plt . style . context ( "default" ): fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) profit_sub . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax , color = plt . cm . tab20 . colors , edgecolor = "black" ) ax . grid ( True ) ax . set_title ( "Profit by Sub-Category" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "profit" ) plt . show () Predict, then reveal ¶ List three things on this chart that do not help the reader, and one question it makes hard to answer. Clarity, not minimalism. Check your understanding 3 The "after" chart removed the value axis. Give one situation where you should keep a value axis instead of writing numbers on the bars. Part 5: Gestalt: what belongs together ¶ Gestalt principles describe how we group what we see. You can use them to decide what the reader compares. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 4 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.2 )) gx , gy = np . meshgrid ( np . arange ( 6 ), np . arange ( 4 )) gx , gy = gx . ravel (), gy . ravel () # Proximity: same dots, but columns pushed into pairs axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( gx + ( gx // 2 ) * 0.9 , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Proximity" ) # Similarity: equal spacing, rows coloured alternately axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = [ ORANGE if row % 2 else BLUE for row in gy ]) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Similarity" ) # Enclosure: equal spacing and colour, one box axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) axes [ 2 ] . add_patch ( Rectangle (( 1.6 , - 0.5 ), 1.8 , 4 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.5 , zorder = 0 )) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Enclosure" ) # Connection: equal spacing, some dots joined axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) for x0 in ( 0 , 2 , 4 ): for y0 in ( 0 , 2 ): axes [ 3 ] . plot ([ x0 , x0 + 1 ], [ y0 , y0 + 1 ], color = INK , linewidth = 1.5 , zorder = 0 ) axes [ 3 ] . set_title ( "Connection" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) ax . set_aspect ( "equal" ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Principle What you saw Use in charts Proximity Pairs of columns Bars placed close together are compared first Similarity Rows, even though spacing is equal Same colour = same category across panels Enclosure The boxed columns form a group Shade a period (a promotion, a recession) Connection Joined dots read as pairs Lines join points that belong to one series Proximity decides the comparison ¶ The same Sales numbers, grouped two ways. Which question does each chart answer easily? pivot = df . groupby ([ "region" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 ), sharey = True ) pivot . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax1 , rot = 0 , color = [ BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN ], width = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Grouped by region: compare segments within a region" , fontsize = 10 ) pivot . T . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax2 , rot = 0 , color = OKABE_ITO [: 4 ], width = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Grouped by segment: compare regions within a segment" , fontsize = 10 ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 8 ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax1 ) plt . show () Bars that sit next to each other get compared. Put next to each other the things your question compares. Part 6: Colour with a job ¶ Colour should do one of three jobs. Match the palette to the job. Data Palette type Example Rule Categories with no order Categorical: distinct hues Segments, regions At most about six; same category, same colour everywhere Ordered amounts from low to high Sequential: one hue, light to dark Sales by region and year Darker = more Values around a meaningful middle Diverging: two hues, neutral centre Profit ratio around 0% The neutral colour must sit exactly at the middle value Sequential: amounts ¶ The helper below draws a table as a heatmap and writes each value in its cell, in white on dark cells and black on light cells. def heatmap ( ax , table , cmap , norm = None , fmt = " {:,.0f} " ): image = ax . imshow ( table . values , cmap = cmap , norm = norm , aspect = "auto" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( table . shape [ 1 ]), table . columns ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( table . shape [ 0 ]), table . index ) ax . grid ( False ) for ( i , j ), value in np . ndenumerate ( table . values ): r , g , b , _ = image . cmap ( image . norm ( value )) text_colour = "white" if 0.299 * r + 0.587 * g + 0.114 * b < 0.5 else "black" ax . text ( j , i , fmt . format ( value ), ha = "center" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = text_colour ) return image sales_year = df . assign ( year = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year ) . pivot_table ( index = "region" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" , aggfunc = "sum" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.2 )) heatmap ( ax , sales_year , cmap = "Blues" ) ax . set_title ( "Sales by region and order year (darker = more)" ) plt . show () Predict, then reveal: diverging ¶ Profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales) for each sub-category and region. Zero is special: above it the business makes money, below it loses money. First, a sequential palette. Can you tell at a glance which cells are losses ? totals = df . groupby ([ "sub_category" , "region" ])[[ "profit" , "sales" ]] . sum () profit_ratio = ( totals [ "profit" ] / totals [ "sales" ] * 100 ) . unstack () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) heatmap ( ax , profit_ratio , cmap = "viridis" , fmt = " {:.0f} " ) ax . set_title ( "Profit ratio (%), sequential palette" ) plt . show () limit = profit_ratio . abs () . max () . max () centred = TwoSlopeNorm ( vcenter = 0 , vmin =- limit , vmax = limit ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) heatmap ( ax , profit_ratio , cmap = "RdBu" , norm = centred , fmt = " {:.0f} " ) ax . set_title ( "Profit ratio (%), diverging palette centred on 0: red = loss" ) plt . show () With the diverging palette, every loss is red and every profit blue, and the palest cells are close to break-even. The sequential palette hid the most important boundary in the data. Colour-blind safety About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some colour-vision deficiency, most often red–green. Safe habits: Avoid red-versus-green as the only difference. Red–blue (as above) or orange–blue are safer. Use a tested palette such as Okabe–Ito ( OKABE_ITO above) for categories. Do not rely on colour alone: add labels, positions or patterns. Highlight one series, grey the rest ¶ Seventeen sub-categories over time with default colours: the default cycle has only ten colours, so some lines share a colour. quarter = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "Q" ) . dt . to_timestamp () by_quarter = df . groupby ([ quarter , "sub_category" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () . fillna ( 0 ) # no lines = no Sales with plt . style . context ( "default" ): ax = by_quarter . plot ( figsize = ( 10 , 5 ), title = "Quarterly sales by sub-category" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 7 , ncol = 2 , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Now decide what the chart is about . Here: the sub-category whose yearly Sales grew most, in source monetary units, between the first and last year. The code finds it; the chart puts it in colour and everything else in grey context. import datetime yearly = df . groupby ([ df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year , "sub_category" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () growth = ( yearly . iloc [ - 1 ] - yearly . iloc [ 0 ]) . sort_values () focus = growth . index [ - 1 ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 10 , 4.5 )) for name in by_quarter . columns : if name != focus : ax . plot ( by_quarter . index , by_quarter [ name ], color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . plot ( by_quarter . index , by_quarter [ focus ], color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2.8 ) ax . text ( by_quarter . index [ - 1 ], by_quarter [ focus ] . iloc [ - 1 ], f " { focus } " , color = ORANGE , va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" ) ax . set_xlim ( right = by_quarter . index [ - 1 ] . to_pydatetime () + datetime . timedelta ( days = 200 )) ax . set_title ( f " { focus } added more Sales than any other sub-category, { yearly . index [ 0 ] } to { yearly . index [ - 1 ] } " , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Quarterly Sales; grey lines are the other sub-categories" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax ) plt . show () print ( f " { focus } yearly Sales, { yearly . index [ 0 ] } : { yearly [ focus ] . iloc [ 0 ] : ,.0f } | { yearly . index [ - 1 ] } : { yearly [ focus ] . iloc [ - 1 ] : ,.0f } " ) Copiers yearly Sales, 2023: 12,050 | 2025: 49,599 Check your understanding 4 Which palette type (categorical, sequential or diverging) fits each case, and why? Customer satisfaction score from 1 to 10 for each store. Change in headcount versus last year, by department (some up, some down). Five product lines on one line chart. Part 7: Honest axes ¶ Bars must start at zero ¶ A bar's length is the encoding. If the axis does not start at zero, the lengths lie. Average order value (AOV = Sales ÷ distinct orders) by region: region_totals = df . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), orders = ( "order_id" , "nunique" )) aov = ( region_totals [ "sales" ] / region_totals [ "orders" ]) . sort_values () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . bar ( aov . index , aov , color = BLUE ) ax1 . set_ylim ( aov . min () * 0.97 , aov . max () * 1.01 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Truncated axis" ) ax2 . bar ( aov . index , aov , color = BLUE ) for i , value in enumerate ( aov ): ax2 . text ( i , value , f " { value : ,.0f } " , ha = "center" , va = "bottom" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax2 . set_title ( "Axis from zero" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Average order value" ) plt . show () print ( "Largest AOV divided by smallest:" , round ( aov . max () / aov . min (), 2 )) Largest AOV divided by smallest: 1.11 On the left, the tallest bar looks several times taller than the shortest. The printed ratio shows the true difference. Lines are different. A line's message is its shape (rising, falling, seasonal), read from position, not length. A line chart may zoom in to the range of the data, as long as the axis is labelled. The rule is: bars from zero; lines may zoom, with labels . Dual axes: two scales, any story you like ¶ A dual-axis chart puts two measures on one picture, each with its own scale. The person drawing it chooses both scales, and with them the "story". Two made-up monthly series: months = pd . date_range ( "2024-01-01" , periods = 24 , freq = "MS" ) visits = pd . Series ( 50_000 + np . arange ( 24 ) * 800 + rng . normal ( 0 , 1_500 , 24 ), index = months ) revenue = pd . Series ( 200_000 + np . arange ( 24 ) * 1_200 + rng . normal ( 0 , 6_000 , 24 ), index = months ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.8 )) right_limits = [( 190_000 , 240_000 ), ( 0 , 600_000 )] titles = [ "Version A: revenue races ahead of visits?" , "Version B: revenue flat while visits grow?" ] for ax , ( low , high ), title in zip ( axes , right_limits , titles ): ax . plot ( visits , color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_ylim ( 40_000 , 75_000 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Website visits" , color = BLUE ) right = ax . twinx () right . plot ( revenue , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) right . set_ylim ( low , high ) right . set_ylabel ( "Revenue" , color = ORANGE ) right . grid ( False ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "x" , labelrotation = 45 ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Same data, opposite impressions, and the crossing point of the two lines means nothing at all. A fairer comparison of growth puts both on one scale by indexing : divide each series by its first value and multiply by 100. import datetime indexed = pd . DataFrame ({ "Website visits" : visits / visits . iloc [ 0 ] * 100 , "Revenue" : revenue / revenue . iloc [ 0 ] * 100 , }) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) ax . plot ( indexed . index , indexed [ "Website visits" ], color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . plot ( indexed . index , indexed [ "Revenue" ], color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . axhline ( 100 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) for name , colour in [( "Website visits" , BLUE ), ( "Revenue" , ORANGE )]: ax . text ( indexed . index [ - 1 ], indexed [ name ] . iloc [ - 1 ], f " { name } " , color = colour , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlim ( right = indexed . index [ - 1 ] . to_pydatetime () + datetime . timedelta ( days = 150 )) growth_v = indexed [ "Website visits" ] . iloc [ - 1 ] - 100 growth_r = indexed [ "Revenue" ] . iloc [ - 1 ] - 100 ax . set_title ( f "Visits grew { growth_v : .0f } % and revenue { growth_r : .0f } % over two years" , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Index, January 2024 = 100 (made-up data)" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) plt . show () Check your understanding 5 For each, is a non-zero axis acceptable? Explain in one sentence. A bar chart of profit ratio by segment. A line chart of daily share price over one month. A dot plot of average delivery days by carrier, with the axis labelled. Part 8: Message titles and annotation ¶ A descriptive title ("Monthly sales") tells the reader what is on the chart. A message title tells them what to see ("Sales peak in the last months of every year"). Managers read titles first and sometimes only titles. Two rules: The message must be true for the chart as drawn : same period, same filters. If the data change, re-check the title. Keep the scope (period, population, units) in a subtitle or note, so the message stays short. Before: monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 3.8 )) ax . plot ( monthly . index , monthly ) ax . set_title ( "Monthly sales" ) plt . show () After: the line in grey, each year's highest month marked in orange and labelled, and a message title. The code checks the claim before it writes it: the title only says "every year" if each year's peak really falls in the last four months. peaks = monthly . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . idxmax () if all ( month . month >= 9 for month in peaks ): message = "Sales peak in the last four months of every year" else : message = "The busiest month changes from year to year" fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) ax . plot ( monthly . index , monthly , color = GREY , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( peaks , monthly [ peaks ], color = ORANGE , s = 50 , zorder = 3 ) for month in peaks : ax . annotate ( month . strftime ( "%b %Y" ), ( month , monthly [ month ]), xytext = ( 0 , 8 ), textcoords = "offset points" , ha = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , monthly . max () * 1.15 ) ax . set_title ( message , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Monthly Sales, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units); orange = each year's highest month" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax ) plt . show () Annotation is text on the chart that explains one thing at the place it happens: a peak, a policy change, a missing month. Use it sparingly: one to three notes per chart. Check your understanding 6 Rewrite each descriptive title as a message title. Invent a plausible finding; the point is the form. "Returns by region, 2025" "Average delivery days by carrier" Part 9: Small multiples ¶ When one chart has too many series, draw many small charts with the same axes , one per group. Tufte called these small multiples . The shared axes make every panel comparable; the repetition means the reader learns to read the first panel and then reads the rest instantly. Here each panel shows one region's quarterly Sales in blue, with the other regions in grey for context. Panels are ordered by total Sales, largest first. by_region = df . groupby ([ quarter , "region" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () by_region = by_region [ by_region . sum () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . index ] # biggest region first fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 6 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax , region in zip ( axes . flat , by_region . columns ): for other in by_region . columns : if other != region : ax . plot ( by_region . index , by_region [ other ], color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . plot ( by_region . index , by_region [ region ], color = BLUE , linewidth = 2.2 ) ax . set_title ( region , fontsize = 10 ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "x" , labelsize = 8 , labelrotation = 45 ) commas ( ax ) fig . suptitle ( "Quarterly Sales by region, largest region first: each panel highlights one region" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . supylabel ( "Sales" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Small multiples checklist Same axes in every panel ( sharex=True, sharey=True ), unless you say clearly that they differ. Panels in a meaningful order (by size, by geography, by time), not alphabetical by default. One highlight colour, the same in every panel. Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Task first Compare → bars; distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter; time → line Encodings Position and length are read best; angle, area and colour worse Pre-attentive One strong colour against grey; never several highlights Data-ink Remove what does not carry data; keep units, scope and meaningful reference lines Gestalt Put next to each other what the reader must compare Colour Categorical, sequential or diverging by the data; colour-blind safe; not colour alone Honest axes Bars from zero; lines may zoom with labels; avoid dual axes, index instead Titles Message title, scope in a subtitle, one to three annotations Small multiples Same axes, many panels, one highlight Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Name the five chart tasks from Part 1 and a good first chart for each. Why is a pie chart with ten slices hard to read? Use the word "encoding" in your answer. What is a pre-attentive attribute? Give two examples and one way to misuse them. Name three kinds of non-data ink you would remove from a default chart, and one element you must keep. Which Gestalt principle explains why grouping bars by region makes segment comparisons easy? You show profit change by department, where some departments improved and some got worse. Which palette type do you use, and where must its neutral colour sit? Why must a bar chart start at zero when a line chart need not? A colleague's dual-axis chart shows revenue and visits "crossing" in March. What do you tell them, and what would you draw instead? In the Lab ¶ In the Session 6 lab you will: Build a small style helper you can reuse for every chart in the course. Redesign three bad charts on the Superstore data: a crowded pie, a truncated bar axis and a rainbow line "spaghetti". Draw one-, two- and many-variable views: a histogram, a discount-versus-profit scatter and small multiples by region. Challenge: build one decision chart with a message title and annotation, and critique a colleague's dual-axis chart. Evidence to bring back: before/after chart pairs, each with a short written critique.

docs.text: A chart is an argument made with shapes and colours. This lecture shows how the eye reads a chart, which choices make a comparison easy or hard, and how to turn a default plot into one a manager understands in seconds. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive .

docs.text: How to choose a chart from the task the reader has to do. Why some encodings (position, length) are read more accurately than others (angle, area, colour). Which pre-attentive attributes make one thing stand out, and how to use only one at a time. How to remove non-data ink without removing meaning. How the Gestalt principles decide what the reader compares. When to use categorical , sequential and diverging colour, and how to stay colour-blind safe. When an axis must start at zero, and why dual axes are dangerous. How to write a message title , add annotations and use small multiples . Part Topic 1 Choose the chart from the task 2 How accurately we read encodings 3 Pre-attentive attributes 4 Data-ink and decluttering 5 Gestalt: what belongs together 6 Colour with a job 7 Honest axes 8 Message titles and annotation 9 Small multiples This lecture goes deeper than the Foundations pages Designing clear visuals and How statistics can mislead . Read them first if you have not. How to use this notebook Every idea comes as a before and an after chart, both drawn by code. When you see Predict, then reveal , write your answer first and only then run the next cell. Run the setup cell first. It prepares pandas, the course chart style and the retail table. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. The next cell loads the table and defines a few colours used throughout. GREY is for context, one strong colour is for the thing that matters. OKABE_ITO is a palette designed to stay distinguishable for people with the common forms of colour blindness. The small commas helper writes axis numbers with thousands separators. import numpy as np from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle df = load_orders () BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" OKABE_ITO = [ "#E69F00" , "#56B4E9" , "#009E73" , "#F0E442" , "#0072B2" , "#D55E00" , "#CC79A7" , "#000000" ] rng = np . random . default_rng ( 6 ) # fixed seed: the made-up examples look the same every run def commas ( ax , axis = "y" ): # Write large axis numbers with thousands separators: 250,000 instead of 250000. target = ax . yaxis if axis == "y" else ax . xaxis target . set_major_formatter ( " {x:,.0f} " ) print ( "Order lines loaded:" , len ( df )) Order lines loaded: 6815

Stacked bar, or a bar of shares; a pie only for two or three parts Pie with many slices Distribution What values are typical, how spread, any outliers? Histogram, box plot, strip plot Bar of the average alone Relationship Do two measures move together? Scatter plot Two lines on dual axes Change over time Rising, falling, seasonal? Line chart (time on the x-axis) Unsorted bars, pie per year

Roughly how many times bigger is the largest slice than the third largest? by_sub = df . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) ax . pie ( by_sub , labels = by_sub . index , startangle = 90 , counterclock = False , textprops = { "fontsize" : 8 }) ax . set_title ( "Sales by sub-category" ) plt . show () Now the same numbers as a sorted bar chart. Check your two answers. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( by_sub . index [:: - 1 ], by_sub . values [:: - 1 ], color = BLUE ) ax . grid ( axis = "y" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Sales by sub-category, orders placed 2023–2025" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) plt . show () top = by_sub . iloc [ 0 ] print ( "Fifth largest:" , by_sub . index [ 4 ]) print ( "Largest divided by third largest:" , round ( top / by_sub . iloc [ 2 ], 2 )) Fifth largest: Machines Largest divided by third largest: 1.54 With the bars, the ranking is the order on the page and the size ratio is a comparison of lengths from a common baseline. docs.title: Predict, then reveal

docs.text: An encoding is how a number becomes something visible: a position, a length, an angle, an area, a colour. Experiments by William Cleveland and Robert McGill (1984), repeated many times since, found that people judge some encodings much more accurately than others. Rank Encoding Example 1 (most accurate) Position on a common scale Dots or bar ends against one axis 2 Length Bars that start at the same baseline 3 Angle and slope Pie slices, line steepness 4 Area Bubbles, treemaps 5 (least accurate) Colour intensity and hue Shaded maps, heatmaps So: put the most important comparison on position or length . Use colour and area for secondary information, or for highlighting.
docs.title: Part 2: How accurately we read encodings

docs.text: Five made-up values are shown as pie slices and as bubbles. Rank them from largest to smallest using only these two pictures, and write your ranking down. values = pd . Series ({ "A" : 20 , "B" : 23 , "C" : 17 , "D" : 21 , "E" : 19 }) fig , ( ax_pie , ax_bubble ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) ax_pie . pie ( values , labels = values . index , startangle = 90 , counterclock = False , colors = OKABE_ITO [: 5 ]) ax_pie . set_title ( "Angle and area" ) ax_bubble . scatter ( range ( len ( values )), [ 0 ] * len ( values ), s = values * 60 , color = BLUE ) for i , label in enumerate ( values . index ): ax_bubble . text ( i , - 0.35 , label , ha = "center" ) ax_bubble . set_xlim ( - 0.7 , 4.7 ) ax_bubble . set_ylim ( - 0.6 , 0.6 ) ax_bubble . axis ( "off" ) ax_bubble . set_title ( "Area only" ) plt . show () Now the same five values as bars on a common baseline. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.5 )) ax . bar ( values . index , values , color = BLUE ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Position and length: the ranking is easy" ) plt . show () print ( "True ranking:" , ", " . join ( values . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . index )) True ranking: B, D, A, E, C Most people get the bubbles and slices partly wrong when the values are close, and nearly everyone gets the bars right. This is the main reason analysts prefer bars and dots. Check your understanding 2 A colleague shows a map where each region's profit is shown only by its shade of green. Name one question about the regions this map answers badly, and suggest a chart that answers it better.
docs.title: Predict, then reveal

docs.text: Some differences are seen in a fraction of a second, before you consciously search: colour , size , position , orientation , shape , enclosure . They are called pre-attentive attributes.
docs.title: Part 3: Pre-attentive attributes

docs.text: The next cell draws two panels. In each, find the odd one out. Which panel is faster, and why? fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 4.2 )) xy = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 1 :, 0 ], xy [ 1 :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = GREY ) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 0 , 0 ], xy [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE ) ax1 . set_title ( "Find the odd one out (colour only)" ) xy2 = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) half = len ( xy2 ) // 2 ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 1 : half , 0 ], xy2 [ 1 : half , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "s" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ half :, 0 ], xy2 [ half :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = BLUE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 0 , 0 ], xy2 [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . set_title ( "Find the orange circle (colour AND shape)" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) plt . show () In the left panel the orange dot "pops out" at once. In the right panel you must scan, because the target differs only by a combination of colour and shape, and combinations are not pre-attentive. Lesson for charts: Use one pre-attentive attribute to mark what matters, usually a single strong colour against grey. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Five bright colours give the eye five places to look. Do not ask the reader to decode combinations ("orange squares are 2024 West").

docs.text: Edward Tufte's data-ink ratio asks: how much of the ink shows data? Everything else (heavy grids, borders, colours with no meaning, rotated labels) costs the reader attention. Here is matplotlib's default style with Profit by sub-category. The plt.style.context("default") line switches off the course style for this one chart. profit_sub = df . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () with plt . style . context ( "default" ): fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) profit_sub . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax , color = plt . cm . tab20 . colors , edgecolor = "black" ) ax . grid ( True ) ax . set_title ( "Profit by Sub-Category" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "profit" ) plt . show ()
docs.title: Part 4: Data-ink and decluttering

docs.text: List three things on this chart that do not help the reader, and one question it makes hard to answer. Then run the next cell. profit_sorted = profit_sub . sort_values () colours = [ ORANGE if value < 0 else GREY for value in profit_sorted ] offset = 0.015 * profit_sorted . abs () . max () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( profit_sorted . index , profit_sorted , color = colours ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) for name , value in profit_sorted . items (): ax . text ( value + offset if value >= 0 else value - offset , name , f " { value : ,.0f } " , va = "center" , ha = "left" if value >= 0 else "right" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( profit_sorted . min () * 1.6 , profit_sorted . max () * 1.18 ) ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) for side in ( "left" , "bottom" ): ax . spines [ side ] . set_visible ( False ) losers = ( profit_sorted < 0 ) . sum () ax . set_title ( f " { losers } sub-categories lost money over 2023–2025" , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Total Profit by sub-category, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units)" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) plt . show () What changed, and why: Change Principle Sorted by value The ranking is now the reading order Horizontal bars Long labels are readable without tilting your head One colour with meaning (orange = loss), grey for the rest One pre-attentive attribute, one message Values written on the bars, value axis removed Exact numbers without a grid to trace A zero line kept It separates profit from loss, so it carries data Title states the finding; subtitle states scope and units The reader knows what to look for and what was counted Do not overdo it Decluttering stops when removing something would lose meaning: units, the period, the scope or a zero line. Clarity, not minimalism. Check your understanding 3 The "after" chart removed the value axis. Give one situation where you should keep a value axis instead of writing numbers on the bars.

docs.text: Gestalt principles describe how we group what we see. You can use them to decide what the reader compares. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 4 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.2 )) gx , gy = np . meshgrid ( np . arange ( 6 ), np . arange ( 4 )) gx , gy = gx . ravel (), gy . ravel () # Proximity: same dots, but columns pushed into pairs axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( gx + ( gx // 2 ) * 0.9 , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Proximity" ) # Similarity: equal spacing, rows coloured alternately axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = [ ORANGE if row % 2 else BLUE for row in gy ]) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Similarity" ) # Enclosure: equal spacing and colour, one box axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) axes [ 2 ] . add_patch ( Rectangle (( 1.6 , - 0.5 ), 1.8 , 4 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.5 , zorder = 0 )) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Enclosure" ) # Connection: equal spacing, some dots joined axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) for x0 in ( 0 , 2 , 4 ): for y0 in ( 0 , 2 ): axes [ 3 ] . plot ([ x0 , x0 + 1 ], [ y0 , y0 + 1 ], color = INK , linewidth = 1.5 , zorder = 0 ) axes [ 3 ] . set_title ( "Connection" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) ax . set_aspect ( "equal" ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Principle What you saw Use in charts Proximity Pairs of columns Bars placed close together are compared first Similarity Rows, even though spacing is equal Same colour = same category across panels Enclosure The boxed columns form a group Shade a period (a promotion, a recession) Connection Joined dots read as pairs Lines join points that belong to one series
docs.title: Part 5: Gestalt: what belongs together

docs.text: The same Sales numbers, grouped two ways. Which question does each chart answer easily? pivot = df . groupby ([ "region" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 ), sharey = True ) pivot . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax1 , rot = 0 , color = [ BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN ], width = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Grouped by region: compare segments within a region" , fontsize = 10 ) pivot . T . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax2 , rot = 0 , color = OKABE_ITO [: 4 ], width = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Grouped by segment: compare regions within a segment" , fontsize = 10 ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 8 ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax1 ) plt . show () Bars that sit next to each other get compared. Put next to each other the things your question compares.
docs.title: Proximity decides the comparison

docs.text: Colour should do one of three jobs. Match the palette to the job. Data Palette type Example Rule Categories with no order Categorical: distinct hues Segments, regions At most about six; same category, same colour everywhere Ordered amounts from low to high Sequential: one hue, light to dark Sales by region and year Darker = more Values around a meaningful middle Diverging: two hues, neutral centre Profit ratio around 0% The neutral colour must sit exactly at the middle value
docs.title: Part 6: Colour with a job

docs.text: The helper below draws a table as a heatmap and writes each value in its cell, in white on dark cells and black on light cells. def heatmap ( ax , table , cmap , norm = None , fmt = " {:,.0f} " ): image = ax . imshow ( table . values , cmap = cmap , norm = norm , aspect = "auto" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( table . shape [ 1 ]), table . columns ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( table . shape [ 0 ]), table . index ) ax . grid ( False ) for ( i , j ), value in np . ndenumerate ( table . values ): r , g , b , _ = image . cmap ( image . norm ( value )) text_colour = "white" if 0.299 * r + 0.587 * g + 0.114 * b < 0.5 else "black" ax . text ( j , i , fmt . format ( value ), ha = "center" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = text_colour ) return image sales_year = df . assign ( year = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year ) . pivot_table ( index = "region" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" , aggfunc = "sum" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.2 )) heatmap ( ax , sales_year , cmap = "Blues" ) ax . set_title ( "Sales by region and order year (darker = more)" ) plt . show ()
docs.title: Sequential: amounts

docs.text: Profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales) for each sub-category and region. Zero is special: above it the business makes money, below it loses money. First, a sequential palette. Can you tell at a glance which cells are losses ? totals = df . groupby ([ "sub_category" , "region" ])[[ "profit" , "sales" ]] . sum () profit_ratio = ( totals [ "profit" ] / totals [ "sales" ] * 100 ) . unstack () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) heatmap ( ax , profit_ratio , cmap = "viridis" , fmt = " {:.0f} " ) ax . set_title ( "Profit ratio (%), sequential palette" ) plt . show () limit = profit_ratio . abs () . max () . max () centred = TwoSlopeNorm ( vcenter = 0 , vmin =- limit , vmax = limit ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) heatmap ( ax , profit_ratio , cmap = "RdBu" , norm = centred , fmt = " {:.0f} " ) ax . set_title ( "Profit ratio (%), diverging palette centred on 0: red = loss" ) plt . show () With the diverging palette, every loss is red and every profit blue, and the palest cells are close to break-even. The sequential palette hid the most important boundary in the data. Colour-blind safety About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some colour-vision deficiency, most often red–green. Safe habits: Avoid red-versus-green as the only difference. Red–blue (as above) or orange–blue are safer. Use a tested palette such as Okabe–Ito ( OKABE_ITO above) for categories. Do not rely on colour alone: add labels, positions or patterns.
docs.title: Predict, then reveal: diverging

docs.text: Seventeen sub-categories over time with default colours: the default cycle has only ten colours, so some lines share a colour. quarter = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "Q" ) . dt . to_timestamp () by_quarter = df . groupby ([ quarter , "sub_category" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () . fillna ( 0 ) # no lines = no Sales with plt . style . context ( "default" ): ax = by_quarter . plot ( figsize = ( 10 , 5 ), title = "Quarterly sales by sub-category" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 7 , ncol = 2 , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Now decide what the chart is about . Here: the sub-category whose yearly Sales grew most, in source monetary units, between the first and last year. The code finds it; the chart puts it in colour and everything else in grey context. import datetime yearly = df . groupby ([ df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year , "sub_category" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () growth = ( yearly . iloc [ - 1 ] - yearly . iloc [ 0 ]) . sort_values () focus = growth . index [ - 1 ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 10 , 4.5 )) for name in by_quarter . columns : if name != focus : ax . plot ( by_quarter . index , by_quarter [ name ], color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . plot ( by_quarter . index , by_quarter [ focus ], color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2.8 ) ax . text ( by_quarter . index [ - 1 ], by_quarter [ focus ] . iloc [ - 1 ], f " { focus } " , color = ORANGE , va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" ) ax . set_xlim ( right = by_quarter . index [ - 1 ] . to_pydatetime () + datetime . timedelta ( days = 200 )) ax . set_title ( f " { focus } added more Sales than any other sub-category, { yearly . index [ 0 ] } to { yearly . index [ - 1 ] } " , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Quarterly Sales; grey lines are the other sub-categories" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax ) plt . show () print ( f " { focus } yearly Sales, { yearly . index [ 0 ] } : { yearly [ focus ] . iloc [ 0 ] : ,.0f } | { yearly . index [ - 1 ] } : { yearly [ focus ] . iloc [ - 1 ] : ,.0f } " ) Copiers yearly Sales, 2023: 12,050 | 2025: 49,599 Check your understanding 4 Which palette type (categorical, sequential or diverging) fits each case, and why? Customer satisfaction score from 1 to 10 for each store. Change in headcount versus last year, by department (some up, some down). Five product lines on one line chart.
docs.title: Highlight one series, grey the rest

docs.text: A bar's length is the encoding. If the axis does not start at zero, the lengths lie. Average order value (AOV = Sales ÷ distinct orders) by region: region_totals = df . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), orders = ( "order_id" , "nunique" )) aov = ( region_totals [ "sales" ] / region_totals [ "orders" ]) . sort_values () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . bar ( aov . index , aov , color = BLUE ) ax1 . set_ylim ( aov . min () * 0.97 , aov . max () * 1.01 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Truncated axis" ) ax2 . bar ( aov . index , aov , color = BLUE ) for i , value in enumerate ( aov ): ax2 . text ( i , value , f " { value : ,.0f } " , ha = "center" , va = "bottom" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax2 . set_title ( "Axis from zero" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Average order value" ) plt . show () print ( "Largest AOV divided by smallest:" , round ( aov . max () / aov . min (), 2 )) Largest AOV divided by smallest: 1.11 On the left, the tallest bar looks several times taller than the shortest. The printed ratio shows the true difference. Lines are different. A line's message is its shape (rising, falling, seasonal), read from position, not length. A line chart may zoom in to the range of the data, as long as the axis is labelled. The rule is: bars from zero; lines may zoom, with labels .
docs.title: Bars must start at zero

docs.text: A dual-axis chart puts two measures on one picture, each with its own scale. The person drawing it chooses both scales, and with them the "story". Two made-up monthly series: months = pd . date_range ( "2024-01-01" , periods = 24 , freq = "MS" ) visits = pd . Series ( 50_000 + np . arange ( 24 ) * 800 + rng . normal ( 0 , 1_500 , 24 ), index = months ) revenue = pd . Series ( 200_000 + np . arange ( 24 ) * 1_200 + rng . normal ( 0 , 6_000 , 24 ), index = months ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.8 )) right_limits = [( 190_000 , 240_000 ), ( 0 , 600_000 )] titles = [ "Version A: revenue races ahead of visits?" , "Version B: revenue flat while visits grow?" ] for ax , ( low , high ), title in zip ( axes , right_limits , titles ): ax . plot ( visits , color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_ylim ( 40_000 , 75_000 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Website visits" , color = BLUE ) right = ax . twinx () right . plot ( revenue , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) right . set_ylim ( low , high ) right . set_ylabel ( "Revenue" , color = ORANGE ) right . grid ( False ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "x" , labelrotation = 45 ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Same data, opposite impressions, and the crossing point of the two lines means nothing at all. A fairer comparison of growth puts both on one scale by indexing : divide each series by its first value and multiply by 100. import datetime indexed = pd . DataFrame ({ "Website visits" : visits / visits . iloc [ 0 ] * 100 , "Revenue" : revenue / revenue . iloc [ 0 ] * 100 , }) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) ax . plot ( indexed . index , indexed [ "Website visits" ], color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . plot ( indexed . index , indexed [ "Revenue" ], color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . axhline ( 100 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) for name , colour in [( "Website visits" , BLUE ), ( "Revenue" , ORANGE )]: ax . text ( indexed . index [ - 1 ], indexed [ name ] . iloc [ - 1 ], f " { name } " , color = colour , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlim ( right = indexed . index [ - 1 ] . to_pydatetime () + datetime . timedelta ( days = 150 )) growth_v = indexed [ "Website visits" ] . iloc [ - 1 ] - 100 growth_r = indexed [ "Revenue" ] . iloc [ - 1 ] - 100 ax . set_title ( f "Visits grew { growth_v : .0f } % and revenue { growth_r : .0f } % over two years" , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Index, January 2024 = 100 (made-up data)" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) plt . show () Check your understanding 5 For each, is a non-zero axis acceptable? Explain in one sentence. A bar chart of profit ratio by segment. A line chart of daily share price over one month. A dot plot of average delivery days by carrier, with the axis labelled.
docs.title: Dual axes: two scales, any story you like

docs.text: A descriptive title ("Monthly sales") tells the reader what is on the chart. A message title tells them what to see ("Sales peak in the last months of every year"). Managers read titles first and sometimes only titles. Two rules: The message must be true for the chart as drawn : same period, same filters. If the data change, re-check the title. Keep the scope (period, population, units) in a subtitle or note, so the message stays short. Before: monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 3.8 )) ax . plot ( monthly . index , monthly ) ax . set_title ( "Monthly sales" ) plt . show () After: the line in grey, each year's highest month marked in orange and labelled, and a message title. The code checks the claim before it writes it: the title only says "every year" if each year's peak really falls in the last four months. peaks = monthly . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . idxmax () if all ( month . month >= 9 for month in peaks ): message = "Sales peak in the last four months of every year" else : message = "The busiest month changes from year to year" fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) ax . plot ( monthly . index , monthly , color = GREY , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( peaks , monthly [ peaks ], color = ORANGE , s = 50 , zorder = 3 ) for month in peaks : ax . annotate ( month . strftime ( "%b %Y" ), ( month , monthly [ month ]), xytext = ( 0 , 8 ), textcoords = "offset points" , ha = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , monthly . max () * 1.15 ) ax . set_title ( message , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Monthly Sales, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units); orange = each year's highest month" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales" ) commas ( ax ) plt . show () Annotation is text on the chart that explains one thing at the place it happens: a peak, a policy change, a missing month. Use it sparingly: one to three notes per chart. Check your understanding 6 Rewrite each descriptive title as a message title. Invent a plausible finding; the point is the form. "Returns by region, 2025" "Average delivery days by carrier"
docs.title: Part 8: Message titles and annotation

docs.text: When one chart has too many series, draw many small charts with the same axes , one per group. Tufte called these small multiples . The shared axes make every panel comparable; the repetition means the reader learns to read the first panel and then reads the rest instantly. Here each panel shows one region's quarterly Sales in blue, with the other regions in grey for context. Panels are ordered by total Sales, largest first. by_region = df . groupby ([ quarter , "region" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () by_region = by_region [ by_region . sum () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . index ] # biggest region first fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 6 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax , region in zip ( axes . flat , by_region . columns ): for other in by_region . columns : if other != region : ax . plot ( by_region . index , by_region [ other ], color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . plot ( by_region . index , by_region [ region ], color = BLUE , linewidth = 2.2 ) ax . set_title ( region , fontsize = 10 ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "x" , labelsize = 8 , labelrotation = 45 ) commas ( ax ) fig . suptitle ( "Quarterly Sales by region, largest region first: each panel highlights one region" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . supylabel ( "Sales" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Small multiples checklist Same axes in every panel ( sharex=True, sharey=True ), unless you say clearly that they differ. Panels in a meaningful order (by size, by geography, by time), not alphabetical by default. One highlight colour, the same in every panel.
docs.title: Part 9: Small multiples

docs.text: Idea One-line takeaway Task first Compare → bars; distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter; time → line Encodings Position and length are read best; angle, area and colour worse Pre-attentive One strong colour against grey; never several highlights Data-ink Remove what does not carry data; keep units, scope and meaningful reference lines Gestalt Put next to each other what the reader must compare Colour Categorical, sequential or diverging by the data; colour-blind safe; not colour alone Honest axes Bars from zero; lines may zoom with labels; avoid dual axes, index instead Titles Message title, scope in a subtitle, one to three annotations Small multiples Same axes, many panels, one highlight
docs.title: Summary

docs.text: Session 7 lab: Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ¶ Add time to your segment comparison, read growth figures without being fooled by the seasons, use the returns list carefully, apply the same ideas to official construction spending, and bring it together in one dashboard with a recommendation. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales are in the file's own source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. A pattern over time shows when something happened, not why . US construction spending comes from the U.S. Census Bureau 's monthly Construction Spending survey (value of construction put in place), as mirrored in Tableau's sample-data catalog. Values are in millions of US dollars of each month , not adjusted for inflation. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G6 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I7 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Build a complete monthly series and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Explain why a blank growth value means "no comparison", and why filtering too early creates blanks. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Select one consistent series from an official statistics file and compare part-years fairly. Combine three charts into one dashboard and write a recommendation for a test. Evidence you keep: your dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, your construction-spending chart with its series definition, and a five-sentence recommendation. G3 (Core): Two kinds of growth ¶ Growth type Compares each month with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous calendar month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month one year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Both use the same formula: (this month − comparison month) ÷ comparison month . Only on a complete monthly series pct_change compares each row with the row above it (or 12 rows above). That only means "previous month" or "same month last year" because we checked that all 36 months are present and in order. To see what is being compared, the table below also keeps the comparison values. shift(1) moves each value down one row; shift(12) moves it down twelve rows. growth = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : monthly }) growth [ "previous_month" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 1 ) growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change () growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 12 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) # A comparison month with zero Sales gives no fair growth figure: treat it as blank. growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "mom_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "previous_month" ] != 0 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "yoy_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] != 0 ) The full table has 36 rows. Name the months you compared. I4 (Core): Recommend a test ¶ Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns-list share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison you would use to judge the test, such as YoY Sales for the same months, or the same months in a similar group that did not get the change. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A segment growing at the same time as something else happened is an association , not proof that one caused the other. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works. Which growth measure would you show instead, and what does it say? Why did January's month-on-month growth become blank after filtering to 2025? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate. Mention the comparison month you used. Hint Look at what happened every January in the seasonal chart, not just in 2025. Then go back to Part 3. C2 (Challenge): "2016 was the weakest year in a decade" ¶ Another colleague adds up construction spending by calendar year and posts: "Construction spending in 2016 was the lowest yearly total since 2012. The boom is over." Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # The colleague's code. It runs, but the comparison is unfair. # 1. Find what is wrong with the 2016 figure. # 2. Fix the comparison so every year covers the same months. # 3. Rewrite the colleague's sentence so it is accurate, naming the months compared. yearly = spend . groupby ( spend . index . year ) . sum () / 1000 print ( "Yearly totals ($bn), the colleague's version:" ) print ( yearly . tail ( 6 ) . round ( 1 )) Yearly totals ($bn), the colleague's version: 2011 788.30 2012 850.50 2013 906.40 2014 1,005.60 2015 1,112.40 2016 863.20 Name: val, dtype: float64 Hint Count the months behind each total. Then go back to I3. Validation checklist ¶ The Superstore monthly series has all 36 months, Jan 2023 to Dec 2025, with no gaps. Growth was computed on the complete series before filtering to a period. Blanks appear only where no comparison exists, and are never shown as 0%. Returns are counted as distinct orders , not lines, and called "share of orders on the returns list". Segment order counts add up to the all-segments total. The construction series is exactly one series (category, data type, estimate, geography, adjustment), with one row per month and its units stated. Part-years are compared only with the same months of earlier years. Every chart has a message title, labelled axes with units, and the dashboard has a scope note. Exit ticket ¶ Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? Why does filtering to one year before computing growth create blanks? What is one thing the returns list cannot tell you? Why can you not compare the 2016 construction total with the 2015 total directly? What would you measure to judge whether your proposed test worked? docs.text: The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales are in the file's own source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. A pattern over time shows when something happened, not why . US construction spending comes from the U.S. Census Bureau 's monthly Construction Spending survey (value of construction put in place), as mirrored in Tableau's sample-data catalog. Values are in millions of US dollars of each month , not adjusted for inflation.

docs.text: Run the setup cell, then load the table. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. df = load_orders () print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 Every row has an order_month column: the first day of the month the order was placed. Grouping by it gives one Sales total per calendar month. monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () monthly . head ( 6 ) order_month 2023-01-01 14,518.06 2023-02-01 4,519.89 2023-03-01 56,933.91 2023-04-01 28,295.35 2023-05-01 26,319.77 2023-06-01 34,669.48 Name: sales, dtype: float64

DataFrame ({ "year" : monthly . index . year , "month" : monthly . index . month , "sales" : monthly . values , }) seasons = by_year . pivot ( index = "month" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" ) seasons . plot ( title = "Monthly Sales, one line per year" ) plt . xlabel ( "Month of the year (1 = January)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) plt . xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 )) plt . legend ( title = "Year" ) plt . show () A quick text check: the three highest and two lowest months in each year. for year , sales in monthly . groupby ( monthly . index . year ): highest = ", " . join ( sales . nlargest ( 3 ) . index . strftime ( "%b" )) lowest = ", " . join ( sales . nsmallest ( 2 ) . index . strftime ( "%b" )) print ( year , "| highest:" , highest , "| lowest:" , lowest ) 2023 | highest: Sep, Nov, Dec | lowest: Feb, Jan 2024 | highest: Nov, Dec, Sep | lowest: Feb, Jan 2025 | highest: Dec, Nov, Sep | lowest: Jan, Feb What do you notice?
