docs.title: G2 (Core): Segments and seasons

docs.text: Growth type Compares each month with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous calendar month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month one year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Both use the same formula: (this month − comparison month) ÷ comparison month . Only on a complete monthly series pct_change compares each row with the row above it (or 12 rows above). That only means "previous month" or "same month last year" because we checked that all 36 months are present and in order. To see what is being compared, the table below also keeps the comparison values. shift(1) moves each value down one row; shift(12) moves it down twelve rows. growth = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : monthly }) growth [ "previous_month" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 1 ) growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change () growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 12 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) # A comparison month with zero Sales gives no fair growth figure: treat it as blank. growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "mom_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "previous_month" ] != 0 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "yoy_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] != 0 ) The full table has 36 rows. To keep it readable we show a few months and format growth as percentages. as_pct writes a blank growth value as the words "no comparison". def as_pct ( value ): if pd . isna ( value ): return "no comparison" return f " { value : +.1% } " def growth_table ( table , months ): rows = table . loc [ months ] return pd . DataFrame ({ "Sales" : rows [ "sales" ] . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ), "MoM growth" : rows [ "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY growth" : rows [ "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), }, index = rows . index . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) growth_table ( growth , [ "2023-01-01" , "2023-02-01" , "2023-03-01" , "2024-01-01" , "2025-01-01" , "2025-12-01" ]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Sales MoM growth YoY growth Jan 2023 14,518 no comparison no comparison Feb 2023 4,520 -68.9% no comparison Mar 2023 56,934 +1159.6% no comparison Jan 2024 18,462 -74.4% +27.2% Jan 2025 18,830 -75.1% +2.0% Dec 2025 97,502 +22.8% +29.1% Read the output above row by row: January 2023 is the first month in the file, so it has no previous month and no month a year earlier. Every 2023 month has no year-earlier month in the file, so its YoY growth is blank. Look at March 2023 . A very large MoM figure often just means the previous month was small, not that something remarkable happened. Compare January 2025 MoM with January 2025 YoY. Do they tell the same story?

docs.text: Suppose you only care about 2025. There are two orders of work: Filter, then compute: keep only 2025 rows, then calculate growth. Compute, then filter: calculate growth on all 36 months, then show only 2025. Run both and compare January and February 2025. # 1. Filter first, then compute growth only_2025 = df [ df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year == 2025 ] monthly_2025 = only_2025 . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = pd . DataFrame ({ "mom_growth" : monthly_2025 . pct_change (), "yoy_growth" : monthly_2025 . pct_change ( periods = 12 ), }) # 2. Compute growth on all months first, then keep 2025 compute_first = growth . loc [ "2025" , [ "mom_growth" , "yoy_growth" ]] check_months = [ "2025-01-01" , "2025-02-01" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "MoM, filter first" : filter_first . loc [ check_months , "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "MoM, compute first" : compute_first . loc [ check_months , "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, filter first" : filter_first . loc [ check_months , "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute first" : compute_first . loc [ check_months , "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), }, index = pd . DatetimeIndex ( check_months ) . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MoM, filter first MoM, compute first YoY, filter first YoY, compute first Jan 2025 no comparison -75.1% no comparison +2.0% Feb 2025 +22.0% +22.0% no comparison +92.3% In the output above, filtering first leaves January 2025 with no row above it, so its MoM growth becomes blank. And because the filtered series holds only 12 months, every YoY value becomes blank: December 2024 and all of 2024 were removed before the calculation could see them. Rule Compute growth on the complete monthly series first. Filter or highlight the period you want to show afterwards. If you must filter first, say clearly that the comparison months were removed. Filtering by segment or region is different: it changes which lines count, and it applies equally to both months being compared. That is fine, as long as you build the full 36-month series for that group and state the filter.
docs.title: G4 (Core): Filtering can remove the comparison

docs.text: From the Session 2 lab, returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . It is an order-level flag: every line of a listed order has 1. So we count distinct orders , never lines. returned = df [ df [ "returned_order_flag" ] == 1 ] returns_by_segment = pd . DataFrame ({ "orders" : df . groupby ( "segment" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique (), "orders_on_returns_list" : returned . groupby ( "segment" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique (), }) returns_by_segment . loc [ "All segments" ] = [ df [ "order_id" ] . nunique (), returned [ "order_id" ] . nunique (), ] returns_by_segment [ "share_on_list" ] = ( returns_by_segment [ "orders_on_returns_list" ] / returns_by_segment [ "orders" ] ) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) returns_by_segment .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } orders orders_on_returns_list share_on_list segment Consumer 1738 99 5.7% Corporate 1044 61 5.8% Home Office 606 31 5.1% All segments 3388 191 5.6% The All segments row is calculated from the whole table, not by adding the segment rows. Check that the segment counts add up to it: if an order appeared in two segments it would be counted twice. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it.
docs.title: G5 (Core): The returns list

docs.text: In Python, a simple dashboard is one figure with several charts (called subplots ). plt.subplots(3, 1) creates three charts stacked vertically; each one has its own ax to draw on. The code is wrapped in a function , draw_dashboard , so you can redraw the whole dashboard for one region later by changing a single line. That is the Python version of one filter that controls every view. The function: builds a segment KPI table (Sales and share of orders on the returns list); builds a complete 36-month Sales series, putting 0 in any month where the selection has no lines; computes YoY growth on the full series before anything is hidden; draws three panels with message titles and a scope note. def draw_dashboard ( data , scope ): # 1. Segment KPIs kpis = pd . docs.text: Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns-list share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison you would use to judge the test, such as YoY Sales for the same months, or the same months in a similar group that did not get the change. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A segment growing at the same time as something else happened is an association , not proof that one caused the other. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works.

docs.text: Session 7 lecture: Time series and trends ¶ A number on its own says little; the same number compared with the right earlier period says a lot. This lecture shows how to read a series over time, pick a fair comparison, smooth out the noise and avoid the traps that make ordinary months look like disasters. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer the quiz at the end of the Session 6 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. What you will be able to explain ¶ The three components of a time series: trend, seasonality and noise. When month-on-month and when year-on-year growth is the fair comparison. How a rolling average smooths a series, and the difference between trailing and centred windows. How index numbers (base = 100) let you compare series of very different sizes. What a seasonally adjusted series is, and why official statistics publish one. Why incomplete and missing periods break comparisons, and how to guard against them. Why growth must be computed before you filter to a period. This lecture builds on the section on cherry-picked time windows in How statistics can mislead . In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to official US construction spending. Most business series are a mix of three parts: Component What it is Example Trend The slow, long-run direction A shop growing a little every year Seasonality A pattern that repeats at the same time every year (or week, or day) Busy Novembers and Decembers, quiet Januaries Noise Irregular ups and downs with no pattern A delivery delay, one big one-off order The cell below builds a series from these three parts, so we know exactly what is inside it. Real data never tells you its parts; you have to infer them. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 7 ) months = pd . date_range ( "2021-01-01" , "2024-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) t = np . arange ( len ( months )) trend = 100 + 1.5 * t # grows steadily every month season_by_month = [ - 25 , - 20 , - 5 , 0 , 5 , 0 , - 5 , 0 , 10 , 5 , 15 , 20 ] # same shape every year seasonal = np . array ([ season_by_month [ m . month - 1 ] for m in months ]) noise = rng . normal ( 0 , 5 , len ( months )) demo = pd . DataFrame ({ "trend" : trend , "seasonal" : seasonal , "noise" : noise }, index = months ) demo [ "sales" ] = demo [ "trend" ] + demo [ "seasonal" ] + demo [ "noise" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , col , colour in zip ( axes , [ "sales" , "trend" , "seasonal" , "noise" ], [ "#2a78d6" , "#555555" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]): ax . plot ( demo . index , demo [ col ], color = colour ) ax . set_title ( col . capitalize () if col != "sales" else "Sales = trend + seasonal + noise" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look only at the top panel. Between December and January of each year, does the series go up or down? Is that the trend changing, or something else? Now look at the three panels underneath and check. The top line drops every January even though the trend never stops rising. A manager looking only at the latest two months would see a "fall" that is entirely seasonal. Check your understanding 1 Name one business series you know and describe its likely trend, its seasonality and one source of noise. Part 2: Month-on-month versus year-on-year ¶ Growth always compares two values: (this period − comparison period) ÷ comparison period . The question is which comparison period. Growth type Compares with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month a year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Predict, then reveal In the simulated series, the trend rises a little every month. What do you expect January's MoM growth to look like? And January's YoY growth? demo [ "mom" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change () demo [ "yoy" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 5.5 ), sharex = True ) ax1 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "mom" ] * 100 , width = 20 ) ax1 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Month-on-month growth: big swings driven by the seasons" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "MoM (%)" ) ax2 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "yoy" ] * 100 , width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Year-on-year growth: steady, close to the real trend (first year has no comparison)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "YoY (%)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () def as_pct ( value ): return "no comparison" if pd . isna ( value ) else f " { value : +.1% } " januaries = demo [ demo . index . month == 1 ][[ "sales" , "mom" , "yoy" ]] januaries . assign ( mom = januaries [ "mom" ] . map ( as_pct ), yoy = januaries [ "yoy" ] . map ( as_pct )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales mom yoy 2021-01-01 75.01 no comparison no comparison 2022-01-01 93.53 -32.4% +24.7% 2023-01-01 111.78 -28.3% +19.5% 2024-01-01 128.84 -23.5% +15.3% Read the table above. Every January has a large negative MoM figure, while YoY stays positive. The first January has no comparison at all: pandas stores it as NaN ( not a number ), and our as_pct helper prints it as "no comparison", never as zero. Use… When… Watch out for… MoM You need to spot a sudden change quickly, and the series is not strongly seasonal Seasonal swings that look like booms and crashes YoY The business is seasonal and you want like-for-like A one-off event in the same month last year; it reacts slowly to new changes Blank is not zero A growth value with no comparison period is not available . It is not 0%. Never fill it with 0. Check your understanding 2 A colleague reports "Sales up 40% month-on-month in November". What extra comparison would you ask for before celebrating, and why? Part 3: Rolling averages, trailing and centred ¶ A rolling average (or moving average) replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. A 12-month window covers exactly one full year, so every month of the season appears once and the seasonal pattern cancels out. Window Uses Good for Cost Trailing this month and the 11 before it Dashboards: only uses data you already have It lags : it turns late Centred about 6 months either side Seeing exactly when the trend turned Needs future data, so the last months are blank We add a sudden step : from mid-2023, sales jump by 40 and stay there. stepped = demo [ "sales" ] + np . where ( demo . index >= "2023-07-01" , 40 , 0 ) smooth = pd . DataFrame ({ "monthly" : stepped , "trailing 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 ) . mean (), "centred 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean (), }) ax = smooth [ "monthly" ] . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly value" ) smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) smooth [ "centred 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2.5 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . axvline ( pd . Timestamp ( "2023-07-01" ), color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "A level change in July 2023: the trailing average reacts late" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () print ( "Blank trailing values:" , smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . isna () . sum (), "| blank centred values:" , smooth [ "centred 12" ] . isna () . sum ()) Blank trailing values: 11 | blank centred values: 11 Predict, then reveal Before reading the chart: which line will finish its climb closer to the vertical line in July 2023, the trailing or the centred average? Where will each line be blank? The trailing average needs 11 earlier months, so it is blank at the start . The centred average needs months on both sides, so it is blank at both ends , including the most recent months a manager usually cares about most. Check your understanding 3 You are building a monthly dashboard that updates on the first day of each month. Which rolling average can you show for the latest month, and what will it hide? Part 4: Index numbers (base = 100) ¶ Two series of very different sizes are hard to compare on one chart: the big one squashes the small one flat. An index divides every value by the value in a chosen base period and multiplies by 100. index = value ÷ base value × 100 So the base period is 100 for every series, and 120 later means "20% above the base period". We add up each segment's Sales by year and use 2023 as the base year. A whole year as the base means one unusual month cannot distort it. seg_monthly = df . groupby ([ "order_month" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () seg_yearly = seg_monthly . groupby ( seg_monthly . index . year ) . sum () base = seg_yearly . loc [ 2023 ] index = seg_yearly / base * 100 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) seg_yearly . plot ( ax = ax1 , marker = "o" , title = "Yearly Sales by segment" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . set_xticks ( seg_yearly . index ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) index . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , title = "Indexed: 2023 = 100" , legend = False ) ax2 . axhline ( 100 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Index (2023 = 100)" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( index . index ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () index . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } segment Consumer Corporate Home Office order_month 2023 100.00 100.00 100.00 2024 99.50 98.70 81.00 2025 111.50 158.80 112.70 On the left, the largest segment dominates. On the right, every segment starts at 100, so you compare growth paths , not sizes. Check your understanding 4 An index reads 85 in the latest year with base year 2023 = 100. Say in plain words what happened. Does the index tell you which segment is the largest? Part 5: Seasonally adjusted series ¶ National statistics offices publish many series twice: Not seasonally adjusted (NSA): the actual amount in each month. Seasonally adjusted (SA): the same series with the usual seasonal pattern taken out, so one month can be compared directly with the month before. Official agencies use detailed methods (for example, the US Census Bureau uses a program called X-13ARIMA-SEATS). The core idea is simple enough to build by hand: Estimate the trend with a centred 12-month average. For each month, see how far the actual value sits above or below that trend. Average those gaps by calendar month: that is the seasonal factor for January, February and so on. Subtract each month's seasonal factor from the actual value. sales = demo [ "sales" ] trend_est = sales . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean () gap = sales - trend_est seasonal_factor = gap . groupby ( gap . index . month ) . mean () adjusted = sales - seasonal_factor . reindex ( sales . index . month ) . values ax = sales . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Not adjusted (actual)" ) adjusted . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Seasonally adjusted (our estimate)" ) demo [ "trend" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "black" , linestyle = ":" , label = "True trend (known only because we built it)" ) ax . set_title ( "Removing the seasonal pattern leaves trend plus noise" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () pd . DataFrame ({ "estimated factor" : seasonal_factor . round ( 1 ), "true factor" : season_by_month }, index = pd . Index ( range ( 1 , 13 ), name = "month" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimated factor true factor month 1 -22.00 -25 2 -17.60 -20 3 -7.30 -5 4 2.80 0 5 5.70 5 6 2.30 0 7 -8.30 -5 8 2.30 0 9 7.40 10 10 5.20 5 11 18.30 15 12 22.40 20 The estimated seasonal factors come out close to the true ones we built in, and the adjusted line follows the trend plus noise. Annual rates Some official monthly series are published as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) : the adjusted monthly value multiplied up to a full year. A SAAR of 1,200 means "if every month were like this one, the year would total about 1,200". Divide by 12 to compare it with a monthly amount, and never add up annual-rate values across months. Check your understanding 5 A news report says spending "fell 8% in January". Which would you rather see: the adjusted or the unadjusted series? Why? Part 6: Incomplete and missing periods ¶ Two quiet traps. An incomplete last period. If data were pulled on the 10th of a month, that month holds about a third of its orders. On a chart it looks like a collapse. cut = demo [ "sales" ] . copy () cut . iloc [ - 1 ] = cut . iloc [ - 1 ] * 10 / 31 # data pulled on the 10th of the last month ax = cut . plot ( marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax . annotate ( "Only 10 of 31 days \n loaded so far" , xy = ( cut . index [ - 1 ], cut . iloc [ - 1 ]), xytext = ( - 130 , - 10 ), textcoords = "offset points" , arrowprops = { "arrowstyle" : "->" }) ax . set_title ( "An incomplete last month looks like a crash" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) plt . show () print ( "Last month MoM growth:" , f " { cut . pct_change () . iloc [ - 1 ] : +.1% } " ) Last month MoM growth: -67.3% A missing month. pct_change() compares each row with the row above. If a month is missing, "the row above" is two months earlier, and nothing warns you. The fix is to line the series up against the full calendar first. gappy = demo [ "sales" ] . drop ( pd . Timestamp ( "2024-06-01" )) print ( "Rows:" , len ( gappy ), "| months in the calendar:" , len ( months )) wrong = gappy . pct_change () . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] safe = gappy . reindex ( months ) . pct_change ( fill_method = None ) . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] print ( "July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: " , f " { wrong : +.1% } <- silently compared with May" ) print ( "July 2024 MoM, after reindex: " , safe , " <- no comparison available" ) Rows: 47 | months in the calendar: 48 July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: -8.3% <- silently compared with May July 2024 MoM, after reindex: nan <- no comparison available Rules for periods Check the first and last date, and whether the last period is complete. Build the full calendar with pd.date_range and reindex against it, so gaps show as blanks. Compare like with like : a part-year only with the same part of earlier years (for example January–September with January–September). Check your understanding 6 A file has nine months of 2016 and twelve months of every earlier year. A colleague compares yearly totals and reports that 2016 was the weakest year. What should you check, and what fair comparison would you make instead? Part 7: Growth after filtering, the trap ¶ You want a table of 2025 only. If you filter first , the earlier months the growth formula needs are gone. monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = monthly . loc [ "2025" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) compute_first = monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) . loc [ "2025" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "YoY, filter then compute" : filter_first . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute then filter" : compute_first . map ( as_pct )}) . head ( 4 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } YoY, filter then compute YoY, compute then filter order_month 2025-01-01 no comparison +2.0% 2025-02-01 no comparison +92.3% 2025-03-01 no comparison +32.6% 2025-04-01 no comparison +13.6% Predict, then reveal Before running the cell above: how many of the twelve 2025 months will have a YoY value when you filter first? Filtering to one year leaves only twelve rows, so no row has a partner twelve rows above it. Every YoY value becomes blank ("no comparison"). Rule Compute growth on the complete series first, then filter or highlight the period you want to show. Filtering by a group such as a segment is fine, because it applies to both months in the comparison; build that group's complete series first. Part 8: Worked case — Superstore monthly Sales ¶ We put the pieces together on the retail orders. Step 1: Check the calendar ¶ all_months = pd . date_range ( "2023-01-01" , "2025-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) print ( "First order month:" , monthly . index . min () . date (), "| last:" , monthly . index . max () . date ()) print ( "Months expected:" , len ( all_months ), "| months present:" , len ( monthly ), "| missing:" , len ( all_months . difference ( monthly . index ))) monthly = monthly . reindex ( all_months ) First order month: 2023-01-01 | last: 2025-12-01 Months expected: 36 | months present: 36 | missing: 0 Step 2: Trend and seasonality in one view ¶ A light line for the actual months, a strong line for the trailing 12-month average, and a year-overlay chart for the season. rolling_12 = monthly . rolling ( 12 ) . mean () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . plot ( monthly . index , monthly , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly Sales" ) ax1 . plot ( rolling_12 . index , rolling_12 , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) ax1 . set_title ( "Underlying level, without the season" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) overlay = pd . DataFrame ({ "year" : monthly . index . year , "month" : monthly . index . month , "sales" : monthly . values }) overlay . pivot ( index = "month" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" ) . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax2 . set_title ( "The same seasonal shape every year" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Month of the year" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 )) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Step 3: Which comparison is fair for January 2025? ¶ jan = pd . Timestamp ( "2025-01-01" ) print ( "January 2025 Sales:" , f " { monthly [ jan ] : ,.0f } " ) print ( "MoM (vs December 2024):" , f " { monthly . pct_change ()[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) print ( "YoY (vs January 2024): " , f " { monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 )[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) January 2025 Sales: 18,830 MoM (vs December 2024): -75.1% YoY (vs January 2024): +2.0% Read the two growth figures above alongside the year-overlay chart. The month-on-month figure repeats the usual January drop; the year-on-year figure compares January with January. For a seasonal business, the YoY figure is the fair headline, and the trailing average shows whether the underlying level is rising. Summary ¶ Question Tool Trap to avoid Is there a pattern by time of year? Year-overlay chart Reading one month in isolation Did this month grow? YoY for seasonal series; MoM for non-seasonal Calling a seasonal dip a crash What is the underlying level? Trailing 12-month average Forgetting it lags When exactly did it turn? Centred average (on history) Expecting it for the latest months How do different-sized series compare? Index, base = 100 Choosing an unusual base period Is this month normal for the season? Seasonally adjusted series Adding up annual-rate values Can I trust the comparison? Full calendar, complete periods Missing months, part-years, filtering first Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Name the three components of a time series and give a one-line example of each. Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What does year-on-year growth compare, and when can it still mislead? A trailing and a centred 12-month average are drawn on the same series. Which turns later after a sudden change, and which is blank for the latest months? An index with base year 2023 = 100 reads 112 in 2025. What does that mean? What does a seasonally adjusted series remove, and why do official agencies publish one? Why should you never fill a blank growth value with 0%? You filter a monthly table to one year and then compute YoY growth. What happens, and what should you do instead? Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you: Build the monthly Superstore series, check it is complete and read its seasons. Calculate MoM and YoY growth and see how filtering removes the comparison. Measure the share of orders on the returns list and build a three-panel dashboard. Select one consistent series from official US construction spending, read its seasons and compare part-years fairly. Debug a "75% crash" and a "weakest year ever" claim. Write a five-sentence test recommendation for the commercial lead. Open the Session 7 lab .

docs.text: A number on its own says little; the same number compared with the right earlier period says a lot. This lecture shows how to read a series over time, pick a fair comparison, smooth out the noise and avoid the traps that make ordinary months look like disasters. docs.text: The three components of a time series: trend, seasonality and noise. When month-on-month and when year-on-year growth is the fair comparison. How a rolling average smooths a series, and the difference between trailing and centred windows. How index numbers (base = 100) let you compare series of very different sizes. What a seasonally adjusted series is, and why official statistics publish one. Why incomplete and missing periods break comparisons, and how to guard against them. Why growth must be computed before you filter to a period. This lecture builds on the section on cherry-picked time windows in How statistics can mislead . In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to official US construction spending. docs.text: A time series is one measure recorded at regular intervals: Sales per month, visitors per day, spending per quarter. Most business series are a mix of three parts: Component What it is Example Trend The slow, long-run direction A shop growing a little every year Seasonality A pattern that repeats at the same time every year (or week, or day) Busy Novembers and Decembers, quiet Januaries Noise Irregular ups and downs with no pattern A delivery delay, one big one-off order The cell below builds a series from these three parts, so we know exactly what is inside it. Real data never tells you its parts; you have to infer them. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 7 ) months = pd . date_range ( "2021-01-01" , "2024-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) t = np . arange ( len ( months )) trend = 100 + 1.5 * t # grows steadily every month season_by_month = [ - 25 , - 20 , - 5 , 0 , 5 , 0 , - 5 , 0 , 10 , 5 , 15 , 20 ] # same shape every year seasonal = np . array ([ season_by_month [ m . month - 1 ] for m in months ]) noise = rng . normal ( 0 , 5 , len ( months )) demo = pd . DataFrame ({ "trend" : trend , "seasonal" : seasonal , "noise" : noise }, index = months ) demo [ "sales" ] = demo [ "trend" ] + demo [ "seasonal" ] + demo [ "noise" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , col , colour in zip ( axes , [ "sales" , "trend" , "seasonal" , "noise" ], [ "#2a78d6" , "#555555" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]): ax . plot ( demo . index , demo [ col ], color = colour ) ax . set_title ( col . capitalize () if col != "sales" else "Sales = trend + seasonal + noise" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look only at the top panel. Between December and January of each year, does the series go up or down? Is that the trend changing, or something else? Now look at the three panels underneath and check. The top line drops every January even though the trend never stops rising. A manager looking only at the latest two months would see a "fall" that is entirely seasonal. Check your understanding 1 Name one business series you know and describe its likely trend, its seasonality and one source of noise.
docs.title: Part 1: The three components of a series

docs.text: Growth always compares two values: (this period − comparison period) ÷ comparison period . The question is which comparison period. Growth type Compares with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month a year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Predict, then reveal In the simulated series, the trend rises a little every month. What do you expect January's MoM growth to look like? And January's YoY growth? demo [ "mom" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change () demo [ "yoy" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 5.5 ), sharex = True ) ax1 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "mom" ] * 100 , width = 20 ) ax1 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Month-on-month growth: big swings driven by the seasons" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "MoM (%)" ) ax2 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "yoy" ] * 100 , width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Year-on-year growth: steady, close to the real trend (first year has no comparison)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "YoY (%)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () def as_pct ( value ): return "no comparison" if pd . isna ( value ) else f " { value : +.1% } " januaries = demo [ demo . index . month == 1 ][[ "sales" , "mom" , "yoy" ]] januaries . assign ( mom = januaries [ "mom" ] . map ( as_pct ), yoy = januaries [ "yoy" ] . map ( as_pct )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales mom yoy 2021-01-01 75.01 no comparison no comparison 2022-01-01 93.53 -32.4% +24.7% 2023-01-01 111.78 -28.3% +19.5% 2024-01-01 128.84 -23.5% +15.3% Read the table above. Every January has a large negative MoM figure, while YoY stays positive. The first January has no comparison at all: pandas stores it as NaN ( not a number ), and our as_pct helper prints it as "no comparison", never as zero. Use… When… Watch out for… MoM You need to spot a sudden change quickly, and the series is not strongly seasonal Seasonal swings that look like booms and crashes YoY The business is seasonal and you want like-for-like A one-off event in the same month last year; it reacts slowly to new changes Blank is not zero A growth value with no comparison period is not available . It is not 0%. Never fill it with 0. Check your understanding 2 A colleague reports "Sales up 40% month-on-month in November". What extra comparison would you ask for before celebrating, and why?

docs.text: A rolling average (or moving average) replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. A 12-month window covers exactly one full year, so every month of the season appears once and the seasonal pattern cancels out. Window Uses Good for Cost Trailing this month and the 11 before it Dashboards: only uses data you already have It lags : it turns late Centred about 6 months either side Seeing exactly when the trend turned Needs future data, so the last months are blank We add a sudden step : from mid-2023, sales jump by 40 and stay there. stepped = demo [ "sales" ] + np . where ( demo . index >= "2023-07-01" , 40 , 0 ) smooth = pd . DataFrame ({ "monthly" : stepped , "trailing 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 ) . mean (), "centred 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean (), }) ax = smooth [ "monthly" ] . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly value" ) smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) smooth [ "centred 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2.5 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . axvline ( pd . Timestamp ( "2023-07-01" ), color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "A level change in July 2023: the trailing average reacts late" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () print ( "Blank trailing values:" , smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . isna () . sum (), "| blank centred values:" , smooth [ "centred 12" ] . isna () . sum ()) Blank trailing values: 11 | blank centred values: 11 Predict, then reveal Before reading the chart: which line will finish its climb closer to the vertical line in July 2023, the trailing or the centred average? Where will each line be blank? The trailing average needs 11 earlier months, so it is blank at the start . The centred average needs months on both sides, so it is blank at both ends , including the most recent months a manager usually cares about most. docs.text: Two series of very different sizes are hard to compare on one chart: the big one squashes the small one flat. An index divides every value by the value in a chosen base period and multiplies by 100. index = value ÷ base value × 100 So the base period is 100 for every series, and 120 later means "20% above the base period". We add up each segment's Sales by year and use 2023 as the base year. A whole year as the base means one unusual month cannot distort it. seg_monthly = df . groupby ([ "order_month" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () seg_yearly = seg_monthly . groupby ( seg_monthly . index . year ) . sum () base = seg_yearly . loc [ 2023 ] index = seg_yearly / base * 100 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) seg_yearly . plot ( ax = ax1 , marker = "o" , title = "Yearly Sales by segment" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . set_xticks ( seg_yearly . index ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) index . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , title = "Indexed: 2023 = 100" , legend = False ) ax2 . axhline ( 100 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Index (2023 = 100)" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( index . index ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () index . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } segment Consumer Corporate Home Office order_month 2023 100.00 100.00 100.00 2024 99.50 98.70 81.00 2025 111.50 158.80 112.70 On the left, the largest segment dominates. On the right, every segment starts at 100, so you compare growth paths , not sizes. Check your understanding 4 An index reads 85 in the latest year with base year 2023 = 100. docs.text: National statistics offices publish many series twice: Not seasonally adjusted (NSA): the actual amount in each month. Seasonally adjusted (SA): the same series with the usual seasonal pattern taken out, so one month can be compared directly with the month before. Official agencies use detailed methods (for example, the US Census Bureau uses a program called X-13ARIMA-SEATS). The core idea is simple enough to build by hand: Estimate the trend with a centred 12-month average. For each month, see how far the actual value sits above or below that trend. Average those gaps by calendar month: that is the seasonal factor for January, February and so on. Subtract each month's seasonal factor from the actual value. sales = demo [ "sales" ] trend_est = sales . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean () gap = sales - trend_est seasonal_factor = gap . groupby ( gap . index . month ) . mean () adjusted = sales - seasonal_factor . reindex ( sales . index . month ) . values ax = sales . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Not adjusted (actual)" ) adjusted . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Seasonally adjusted (our estimate)" ) demo [ "trend" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "black" , linestyle = ":" , label = "True trend (known only because we built it)" ) ax . set_title ( "Removing the seasonal pattern leaves trend plus noise" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () pd . DataFrame ({ "estimated factor" : seasonal_factor . round ( 1 ), "true factor" : season_by_month }, index = pd . Index ( range ( 1 , 13 ), name = "month" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimated factor true factor month 1 -22.00 -25 2 -17.60 -20 3 -7.30 -5 4 2.80 0 5 5.70 5 6 2.30 0 7 -8.30 -5 8 2.30 0 9 7.40 10 10 5.20 5 11 18.30 15 12 22.40 20 The estimated seasonal factors come out close to the true ones we built in, and the adjusted line follows the trend plus noise. Annual rates Some official monthly series are published as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) : the adjusted monthly value multiplied up to a full year. A SAAR of 1,200 means "if every month were like this one, the year would total about 1,200". Divide by 12 to compare it with a monthly amount, and never add up annual-rate values across months. Check your understanding 5 A news report says spending "fell 8% in January". Which would you rather see: the adjusted or the unadjusted series? Why?

docs.text: Two quiet traps. An incomplete last period. If data were pulled on the 10th of a month, that month holds about a third of its orders. On a chart it looks like a collapse. cut = demo [ "sales" ] . copy () cut . iloc [ - 1 ] = cut . iloc [ - 1 ] * 10 / 31 # data pulled on the 10th of the last month ax = cut . plot ( marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax . annotate ( "Only 10 of 31 days \n loaded so far" , xy = ( cut . index [ - 1 ], cut . iloc [ - 1 ]), xytext = ( - 130 , - 10 ), textcoords = "offset points" , arrowprops = { "arrowstyle" : "->" }) ax . set_title ( "An incomplete last month looks like a crash" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) plt . show () print ( "Last month MoM growth:" , f " { cut . pct_change () . iloc [ - 1 ] : +.1% } " ) Last month MoM growth: -67.3% A missing month. pct_change() compares each row with the row above. If a month is missing, "the row above" is two months earlier, and nothing warns you. The fix is to line the series up against the full calendar first. gappy = demo [ "sales" ] . drop ( pd . Timestamp ( "2024-06-01" )) print ( "Rows:" , len ( gappy ), "| months in the calendar:" , len ( months )) wrong = gappy . pct_change () . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] safe = gappy . reindex ( months ) . pct_change ( fill_method = None ) . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] print ( "July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: " , f " { wrong : +.1% } <- silently compared with May" ) print ( "July 2024 MoM, after reindex: " , safe , " <- no comparison available" ) Rows: 47 | months in the calendar: 48 July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: -8.3% <- silently compared with May July 2024 MoM, after reindex: nan <- no comparison available Rules for periods Check the first and last date, and whether the last period is complete. Build the full calendar with pd.date_range and reindex against it, so gaps show as blanks. Compare like with like : a part-year only with the same part of earlier years (for example January–September with January–September). Check your understanding 6 A file has nine months of 2016 and twelve months of every earlier year. A colleague compares yearly totals and reports that 2016 was the weakest year. What should you check, and what fair comparison would you make instead?
docs.title: Part 6: Incomplete and missing periods

If you filter first , the earlier months the growth formula needs are gone. monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = monthly . loc [ "2025" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) compute_first = monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) . loc [ "2025" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "YoY, filter then compute" : filter_first . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute then filter" : compute_first . map ( as_pct )}) . head ( 4 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } YoY, filter then compute YoY, compute then filter order_month 2025-01-01 no comparison +2.0% 2025-02-01 no comparison +92.3% 2025-03-01 no comparison +32.6% 2025-04-01 no comparison +13.6% Predict, then reveal Before running the cell above: how many of the twelve 2025 months will have a YoY value when you filter first? Filtering to one year leaves only twelve rows, so no row has a partner twelve rows above it. Every YoY value becomes blank ("no comparison"). Rule Compute growth on the complete series first, then filter or highlight the period you want to show. Filtering by a group such as a segment is fine, because it applies to both months in the comparison; build that group's complete series first.

docs.text: Session 8 lab: Discount, profit and advertising spend ¶ Measure how discounts relate to profit in the retail orders, fit and interpret a regression of advertising spend against revenue, read its residuals, and learn to say clearly what a slope can and cannot promise. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ Two managers have questions: Commercial lead: "Do our discounts eat into profit? How strongly?" Marketing lead: "If one unit of search advertising brings in several units of revenue, why don't we double the budget?" Both questions are about two measures moving together . Your job is to measure the relationship honestly, and to say what it does not prove. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. marketing_daily.csv is synthetic : generated for this course, describing no real company, brand or platform. One row per day of 2025 × paid campaign. Amounts are in neutral currency units . How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G5 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I5 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Draw a scatter plot and compute Pearson and Spearman correlation. Aggregate to the right level before computing a ratio, and explain why the level changes the picture. Fit a straight line with np.polyfit , and state its slope, R² and the range of the data in business language. Read a residual plot and spot a missing factor. Flag predictions that are extrapolations. Explain why a regression slope from past data is an association, not the effect of spending more. Evidence you keep: an interpreted regression with one stated limitation (I1–I3), plus your line-versus-order explanation (G4). Before you start ¶ Read the Session 8 lecture . Re-read correlation is not causation . Remember from the Session 5 lab: profit ratio = total Profit ÷ total Sales , a ratio of sums. A line's profit ratio is its Profit ÷ its Sales. Because no line has zero Sales, every line has a ratio. df [ "line_profit_ratio" ] = df [ "profit" ] / df [ "sales" ] ax = df . plot . scatter ( x = "discount" , y = "line_profit_ratio" , s = 8 , alpha = 0.15 ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "Order lines: higher discounts, lower profit ratios" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Discount on the line (share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Line profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales)" ) plt . show () print ( "Different discount values:" , df [ "discount" ] . nunique ()) print ( "Pearson r: " , round ( df [ "discount" ] . corr ( df [ "line_profit_ratio" ]), 3 )) print ( "Spearman: " , round ( df [ "discount" ] . rank () . corr ( df [ "line_profit_ratio" ] . rank ()), 3 )) Different discount values: 12 Pearson r: -0.865 Spearman: -0.65 What do you notice? Why do the dots form vertical stripes ? (Look at the number of different discount values.) Many dots sit on top of each other. Which discount values hold most of the lines? Is the relationship positive or negative? Strong or weak? G2 (Core): Profit ratio by discount level ¶ Because discount takes only a few values, a table can summarise the scatter. For each discount level we add up Sales and Profit and then divide: a ratio of sums, never an average of line ratios. by_discount = df . groupby ( "discount" ) . agg ( lines = ( "row_id" , "count" ), sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" )) by_discount [ "profit_ratio" ] = by_discount [ "profit" ] / by_discount [ "sales" ] ax = by_discount [ "profit_ratio" ] . plot . bar ( color = [ "#2a78d6" if v >= 0 else "#eb6834" for v in by_discount [ "profit_ratio" ]]) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "Profit ratio turns negative at higher discount levels" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Discount on the line (share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit ratio (total Profit ÷ total Sales)" ) plt . show () by_discount . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } lines sales profit profit_ratio discount 0.00 3296 748,350.61 220,093.62 0.29 0.10 67 35,773.77 5,796.92 0.16 0.15 36 18,795.73 881.46 0.05 0.20 2464 521,404.86 57,800.06 0.11 0.30 161 72,640.59 -6,593.19 -0.09 0.32 16 10,776.35 -1,898.91 -0.18 0.40 138 82,397.71 -15,253.23 -0.18 0.45 7 2,975.36 -1,264.67 -0.42 0.50 47 45,117.10 -13,642.04 -0.30 0.60 107 4,953.99 -4,143.39 -0.84 0.70 283 28,646.77 -28,111.59 -0.98 0.80 193 9,134.01 -17,294.58 -1.89 Read the table above. Look at the lines column too: a level with few lines gives a less reliable ratio. G3 (Core): Aggregate to orders first ¶ A manager thinks in orders , not lines. An order can mix discounted and full-price lines. To get one point per order: Add up each order's Sales and Profit. Order profit ratio = order Profit ÷ order Sales (a ratio of sums). Order discount = Sales-weighted average of its lines' discounts: sum of (discount × Sales) ÷ sum of Sales . A big discounted line counts more than a small one. df [ "discount_x_sales" ] = df [ "discount" ] * df [ "sales" ] orders = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . agg ( lines = ( "row_id" , "count" ), sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), discount_x_sales = ( "discount_x_sales" , "sum" ), ) orders [ "order_discount" ] = orders [ "discount_x_sales" ] / orders [ "sales" ] orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] = orders [ "profit" ] / orders [ "sales" ] print ( "Orders:" , len ( orders ), "| orders with more than one line:" , ( orders [ "lines" ] > 1 ) . sum ()) ax = orders . plot . scatter ( x = "order_discount" , y = "order_profit_ratio" , s = 8 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "Orders: the same direction, fewer stripes" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (Sales-weighted, share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Order profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales)" ) plt . show () Orders: 3388 | orders with more than one line: 1691 G4 (Core): Why do the two pictures differ? ¶ Put the two levels side by side. def describe_level ( x , y ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( x , y , 1 ) return { "points" : len ( x ), "Pearson r" : x . corr ( y ), "Spearman" : x . rank () . corr ( y . rank ()), "slope" : slope , "mean of ratios" : y . mean (), } levels = pd . DataFrame ({ "line level" : describe_level ( df [ "discount" ], df [ "line_profit_ratio" ]), "order level" : describe_level ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ]), }) . T . astype ({ "points" : int }) print ( "Profit ratio of all Sales (total Profit ÷ total Sales):" , round ( df [ "profit" ] . sum () / df [ "sales" ] . sum (), 3 )) with pd . option_context ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.3f} " . format ): display ( levels ) Profit ratio of all Sales (total Profit ÷ total Sales): 0.124 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } points Pearson r Spearman slope mean of ratios line level 6815 -0.865 -0.650 -1.923 0.125 order level 3388 -0.863 -0.696 -1.855 0.116 Read the output above and discuss in pairs: Number of points. An order with five lines is five dots at line level and one dot at order level. Which orders count more in the line picture? Mixing. At order level, a discounted line and a full-price line are blended into one point. What happens to the stripes, and to the most extreme negative ratios? Averages. Compare the two "mean of ratios" values with the profit ratio of all Sales printed above. Which number should a report use as the profit ratio? Why can an average of ratios not be trusted, even when it happens to land close? The question. "Do discounted products lose money?" is a line question. "Do orders with deeper discounts lose money?" is an order question. Which did the commercial lead ask? Rule Decide the level of the question first, aggregate to that level, then compute ratios and correlations. State the level in every chart title and sentence. G5 (Core): Fit and interpret a line at order level ¶ A slope per one whole unit of discount (100 percentage points) is hard to picture, so we also state it per 10 points. slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ], 1 ) orders [ "predicted" ] = intercept + slope * orders [ "order_discount" ] orders [ "residual" ] = orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] - orders [ "predicted" ] r_squared = 1 - ( orders [ "residual" ] ** 2 ) . sum () / (( orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] - orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] . mean ()) ** 2 ) . sum () print ( f "Slope: { slope : .3f } profit ratio per 1.0 of discount " f "= { slope * 0.1 * 100 : +.1f } percentage points of profit ratio per 10 points of discount" ) print ( f "Intercept: { intercept : .3f } (predicted profit ratio for an order with no discount)" ) print ( f "R²: { r_squared : .3f } " ) print ( "Order discounts observed:" , round ( orders [ "order_discount" ] . min (), 2 ), "to" , round ( orders [ "order_discount" ] . max (), 2 )) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) xs = np . linspace ( 0 , orders [ "order_discount" ] . max (), 50 ) ax1 . scatter ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ], s = 6 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax1 . plot ( xs , intercept + slope * xs , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Least-squares line, order level" ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (share of list price)" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Order profit ratio" ) ax2 . scatter ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "residual" ], s = 6 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#1baf7a" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Residuals: is a straight line the right shape?" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (share of list price)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Residual (profit ratio)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Slope: -1.855 profit ratio per 1.0 of discount = -18.6 percentage points of profit ratio per 10 points of discount Intercept: 0.403 (predicted profit ratio for an order with no discount) R²: 0.745 Order discounts observed: 0.0 to 0.8 Here the intercept means something: an order with no discount is inside the data. Write it down Complete in your evidence log: "Across all orders placed 2023–2025, each extra 10 points of order discount was associated with a profit ratio about ___ percentage points lower (R² = ___). The residual plot shows ___." Then add one limitation . Ideas: discounts are not given at random (some product groups are discounted far more often, so product mix may be a confounder, see I5); the residuals show the line does not fit equally well everywhere; the data is a fictitious sample. Independent tasks ¶ I1 (Core): One campaign — fit and interpret a line ¶ Load the advertising data. Days with zero spend cannot show what spend buys, so we keep only days with spend above zero. mkt = load_marketing ( "marketing_daily.csv" ) paid = mkt [ mkt [ "spend" ] > 0 ] . copy () print ( "Rows:" , len ( mkt ), "| rows with spend > 0:" , len ( paid )) paid . groupby ([ "channel" , "campaign_id" ])[ "date" ] . count () . rename ( "paid days" ) Rows: 2555 | rows with spend > 0: 2516 channel campaign_id Display DISP-01 362 Email EML-01 353 Search SRCH-01 360 SRCH-02 359 Social SOC-01 360 SOC-02 359 Video VID-01 363 Name: paid days, dtype: int64 The cell below fits daily attributed revenue against daily spend for one campaign and one period . If not, what is wrong (a curve, one outlier, one high-leverage point)? Which residual plot tells you most clearly? C2 (Challenge): "Double the budget" ¶ A colleague posts: "I ran a regression on SRCH-01 for the whole of 2025. Every extra 1 unit of spend brings in more than ten units of revenue. Let's double the current daily budget: that's free money." Reproduce the colleague's number, then look at what they did not check. Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # The colleague's analysis, plus some checks they did not make. # 1. Find at least three problems with the claim. Use the lecture's Part 7 and Part 8. # 2. Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate and states one limitation. search = paid [ paid [ "campaign_id" ] == "SRCH-01" ] full_slope , full_intercept = np . polyfit ( search [ "spend" ], search [ "attributed_revenue" ], 1 ) jan_sep = search [ search [ "date" ] . dt . month <= 9 ] js_slope , _ = np . polyfit ( jan_sep [ "spend" ], jan_sep [ "attributed_revenue" ], 1 ) print ( f "Colleague's slope, all of 2025: { full_slope : .2f } " ) print ( f "Same campaign, January–September: { js_slope : .2f } " ) current = search . loc [ search [ "date" ] . dt . month == 12 , "spend" ] . mean () print ( f "Current daily budget (December average): { current : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Doubled current daily budget: { 2 * current : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Highest daily spend ever seen: { search [ 'spend' ] . max () : ,.0f } " ) print ( "Average daily spend by quarter:" ) print ( search . groupby ( search [ "date" ] . dt . quarter )[ "spend" ] . mean () . round ( 0 ) . to_string ()) Colleague's slope, all of 2025: 13.31 Same campaign, January–September: 5.62 Current daily budget (December average): 1,475 Doubled current daily budget: 2,951 Highest daily spend ever seen: 2,150 Average daily spend by quarter: date 1 926.00 2 885.00 3 913.00 4 1,306.00 Hint Think about what else changed in the months with the highest spend, whether the doubled budget was ever observed , and whether "brings in" is a claim the data can support. Validation checklist ¶ Every scatter plot has a title, labelled axes and units. Profit ratios are ratios of sums at the level of the question (line, discount level, order). Order-level discount is weighted by Sales, and the level is stated in the sentence. Days with zero spend were excluded from the regressions, and you said so. Every slope is written with "associated with", its units, the period and the observed x-range. Every regression has a residual plot, and you described any pattern. Any prediction outside the observed range is labelled as extrapolation. No sentence claims that discounts or spend cause the change. Exit ticket ¶ Why did the line-level and order-level discount pictures look different? What does the slope of your I1 regression mean in one sentence, with units? What did the residual plot tell you that the R² did not? Why is "double the budget" an extrapolation? Name one confounder for spend and revenue, and one for discount and profit ratio. Evidence to keep ¶ Line-level and order-level scatter plots with your explanation of the difference (G1–G4) Order-level slope sentence with one limitation (G5) Interpreted regression with one stated limitation : I1 sentence, residual plot, one in-range prediction (I1–I3) Campaign comparison and what pooling hides (I4, if attempted) Anscombe notes and the corrected "double the budget" message (C1, C2, if attempted) Record in your evidence log the data versions, the period and campaign you used, and which days you excluded. docs.title: Session 8 lab: Discount, profit and advertising spend

docs.text: Two managers have questions: Commercial lead: "Do our discounts eat into profit? How strongly?" Marketing lead: "If one unit of search advertising brings in several units of revenue, why don't we double the budget?" Both questions are about two measures moving together . Your job is to measure the relationship honestly, and to say what it does not prove. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. marketing_daily.csv is synthetic : generated for this course, describing no real company, brand or platform. One row per day of 2025 × paid campaign. Amounts are in neutral currency units .

docs.text: Draw a scatter plot and compute Pearson and Spearman correlation. Aggregate to the right level before computing a ratio, and explain why the level changes the picture. Fit a straight line with np.polyfit , and state its slope, R² and the range of the data in business language. Read a residual plot and spot a missing factor. Flag predictions that are extrapolations. Explain why a regression slope from past data is an association, not the effect of spending more. Evidence you keep: an interpreted regression with one stated limitation (I1–I3), plus your line-versus-order explanation (G4).

docs.title: G2 (Core): Profit ratio by discount level

docs.text: A manager thinks in orders , not lines. An order can mix discounted and full-price lines. To get one point per order: Add up each order's Sales and Profit. Order profit ratio = order Profit ÷ order Sales (a ratio of sums). Order discount = Sales-weighted average of its lines' discounts: sum of (discount × Sales) ÷ sum of Sales . A big discounted line counts more than a small one. df [ "discount_x_sales" ] = df [ "discount" ] * df [ "sales" ] orders = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . agg ( lines = ( "row_id" , "count" ), sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), discount_x_sales = ( "discount_x_sales" , "sum" ), ) orders [ "order_discount" ] = orders [ "discount_x_sales" ] / orders [ "sales" ] orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] = orders [ "profit" ] / orders [ "sales" ] print ( "Orders:" , len ( orders ), "| orders with more than one line:" , ( orders [ "lines" ] > 1 ) . sum ()) ax = orders . plot . scatter ( x = "order_discount" , y = "order_profit_ratio" , s = 8 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "Orders: the same direction, fewer stripes" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (Sales-weighted, share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Order profit ratio (Profit ÷ Sales)" ) plt . show () Orders: 3388 | orders with more than one line: 1691

docs.text: Put the two levels side by side. def describe_level ( x , y ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( x , y , 1 ) return { "points" : len ( x ), "Pearson r" : x . corr ( y ), "Spearman" : x . rank () . corr ( y . rank ()), "slope" : slope , "mean of ratios" : y . mean (), } levels = pd . DataFrame ({ "line level" : describe_level ( df [ "discount" ], df [ "line_profit_ratio" ]), "order level" : describe_level ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ]), }) . T . astype ({ "points" : int }) print ( "Profit ratio of all Sales (total Profit ÷ total Sales):" , round ( df [ "profit" ] . sum () / df [ "sales" ] . sum (), 3 )) with pd . option_context ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.3f} " . format ): display ( levels ) Profit ratio of all Sales (total Profit ÷ total Sales): 0.124 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } points Pearson r Spearman slope mean of ratios line level 6815 -0.865 -0.650 -1.923 0.125 order level 3388 -0.863 -0.696 -1.855 0.116 Read the output above and discuss in pairs: Number of points. An order with five lines is five dots at line level and one dot at order level. Which orders count more in the line picture? Mixing. At order level, a discounted line and a full-price line are blended into one point. What happens to the stripes, and to the most extreme negative ratios? Averages. Compare the two "mean of ratios" values with the profit ratio of all Sales printed above. Which number should a report use as the profit ratio? Why can an average of ratios not be trusted, even when it happens to land close? The question. "Do discounted products lose money?" is a line question. "Do orders with deeper discounts lose money?" is an order question. Which did the commercial lead ask? Rule Decide the level of the question first, aggregate to that level, then compute ratios and correlations. State the level in every chart title and sentence.

docs.text: A slope per one whole unit of discount (100 percentage points) is hard to picture, so we also state it per 10 points. slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ], 1 ) orders [ "predicted" ] = intercept + slope * orders [ "order_discount" ] orders [ "residual" ] = orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] - orders [ "predicted" ] r_squared = 1 - ( orders [ "residual" ] ** 2 ) . sum () / (( orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] - orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ] . mean ()) ** 2 ) . sum () print ( f "Slope: { slope : .3f } profit ratio per 1.0 of discount " f "= { slope * 0.1 * 100 : +.1f } percentage points of profit ratio per 10 points of discount" ) print ( f "Intercept: { intercept : .3f } (predicted profit ratio for an order with no discount)" ) print ( f "R²: { r_squared : .3f } " ) print ( "Order discounts observed:" , round ( orders [ "order_discount" ] . min (), 2 ), "to" , round ( orders [ "order_discount" ] . max (), 2 )) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) xs = np . linspace ( 0 , orders [ "order_discount" ] . max (), 50 ) ax1 . scatter ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "order_profit_ratio" ], s = 6 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax1 . plot ( xs , intercept + slope * xs , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Least-squares line, order level" ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (share of list price)" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Order profit ratio" ) ax2 . scatter ( orders [ "order_discount" ], orders [ "residual" ], s = 6 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "#1baf7a" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Residuals: is a straight line the right shape?" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Order discount (share of list price)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Residual (profit ratio)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Slope: -1.855 profit ratio per 1.0 of discount = -18.6 percentage points of profit ratio per 10 points of discount Intercept: 0.403 (predicted profit ratio for an order with no discount) R²: 0.745 Order discounts observed: 0.0 to 0.8 Here the intercept means something: an order with no discount is inside the data. Write it down Complete in your evidence log: "Across all orders placed 2023–2025, each extra 10 points of order discount was associated with a profit ratio about ___ percentage points lower (R² = ___). The residual plot shows ___." Then add one limitation . Ideas: discounts are not given at random (some product groups are discounted far more often, so product mix may be a confounder, see I5); the residuals show the line does not fit equally well everywhere; the data is a fictitious sample.

Compare the discount–profit relationship within each group. Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell.
