df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. # Marketing data setup (synthetic). Run this cell first. # Downloads the course's synthetic marketing data from GitHub and checks it is the exact version this course uses. import hashlib import io import os import urllib.request import pandas as pd MARKETING_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Aayush181509/AnalyticsLecture/main/data/synthetic/marketing-v1/" MARKETING_SHA256 = { "marketing_daily.csv" : "1cbfc8e1c91ae72d18364b2d13bdf6db513c4aec28c339ef8b91f87a60dc0a07" , "ab_test.csv" : "41a3662997111b66d7ab1eb899f4b32e26bd64c66284ce881db6b8a7300ad47f" , } MARKETING_DIR = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_MARKETING_DIR" , "" ) def load_marketing ( name ): """Load one marketing-v1 file: 'marketing_daily.csv' or 'ab_test.csv'.""" if MARKETING_DIR : with open ( os . path . join ( MARKETING_DIR , name ), "rb" ) as f : data = f . read () else : data = urllib . request . urlopen ( MARKETING_URL + name ) . read () if hashlib . sha256 ( data ) . hexdigest () != MARKETING_SHA256 [ name ]: print ( "WARNING: this file differs from the course version. Ask your facilitator." ) return pd . read_csv ( io . BytesIO ( data ), parse_dates = [ "date" ]) print ( "Marketing setup complete." ) Marketing setup complete. import math import numpy as np df = load_orders () print ( "Order lines:" , len ( df ), "| different orders:" , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Order lines: 6815 | different orders: 3388 Average order value ( AOV ) is about orders , but each row is an order line . So we add up the lines of each order first. The last line of output shows what goes wrong if you skip this step. orders = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "sales" ] . sum () values = orders . to_numpy () print ( f "Orders: { len ( values ) } " ) print ( f "AOV, all orders: { values . mean () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Median order value: { np . median ( values ) : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Average LINE value: { df [ 'sales' ] . mean () : ,.2f } <- wrong grain for AOV" ) Orders: 3388 AOV, all orders: 466.64 Median order value: 151.46 Average LINE value: 231.98 <- wrong grain for AOV A game we play in this lab As in the lecture, we pretend these orders are the whole population of orders, so values.mean() is the true AOV . In real work you rarely see everything. Pretending lets us check whether our methods find the truth. G2 (Core): One sample, one answer ¶ Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. How far is the sample AOV from the true AOV? # 2. Change seed to 2, then 3. Does the sample AOV change? Why? # 3. Change sample_size to 25, then 400. Is the sampling error usually bigger or smaller? seed = 1 sample_size = 100 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) sample = rng . choice ( values , size = sample_size , replace = False ) true_aov = values . mean () print ( f "Sample of { sample_size } orders, AOV: { sample . mean () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "True AOV: { true_aov : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Sampling error: { sample . mean () - true_aov : +,.2f } " ) Sample of 100 orders, AOV: 542.07 True AOV: 466.64 Sampling error: +75.43 G3 (Core): Watch the sampling distribution form ¶ Now repeat G2 a thousand times and keep every sample's AOV. The histogram of those AOVs is the sampling distribution . Its spread is the standard error (SE) . Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. Where is the histogram centred? How does its shape compare with single orders? # 2. Compare "SE by simulation" with "SD / sqrt(n)". Are they close? # 3. Change sample_size to 25, then 400. What happens to the width of the histogram and to the SE? sample_size = 100 repeats = 1000 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 1 ) sample_aovs = np . array ([ rng . choice ( values , size = sample_size , replace = False ) . mean () for _ in range ( repeats )]) ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( sample_aovs , bins = 40 ) ax . axvline ( true_aov , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV" ) ax . set_title ( f "AOVs of { repeats : , } random samples of { sample_size } orders" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Sample AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of samples" ) ax . legend () plt . show () low , high = np . percentile ( sample_aovs , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) print ( f "Average of the sample AOVs: { sample_aovs . mean () : ,.2f } (true AOV { true_aov : ,.2f } )" ) print ( f "Middle 95% of sample AOVs: { low : ,.0f } to { high : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "SE by simulation: { sample_aovs . std () : ,.1f } " ) print ( f "SD / sqrt(n): { values . std () / math . sqrt ( sample_size ) : ,.1f } " ) Average of the sample AOVs: 468.62 (true AOV 466.64) Middle 95% of sample AOVs: 319 to 714 SE by simulation: 99.5 SD / sqrt(n): 97.5 What do you notice? Write down what happened to the SE when you made the sample four times bigger (from 25 to 100, or 100 to 400). Does that match the √n rule from the lecture? G4 (Core): Bootstrap a 95% confidence interval for AOV ¶ In real work you have one sample. Here it is 200 orders. The bootstrap resamples that sample , with replacement, thousands of times, and the middle 95% of the resampled AOVs is the interval. Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. Does each interval contain the true AOV? Are the two intervals close? # 2. Change seed to 3, 6, 7, 8 and 9. Note each time whether the bootstrap interval contains the true AOV. # 3. Change sample_size to 50. What happens to the width of the intervals? seed = 2 sample_size = 200 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) my_sample = rng . choice ( values , size = sample_size , replace = False ) boot_aovs = np . array ([ rng . choice ( my_sample , size = sample_size , replace = True ) . mean () for _ in range ( 5000 )]) boot_low , boot_high = np . percentile ( boot_aovs , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) se = my_sample . std ( ddof = 1 ) / math . sqrt ( sample_size ) formula_low , formula_high = my_sample . mean () - 1.96 * se , my_sample . mean () + 1.96 * se ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( boot_aovs , bins = 50 ) ax . axvline ( boot_low , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Bootstrap 95 % i nterval" ) ax . axvline ( boot_high , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . axvline ( true_aov , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV (normally unknown)" ) ax . set_title ( f "Bootstrap AOVs from one sample of { sample_size } orders" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Bootstrap AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bootstrap samples" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Sample AOV: { my_sample . mean () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI: { boot_low : ,.2f } to { boot_high : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Formula 95% CI: { formula_low : ,.2f } to { formula_high : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Contains true AOV? bootstrap { boot_low <= true_aov <= boot_high } , formula { formula_low <= true_aov <= formula_high } " ) Sample AOV: 495.68 Bootstrap 95% CI: 388.22 to 615.58 Formula 95% CI: 383.40 to 607.96 Contains true AOV? bootstrap True, formula True Over many seeds, about 95% of intervals should contain the true AOV (a little less with these very skewed order values, as the lecture showed). Any single interval may be one of the misses, and you cannot tell from inside it. G5 (Core): Explain the interval to the retail lead ¶ Write two sentences in your evidence log, using your output from G4 with seed = 2 : "From a random sample of ___ orders, the average order value is ___ source monetary units. We are 95% confident that the average across all orders is between ___ and ___; a larger sample would narrow this range." Check your sentence against these rules: It says orders , not lines or customers. It gives the range, not just the single number. It does not say "95% of orders are between…" or "there is a 95% probability…". It states the units. Look at the smallest and largest daily share in B. Is any day far from 50%? # 3. If B had received many more desktop visitors, B could look better just because of its device mix. Random assignment should make the mix similar; the balance check confirms it did. I2 (Core): Conversion, revenue per visitor and lift ¶ results = ab . groupby ( "variant" ) . agg ( visitors = ( "visitor_id" , "count" ), buyers = ( "converted" , "sum" ), revenue = ( "revenue" , "sum" ), ) results [ "conversion_rate" ] = results [ "buyers" ] / results [ "visitors" ] results [ "revenue_per_visitor" ] = results [ "revenue" ] / results [ "visitors" ] for measure in [ "conversion_rate" , "revenue_per_visitor" ]: a , b = results . loc [ "A" , measure ], results . loc [ "B" , measure ] unit = "percentage points" if measure == "conversion_rate" else "currency units per visitor" absolute = ( b - a ) * 100 if measure == "conversion_rate" else b - a print ( f " { measure } : absolute lift { absolute : +.2f } { unit } | relative lift { ( b - a ) / a : +.1% } " ) results . assign ( revenue = results [ "revenue" ] . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ), conversion_rate = results [ "conversion_rate" ] . map ( " {:.2%} " . format ), revenue_per_visitor = results [ "revenue_per_visitor" ] . map ( " {:.2f} " . format ), ) conversion_rate: absolute lift +0.50 percentage points | relative lift +15.8% revenue_per_visitor: absolute lift +0.41 currency units per visitor | relative lift +13.4% .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitors buyers revenue conversion_rate revenue_per_visitor variant A 29873 940 92,066 3.15% 3.08 B 30127 1098 105,280 3.64% 3.49 Revenue per visitor divides by all visitors, including the zeros of those who did not buy. It combines "more people buy" with "buyers spend more or less". I3 (Core): How sure are we? A confidence interval for the lift ¶ The function below bootstraps the difference B − A in the average of any column: resample visitors within each group, recompute both averages, repeat. For a 0/1 column like converted , the average is the conversion rate. def bootstrap_diff ( data , column , reps = 2000 , seed = 1 ): """95% bootstrap percentile interval for mean(B) - mean(A) of one column.""" rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) a = data . loc [ data [ "variant" ] == "A" , column ] . to_numpy () b = data . loc [ data [ "variant" ] == "B" , column ] . to_numpy () diffs = np . array ([ rng . choice ( b , size = len ( b )) . mean () - rng . choice ( a , size = len ( a )) . mean () for _ in range ( reps )]) return b . mean () - a . mean (), np . percentile ( diffs , 2.5 ), np . percentile ( diffs , 97.5 ) def compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors_a , buyers_b , visitors_b ): """Lift (B - A), its 95% interval and a two-sided p-value, by the normal formula.""" rate_a , rate_b = buyers_a / visitors_a , buyers_b / visitors_b lift = rate_b - rate_a se = math . sqrt ( rate_a * ( 1 - rate_a ) / visitors_a + rate_b * ( 1 - rate_b ) / visitors_b ) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) se_null = math . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) z = lift / se_null return { "lift" : lift , "low" : lift - 1.96 * se , "high" : lift + 1.96 * se , "p_value" : math . erfc ( abs ( z ) / math . sqrt ( 2 ))} Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. Does the interval include zero? What is the smallest lift that is still plausible? # 2. Change seed to 2. Does the bootstrap interval move much? # 3. Are the bootstrap and formula intervals close? Why would you expect that here? seed = 1 lift , low , high = bootstrap_diff ( ab , "converted" , seed = seed ) formula = compare_rates ( results . loc [ "A" , "buyers" ], results . loc [ "A" , "visitors" ], results . loc [ "B" , "buyers" ], results . loc [ "B" , "visitors" ]) print ( f "Lift in conversion: { lift * 100 : +.2f } percentage points" ) print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI: { low * 100 : +.2f } to { high * 100 : +.2f } points" ) print ( f "Formula 95% CI: { formula [ 'low' ] * 100 : +.2f } to { formula [ 'high' ] * 100 : +.2f } points" ) Lift in conversion: +0.50 percentage points Bootstrap 95% CI: +0.20 to +0.77 points Formula 95% CI: +0.21 to +0.79 points I4 (Core): Could chance explain it? A permutation p-value ¶ If the new page made no difference, the A/B labels would be arbitrary. Shuffle them, recompute the lift, and count how often a shuffled lift is at least as large (either direction) as the real one. def permutation_p ( data , column , reps = 5000 , seed = 1 ): """Two-sided permutation p-value for mean(B) - mean(A) of one column.""" rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) values = data [ column ] . to_numpy () is_b = ( data [ "variant" ] == "B" ) . to_numpy () observed = values [ is_b ] . mean () - values [ ~ is_b ] . mean () shuffled = np . empty ( reps ) for i in range ( reps ): labels = rng . permutation ( is_b ) shuffled [ i ] = values [ labels ] . mean () - values [ ~ labels ] . mean () extreme = int (( np . abs ( shuffled ) >= abs ( observed )) . sum ()) return extreme , shuffled Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. How many shuffles reached the real lift? What is the p-value? # 2. Change reps to 1000. Does the conclusion change? Why is the p-value rougher with fewer shuffles? # 3. Compare with the formula p-value. Does that show the page "does nothing on desktop"? Does the desktop interval also include the mobile lift? What can you honestly say? Compare the number of significant device × day slices with what A/A tests produce by chance. Is "the desktop effect comes and goes" a finding? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate. Say what a follow-up test would need to show to support a mobile-only roll-out. Hint "Not significant" means "not shown", not "shown to be zero". A subgroup has fewer visitors, so its interval is wider. And 56 slices give noise 56 chances. Validation checklist ¶ AOV was computed on orders (lines added up per order), not on lines. The sampling distribution is centred near the true AOV, and its SE roughly matches SD ÷ √n. The bootstrap and formula intervals were both reported, with units, and read correctly. The A/B test has one row per visitor, about half in each group, and a similar device mix in A and B. Conversion and revenue per visitor divide by all visitors in the group. Lifts state whether they are percentage points or percent . Every lift has a 95% interval; the p-value is explained in plain words. Subgroup and slice results are labelled as exploratory, with their own intervals. Exit ticket ¶ Why must you add up order lines before computing average order value? What does a 95% confidence interval for AOV mean, in one sentence a manager would understand? Your sample becomes four times bigger. What happens to the standard error? The conversion lift is +0.5 percentage points with a 95% interval that excludes zero. Name one more thing you would check before recommending a roll-out. Why does checking a test every day and stopping at the first p < 0.05 produce too many false winners? docs.text: Put an honest range around an average order value, then analyse a checkout-page experiment: check the randomisation, measure the lift, say how sure you are, and explain it to a manager without overselling it. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive .
docs.title: Session 9 lab: How sure are we?

docs.text: Two managers each want a number they can act on: Retail lead: "What is our average order value? I need a figure I can plan with, and I need to know how far off it might be." Marketing lead: "We tested a new checkout page for four weeks. Did it work, by how much, and should we roll it out?" A single number answers neither question honestly. Both need a range and a plain-language explanation of how sure we are. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales are in the file's own source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. ab_test.csv is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: one row per visitor, randomly assigned to the current checkout page ( A , control) or the new one ( B , treatment) over 28 days. Revenue is in neutral currency units .

Bootstrap a 95% confidence interval and compare it with the formula interval. Check that an A/B test was randomised fairly. Measure conversion, revenue per visitor and lift, with an interval and a permutation p-value. Explain a confidence interval and an A/B result to a manager in plain language. Show why peeking and slicing produce false winners. Evidence you keep: a CI for AOV and an A/B result, each explained in plain language for a manager.

The bootstrap resamples that sample , with replacement, thousands of times, and the middle 95% of the resampled AOVs is the interval. Note each time whether the bootstrap interval contains the true AOV. # 3. Change sample_size to 50. What happens to the width of the intervals? seed = 2 sample_size = 200 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) my_sample = rng . choice ( values , size = sample_size , replace = False ) boot_aovs = np . array ([ rng . choice ( my_sample , size = sample_size , replace = True ) . mean () for _ in range ( 5000 )]) boot_low , boot_high = np . percentile ( boot_aovs , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) se = my_sample . std ( ddof = 1 ) / math . sqrt ( sample_size ) formula_low , formula_high = my_sample . mean () - 1.96 * se , my_sample . mean () + 1.96 * se ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( boot_aovs , bins = 50 ) ax . axvline ( boot_low , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Bootstrap 95 % i nterval" ) ax . axvline ( boot_high , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . axvline ( true_aov , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV (normally unknown)" ) ax . set_title ( f "Bootstrap AOVs from one sample of { sample_size } orders" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Bootstrap AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bootstrap samples" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Sample AOV: { my_sample . mean () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI: { boot_low : ,.2f } to { boot_high : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Formula 95% CI: { formula_low : ,.2f } to { formula_high : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Contains true AOV? bootstrap { boot_low <= true_aov <= boot_high } , formula { formula_low <= true_aov <= formula_high } " ) Sample AOV: 495.68 Bootstrap 95% CI: 388.22 to 615.58 Formula 95% CI: 383.40 to 607.96 Contains true AOV? bootstrap True, formula True Over many seeds, about 95% of intervals should contain the true AOV (a little less with these very skewed order values, as the lecture showed). Any single interval may be one of the misses, and you cannot tell from inside it.

docs.text: results = ab . groupby ( "variant" ) . agg ( visitors = ( "visitor_id" , "count" ), buyers = ( "converted" , "sum" ), revenue = ( "revenue" , "sum" ), ) results [ "conversion_rate" ] = results [ "buyers" ] / results [ "visitors" ] results [ "revenue_per_visitor" ] = results [ "revenue" ] / results [ "visitors" ] for measure in [ "conversion_rate" , "revenue_per_visitor" ]: a , b = results . loc [ "A" , measure ], results . loc [ "B" , measure ] unit = "percentage points" if measure == "conversion_rate" else "currency units per visitor" absolute = ( b - a ) * 100 if measure == "conversion_rate" else b - a print ( f " { measure } : absolute lift { absolute : +.2f } { unit } | relative lift { ( b - a ) / a : +.1% } " ) results . assign ( revenue = results [ "revenue" ] . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ), conversion_rate = results [ "conversion_rate" ] . map ( " {:.2%} " . format ), revenue_per_visitor = results [ "revenue_per_visitor" ] . map ( " {:.2f} " . format ), ) conversion_rate: absolute lift +0.50 percentage points | relative lift +15.8% revenue_per_visitor: absolute lift +0.41 currency units per visitor | relative lift +13.4% .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitors buyers revenue conversion_rate revenue_per_visitor variant A 29873 940 92,066 3.15% 3.08 B 30127 1098 105,280 3.64% 3.49 Revenue per visitor divides by all visitors, including the zeros of those who did not buy. docs.text: The function below bootstraps the difference B − A in the average of any column: resample visitors within each group, recompute both averages, repeat. For a 0/1 column like converted , the average is the conversion rate. def bootstrap_diff ( data , column , reps = 2000 , seed = 1 ): """95% bootstrap percentile interval for mean(B) - mean(A) of one column.""" rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) a = data . loc [ data [ "variant" ] == "A" , column ] . to_numpy () b = data . loc [ data [ "variant" ] == "B" , column ] . to_numpy () diffs = np . array ([ rng . choice ( b , size = len ( b )) . mean () - rng . choice ( a , size = len ( a )) . mean () for _ in range ( reps )]) return b . mean () - a . mean (), np . percentile ( diffs , 2.5 ), np . percentile ( diffs , 97.5 ) def compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors_a , buyers_b , visitors_b ): """Lift (B - A), its 95% interval and a two-sided p-value, by the normal formula.""" rate_a , rate_b = buyers_a / visitors_a , buyers_b / visitors_b lift = rate_b - rate_a se = math . sqrt ( rate_a * ( 1 - rate_a ) / visitors_a + rate_b * ( 1 - rate_b ) / visitors_b ) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) se_null = math . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) z = lift / se_null return { "lift" : lift , "low" : lift - 1.96 * se , "high" : lift + 1.96 * se , "p_value" : math . erfc ( abs ( z ) / math . sqrt ( 2 ))} Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. Does the interval include zero? What is the smallest lift that is still plausible? # 2. Change seed to 2. Does the bootstrap interval move much? # 3. Are the bootstrap and formula intervals close? Why would you expect that here? seed = 1 lift , low , high = bootstrap_diff ( ab , "converted" , seed = seed ) formula = compare_rates ( results . loc [ "A" , "buyers" ], results . loc [ "A" , "visitors" ], results . loc [ "B" , "buyers" ], results . loc [ "B" , "visitors" ]) print ( f "Lift in conversion: { lift * 100 : +.2f } percentage points" ) print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI: { low * 100 : +.2f } to { high * 100 : +.2f } points" ) print ( f "Formula 95% CI: { formula [ 'low' ] * 100 : +.2f } to { formula [ 'high' ] * 100 : +.2f } points" ) Lift in conversion: +0.50 percentage points Bootstrap 95% CI: +0.20 to +0.77 points Formula 95% CI: +0.21 to +0.79 points
docs.title: I3 (Core): How sure are we? A confidence interval for the lift

docs.text: If the new page made no difference, the A/B labels would be arbitrary. Shuffle them, recompute the lift, and count how often a shuffled lift is at least as large (either direction) as the real one. def permutation_p ( data , column , reps = 5000 , seed = 1 ): """Two-sided permutation p-value for mean(B) - mean(A) of one column.""" rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) values = data [ column ] . to_numpy () is_b = ( data [ "variant" ] == "B" ) . to_numpy () observed = values [ is_b ] . mean () - values [ ~ is_b ] . mean () shuffled = np . empty ( reps ) for i in range ( reps ): labels = rng . permutation ( is_b ) shuffled [ i ] = values [ labels ] . mean () - values [ ~ labels ] . mean () extreme = int (( np . abs ( shuffled ) >= abs ( observed )) . sum ()) return extreme , shuffled Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. How many shuffles reached the real lift? What is the p-value? # 2. Change reps to 1000. Does the conclusion change? Why is the p-value rougher with fewer shuffles? # 3. Compare with the formula p-value. Do they tell the same story? reps = 5000 extreme , shuffled = permutation_p ( ab , "converted" , reps = reps ) ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( shuffled * 100 , bins = 50 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Shuffled labels" ) ax . axvline ( lift * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Observed lift" ) ax . set_title ( "Lifts produced by chance alone, compared with the real lift" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Lift in conversion (percentage points)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of shuffles" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Shuffles at least as extreme: { extreme } of { reps } " ) print ( f "Permutation p-value: { extreme / reps : .4f } " + ( " (below 1 in " + str ( reps ) + ")" if extreme == 0 else "" )) print ( f "Formula p-value: { formula [ 'p_value' ] : .4f } " ) Shuffles at least as extreme: 1 of 5000 Permutation p-value: 0.0002 Formula p-value: 0.0008
docs.title: I4 (Core): Could chance explain it? A permutation p-value

docs.text: Write three sentences for the marketing lead, using your outputs from I1–I4: What happened , in business units: conversion on A and B, and the lift in percentage points (and, if you like, extra buyers per 10,000 visitors). How sure we are : the 95% interval for the lift, and what the p-value says in plain words ("a gap this large would be very unlikely if the page made no difference"). What it does not tell us : for example, whether the lift is worth the cost of the new page, or whether it holds after the test period. Avoid these phrases "There is a 99.9% chance B is better." "The p-value proves the page works." "B increased conversion by 16%" (without saying it is a relative lift). "Statistically significant, so we must roll it out."

DataFrame ( running ) . set_index ( "date" ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 6 ), sharex = True ) ax1 . plot ( running . index , running [ "lift (points)" ], marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax1 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Running lift, using all visitors up to each day" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Lift (points)" ) ax2 . plot ( running . index , running [ "p_value" ], marker = "o" , markersize = 3 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0.05 , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 0.8 , label = "p = 0.05" ) ax2 . set_title ( "Running p-value" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "p-value" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Test day" ) ax2 . legend () fig . tight_layout () plt . show () first = running [ running [ "p_value" ] < 0.05 ] print ( "First day with p below 0.05:" , first . index [ 0 ] . date () if len ( first ) else "none" ) First day with p below 0.05: 2025-03-16 The real test has a genuine effect built in, so the peeker gets the right direction here. The problem is the rule . To see it, run A/A tests : shuffle the variant labels so there is no real difference, and count how often the peeker's rule still declares a winner. Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell. What share of A/A tests produce a false winner when checked once at the end? When checked daily? # 2. Change check_every to 7 (a weekly check). What happens to the false-winner share? # 3. Explain to the colleague, in two sentences, why stopping at the first significant day misleads. check_every = 1 aa_tests = 500 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 1 ) day = ( ab [ "date" ] - ab [ "date" ] . min ()) . dt . days . to_numpy () converted = ab [ "converted" ] . to_numpy () is_b = ( ab [ "variant" ] == "B" ) . to_numpy () looks = np . arange ( check_every - 1 , day . max () + 1 , check_every ) def running_z ( labels ): vb = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], minlength = day . max () + 1 )) va = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], minlength = day . max () + 1 )) bb = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], weights = converted [ labels ], minlength = day . max () + 1 )) ba = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], weights = converted [ ~ labels ], minlength = day . max () + 1 )) pooled = ( ba + bb ) / ( va + vb ) return ( bb / vb - ba / va ) / np . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / va + 1 / vb )) z = np . array ([ running_z ( rng . permutation ( is_b )) for _ in range ( aa_tests )]) print ( f "Looks per test: { len ( looks ) } " ) print ( f "False winners, one look at the end: { ( np . abs ( z [:, - 1 ]) > 1.96 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "False winners, stop at first p below 0.05: { ( np . abs ( z [:, looks ]) > 1.96 ) . any ( axis = 1 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) Looks per test: 28 False winners, one look at the end: 4.8% False winners, stop at first p below 0.05: 26.4% Hint A 5% false-alarm rate is a promise about one look. Every extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line. Also think about the size of the lift on the day a peeker stops: is it more likely to be too big or too small?

docs.text: Session 9 lecture: Sampling, uncertainty and experiments ¶ Almost every number an analyst reports comes from a sample, and a different sample would have given a slightly different number. This lecture shows how big that wobble is, how to put an honest range around an estimate, and how to read an A/B test without fooling yourself or your manager. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 8 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. The correlation between weekly advertising spend and weekly sales is strongly positive. Say what this tells you, and one thing it does not tell you. A regression of revenue on advertising spend has a slope of 4. Say in plain words what the slope means, with units. Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise and fall together. Why might that be, and what is the general lesson? A correlation is close to zero. Does that prove the two measures are unrelated? Give a reason. Name one thing you should always do before calculating a correlation or fitting a line. What you will be able to explain ¶ The difference between a population and a sample , and why every sample has sampling error . What a sampling distribution is, using simulation rather than formulas. What the standard error measures, and why it shrinks with the square root of the sample size. How to build a confidence interval : by the bootstrap first, then by the formula estimate ± 1.96 × standard error . What " 95% confidence " does and does not mean. How an A/B test works: randomisation, control and treatment, conversion rate and lift . Part 4: Confidence intervals, bootstrap first ¶ Now the real situation: you have one sample of 200 orders and no access to the population. You want a range of plausible values for the true AOV: a confidence interval (CI) . The bootstrap gets one by simulation, using only the sample: Treat your sample as a stand-in for the population. Draw a new sample of the same size from your sample, with replacement (some orders appear twice, some not at all). Compute its AOV. Repeat thousands of times. The middle 95% of those AOVs (the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile) is the bootstrap 95% percentile interval . Predict, then reveal The bootstrap never sees a single order outside your sample. Part 5: What "95% confidence" means ¶ A 95% interval does not mean "there is a 95% chance the true AOV is in this interval". The true AOV is fixed; this interval either contains it or not. Part 9: A p-value by shuffling (permutation test) ¶ A p-value answers one narrow question: if the new page made no difference at all , how often would chance alone produce a gap at least as large as the one we saw? We can answer it by simulation. If the page did nothing, the A and B labels are meaningless, so shuffling them should not matter. We: Shuffle the variant labels across all visitors (keeping group sizes). Recompute the difference in conversion rates. Repeat thousands of times: this is the "no difference" world. The p-value is the share of shuffles with a gap at least as large (in either direction) as the real one. Predict, then reveal In the shuffled world, where will the differences be centred? How many of 5,000 shuffles do you expect to beat the real lift? converted = ab [ "converted" ] . to_numpy () is_b = ( ab [ "variant" ] == "B" ) . to_numpy () shuffled_lifts = np . empty ( 5000 ) for i in range ( 5000 ): labels = rng . permutation ( is_b ) shuffled_lifts [ i ] = converted [ labels ] . mean () - converted [ ~ labels ] . mean () extreme = ( np . abs ( shuffled_lifts ) >= abs ( lift )) . sum () ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( shuffled_lifts * 100 , bins = 50 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Shuffled labels (no real difference)" ) ax . axvline ( lift * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Observed lift" ) ax . axvline ( - lift * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = ":" ) ax . set_title ( "How big are lifts when the page makes no difference?" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Lift (percentage points)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of shuffles" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Shuffles with a gap at least as large: { extreme } of 5000" ) print ( f "Permutation p-value: about { max ( extreme , 1 ) / 5000 : .4f } " + ( " (an upper bound)" if extreme == 0 else "" )) Shuffles with a gap at least as large: 1 of 5000 Permutation p-value: about 0.0002 The grey histogram above is what pure chance produces. The observed lift sits far out in its tail, so very few shuffles (or none) reach it, and the p-value is small. The formula shortcut ¶ There is also a formula (the two-proportion z-test ). It divides the lift by its standard error under the "no difference" assumption and reads the p-value from the bell curve. We wrap it in a function to reuse later; you do not need to memorise it. def compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors_a , buyers_b , visitors_b ): """Lift (B - A), its 95% interval and a two-sided p-value, by the normal formula.""" rate_a , rate_b = buyers_a / visitors_a , buyers_b / visitors_b lift = rate_b - rate_a se = math . sqrt ( rate_a * ( 1 - rate_a ) / visitors_a + rate_b * ( 1 - rate_b ) / visitors_b ) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) # "no difference" rate se_null = math . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) z = lift / se_null p_value = math . erfc ( abs ( z ) / math . sqrt ( 2 )) # two-sided, from the bell curve return { "lift" : lift , "low" : lift - 1.96 * se , "high" : lift + 1.96 * se , "z" : z , "p_value" : p_value } result = compare_rates ( conv_a . sum (), n_a , conv_b . sum (), n_b ) print ( f "Formula p-value: { result [ 'p_value' ] : .4f } (z = { result [ 'z' ] : .2f } )" ) Formula p-value: 0.0008 (z = 3.37) Compare the two p-values in the outputs above. They tell the same story: chance is a poor explanation for the gap. When only a handful of shuffles reach the observed gap, the permutation p-value is rough (one more or one fewer extreme shuffle changes it a lot); more shuffles would sharpen it. With large samples like this one, the formula is a good shortcut. Part 10: Reading a p-value, and practical versus statistical significance ¶ In plain language: "If the new page truly made no difference, a gap this large would happen by chance in about p of tests." A small p-value (by convention below 0.05) means chance is a poor explanation; we call the result statistically significant . Common misreading Why it is wrong "p is the probability that the page has no effect." p assumes no effect and asks how surprising the data are. It is not the probability of the assumption. "1 − p is the probability that B is better." Same mistake in reverse. "p < 0.05, so the effect is big and important." p mixes effect size with sample size. A tiny effect in a huge sample gets a tiny p. "p > 0.05, so there is no difference." Not significant means not shown , not "shown to be zero". Look at the interval. "p = 0.049 is a success and p = 0.051 a failure." 0.05 is a convention, not a cliff. Report the interval and the p-value. Practical significance asks whether the effect is big enough to matter for the business. Statistical significance only asks whether chance is a poor explanation. The confidence interval answers both: its position says whether zero is plausible, its ends say how big the effect could be. Predict, then reveal Two made-up tests. Test 1 has 5 million visitors per group and a true lift of 0.1 percentage points. Test 2 has 1,000 visitors per group and a true lift of 1 percentage point. Which one will be "statistically significant"? Which one matters more for the business? sim = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 21 ) tests = { "Test 1" : ( 5_000_000 , 0.030 , 0.031 ), # visitors per group, true rate A, true rate B "Test 2" : ( 1_000 , 0.030 , 0.040 )} rows = {} for name , ( visitors , true_a , true_b ) in tests . items (): buyers_a , buyers_b = sim . binomial ( visitors , true_a ), sim . binomial ( visitors , true_b ) r = compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors , buyers_b , visitors ) rows [ name ] = { "visitors per group" : f " { visitors : , } " , "lift (points)" : f " { r [ 'lift' ] * 100 : +.2f } " , "95% CI (points)" : f " { r [ 'low' ] * 100 : +.2f } to { r [ 'high' ] * 100 : +.2f } " , "p-value" : f " { r [ 'p_value' ] : .4f } " if r [ "p_value" ] >= 0.0001 else "below 0.0001" } pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . T .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitors per group lift (points) 95% CI (points) p-value Test 1 5,000,000 +0.08 +0.06 to +0.10 below 0.0001 Test 2 1,000 +0.50 -1.03 to +2.03 0.5221 Read the table above. The huge test is clearly "significant", yet its lift is so small it may not pay for the change. The small test was built with a lift that would matter, but its interval is so wide that it cannot tell a worthwhile lift from zero, or even from a loss. Neither "significant" nor "not significant" is the whole story. Always report the interval, in the units the manager cares about. Check your understanding 8 Translate the checkout-page lift and its interval into "extra buyers per 10,000 visitors". Which number would you put in the headline for a manager, the p-value or this? Part 11: Peeking and multiple comparisons ¶ A 5% significance threshold means a false winner 5% of the time when there is no real effect , but only if you look once , at one result, decided in advance. Two everyday habits break that promise. Peeking ¶ A colleague checks the test every day and stops the first day the p-value dips below 0.05. To see what that does, we make an A/A test : we shuffle the variant labels in the real data, so there is no real difference by construction, then follow the running result day by day. Predict, then reveal In A/A tests with no real difference, what share would end with a "winner" if you checked only on the last day? And if you checked every day and stopped at the first significant day? day = ( ab [ "date" ] - ab [ "date" ] . min ()) . dt . days . to_numpy () n_days = day . max () + 1 def daily_z ( labels ): """Running z statistic after each day of the test, for given B labels.""" buyers_b = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], weights = converted [ labels ], minlength = n_days )) visitors_b = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], minlength = n_days )) buyers_a = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], weights = converted [ ~ labels ], minlength = n_days )) visitors_a = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], minlength = n_days )) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) se_null = np . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) return ( buyers_b / visitors_b - buyers_a / visitors_a ) / se_null aa_runs = np . array ([ daily_z ( rng . permutation ( is_b )) for _ in range ( 1000 )]) significant = np . abs ( aa_runs ) > 1.96 # |z| above 1.96 is the same as p below 0.05 print ( f "A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked once, on the last day: { significant [:, - 1 ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked every day: { significant . any ( axis = 1 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) ax = plt . gca () for run in aa_runs [: 40 ]: crosses = ( np . abs ( run ) > 1.96 ) . any () ax . plot ( range ( 1 , n_days + 1 ), run , color = "#2a78d6" if crosses else "#b8b6b0" , linewidth = 1.5 if crosses else 0.8 ) ax . axhline ( 1.96 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Significance threshold (p = 0.05)" ) ax . axhline ( - 1.96 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" ) ax . set_ylim ( - 3.5 , 3.5 ) ax . set_title ( "40 A/A tests: blue runs cross the threshold at least once by chance" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Day of the test" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Running z statistic (A/A, no real effect)" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked once, on the last day: 5.2% A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked every day: 27.1% Read the two shares above. Checked once, A/A tests produce a false winner about 5% of the time, as promised. Checked every day and stopped at the first dip below 0.05, the false-winner rate is several times higher, because a random walk that wanders long enough crosses the line by chance. Multiple comparisons ¶ Another colleague slices the test into 20 slices (2 devices × the first 10 days) and reports any slice where B "wins". Each slice has a 5% false-alarm chance, so with 20 slices a false alarm somewhere is likely: 1 − 0.95²⁰. slice_mask = day < 10 slice_key = day [ slice_mask ] * 2 + ( ab [ "device" ] . to_numpy ()[ slice_mask ] == "mobile" ) conv_s = converted [ slice_mask ] def slice_z ( labels ): """z statistic in each of the 20 device x day slices, for given B labels.""" lab = labels [ slice_mask ] vb = np . bincount ( slice_key [ lab ], minlength = 20 ) va = np . bincount ( slice_key [ ~ lab ], minlength = 20 ) bb = np . bincount ( slice_key [ lab ], weights = conv_s [ lab ], minlength = 20 ) ba = np . bincount ( slice_key [ ~ lab ], weights = conv_s [ ~ lab ], minlength = 20 ) pooled = ( ba + bb ) / ( va + vb ) se_null = np . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / va + 1 / vb )) return ( bb / vb - ba / va ) / se_null aa_slices = np . array ([ slice_z ( rng . permutation ( is_b )) for _ in range ( 1000 )]) print ( f "Chance of at least one false alarm in 20 slices, by the rule: { 1 - 0.95 ** 20 : .0% } " ) print ( f "Chance of at least one 'significant' slice, A/A simulation: { ( np . abs ( aa_slices ) > 1.96 ) . any ( axis = 1 ) . mean () : .0% } " ) Chance of at least one false alarm in 20 slices, by the rule: 64% Chance of at least one 'significant' slice, A/A simulation: 63% With no real effect at all, most A/A tests above still contain at least one "significant" slice. A slice that wins is a lead for a new test , not a finding. Rules that keep a test honest Before the test starts, write down the one primary measure , the sample size or duration , and the decision rule. Look at the result once , at the planned end. (There are methods for planned interim looks; they use stricter thresholds.) Treat subgroup and slice results as hypotheses . Name the few subgroups you care about in advance, and give each one its own interval. Report how many comparisons you made, not only the ones that "worked". Check your understanding 9 A team ran a test for three weeks, looked at 12 measures and found that "time on page" improved with p = 0.03. What would you ask before believing it? Part 12: Worked case — the checkout-page result for a manager ¶ We pull everything together into one result table for the manager: conversion rate (in %) and revenue per visitor (in currency units) for A and B, the difference B − A, and a 95% bootstrap interval for that difference ("CI low" to "CI high"). Then one printed sentence with the permutation p-value for conversion. rev_a = ab . loc [ ab [ "variant" ] == "A" , "revenue" ] . to_numpy () rev_b = ab . loc [ ab [ "variant" ] == "B" , "revenue" ] . to_numpy () boot_rpv = np . empty ( 2000 ) for i in range ( 2000 ): idx_a = rng . integers ( 0 , n_a , n_a ) # resample visitors, keeping each visitor's idx_b = rng . integers ( 0 , n_b , n_b ) # conversion and revenue together boot_rpv [ i ] = rev_b [ idx_b ] . mean () - rev_a [ idx_a ] . mean () summary = pd . DataFrame ({ "A" : [ rate_a * 100 , rev_a . mean ()], "B" : [ rate_b * 100 , rev_b . mean ()], "B − A" : [ lift * 100 , rev_b . mean () - rev_a . mean ()], "CI low" : [ lift_low * 100 , np . percentile ( boot_rpv , 2.5 )], "CI high" : [ lift_high * 100 , np . percentile ( boot_rpv , 97.5 )], }, index = [ "Conversion (%)" , "Revenue per visitor" ]) display ( summary . round ( 2 )) print ( f "The new checkout page converted { rate_b : .2% } of visitors against { rate_a : .2% } on the current page, " f "a lift of { lift * 100 : +.2f } percentage points (95% CI { lift_low * 100 : +.2f } to { lift_high * 100 : +.2f } ). " f "That is about { lift * 10000 : .0f } extra buyers per 10,000 visitors. " f "A gap this large would be very unlikely if the page made no difference (permutation p about { max ( extreme , 1 ) / 5000 : .4f } )." ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } A B B − A CI low CI high Conversion (%) 3.15 3.64 0.50 0.20 0.77 Revenue per visitor 3.08 3.49 0.41 0.09 0.74 The new checkout page converted 3.64% of visitors against 3.15% on the current page, a lift of +0.50 percentage points (95% CI +0.20 to +0.77). That is about 50 extra buyers per 10,000 visitors. A gap this large would be very unlikely if the page made no difference (permutation p about 0.0002). The printed sentence is the evidence a manager needs: what changed, by how much, how sure we are, and in business units. Before recommending a roll-out you would add cost (is the lift worth building and maintaining the page?), and note that this is one pre-planned measure checked once at the end of the test. In the lab you will also look at how the result differs by device, and why that needs care. Summary ¶ Question Tool Trap to avoid How much would a different sample change my number? You do not need any finance knowledge; use common sense. Write short answers. A team budgeted 10,000 currency units for travel and actually spent 12,000. What is the difference in currency units, and as a percentage of the budget? For a cost line, is spending more than budget good news or bad news for the company? What about earning more revenue than budgeted? A new project has a budget of 0 but spent 500. Why can you not calculate a percentage difference, and what would you show instead? Line X is 30% over a budget of 1,000. Line Y is 2% over a budget of 500,000. Which one would you look at first, and why? A department spent much less than its budget. Give one reason that is good news and one reason that might be bad news. A budget table has one row per department per month. You join it to a table of individual invoices and then add up the budget column. What could go wrong? Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you: Draw repeated samples of Superstore orders and watch the sampling distribution form. docs.text: Almost every number an analyst reports comes from a sample, and a different sample would have given a slightly different number. This lecture shows how big that wobble is, how to put an honest range around an estimate, and how to read an A/B test without fooling yourself or your manager. What the standard error measures, and why it shrinks with the square root of the sample size. How to build a confidence interval : by the bootstrap first, then by the formula estimate ± 1.96 × standard error . What " 95% confidence " does and does not mean. How an A/B test works: randomisation, control and treatment, conversion rate and lift . How to get a confidence interval for a lift and a p-value from a permutation test , and how to explain both in plain words. Why practical and statistical significance differ, and why peeking and slicing produce false winners. This lecture builds on How statistics can mislead . docs.text: The Superstore table has one row per order line . Average order value ( AOV ) is a measure of orders , so the cell above added up the lines of each order first. Averaging lines would give the average line value, a different and smaller number. For this lecture we play a game. We pretend the Superstore orders from 2023 to 2025 are the whole population : every order the company took. Then we can compare what a sample tells us with the true answer, something real life never lets you do. Term Meaning In our example Population Everything you want to know about All Superstore orders, 2023–2025 Parameter A number describing the population, usually unknown The true AOV Sample The part you actually observe 50 orders picked at random Statistic The same number calculated on the sample The sample's AOV Sampling error Statistic minus parameter: the luck of the draw Sample AOV − true AOV values = orders . to_numpy () true_mean = values . mean () print ( "Population:" , len ( values ), "orders" ) print ( "True AOV:" , f " { true_mean : ,.2f } source monetary units" ) Population: 3388 orders True AOV: 466.64 source monetary units Predict, then reveal We draw three random samples of 50 orders each. Will the three sample AOVs be the same? Will any of them equal the true AOV exactly? rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 9 ) for i in range ( 3 ): sample = rng . choice ( values , size = 50 , replace = False ) error = sample . mean () - true_mean print ( f "Sample { i + 1 } : AOV { sample . mean () : ,.2f } | sampling error { error : +,.2f } " ) Sample 1: AOV 350.71 | sampling error -115.92 Sample 2: AOV 568.28 | sampling error +101.64 Sample 3: AOV 238.47 | sampling error -228.17 Read the output above. Each sample gives a different AOV, and none hits the true value exactly. That is sampling error . It is not a mistake anyone made: it is the natural wobble of looking at part of the data. The question is never "is there sampling error?" but " how big is it likely to be?"
