docs.title: Part 1: Population, sample and sampling error

docs.text: One sample gives one AOV. If we could repeat the sampling many times, we would get a whole distribution of sample AOVs : the sampling distribution . It shows how far a single sample's answer can land from the truth. We cannot do this in real life (you get one sample), but with our pretend population we can simulate it: draw 2,000 samples of 100 orders and keep each sample's AOV. Predict, then reveal Order values are very skewed: most orders are small and a few are huge. Will the 2,000 sample AOVs be skewed in the same way, or will they look different? n = 100 sample_means = np . array ([ rng . choice ( values , size = n , replace = False ) . mean () for _ in range ( 2000 )]) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . hist ( values , bins = 60 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Single orders: very skewed" ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Order value (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) ax2 . hist ( sample_means , bins = 40 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axvline ( true_mean , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV" ) ax2 . set_title ( f "AOVs of 2,000 samples of { n } orders" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Sample AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Number of samples" ) ax2 . legend () fig . tight_layout () plt . show () low , high = np . percentile ( sample_means , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) print ( f "Middle 95% of sample AOVs: { low : ,.0f } to { high : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Spread (standard deviation) of sample AOVs: { sample_means . std () : ,.1f } " ) Middle 95% of sample AOVs: 318 to 702 Spread (standard deviation) of sample AOVs: 96.3 Three things to notice in the charts and output above: The sample AOVs are centred on the true AOV : random samples are right on average. They are far less spread out than single orders: averaging 100 orders cancels out much of the luck. Their shape is much closer to a symmetric bell curve than the orders themselves. Averages of reasonably large random samples tend towards this shape, whatever the data look like. Statisticians call this the central limit theorem ; you only need the idea. Check your understanding 2 Your colleague says: "The sampling distribution is the histogram of my data." What is the difference between the distribution of the data and the sampling distribution of the AOV?
docs.title: Part 2: The sampling distribution, by simulation

docs.text: The spread of the sampling distribution has a name: the standard error (SE) . It is the typical size of the sampling error. A small SE means one sample's answer is probably close to the truth. Predict, then reveal If you make the sample four times bigger , does the standard error become four times smaller, twice as small, or stay the same? rows = [] for size in [ 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 ]: means = np . array ([ rng . choice ( values , size = size , replace = False ) . mean () for _ in range ( 2000 )]) rows . append ({ "sample size" : size , "SE by simulation" : means . std (), "SD of orders / √n" : values . std () / math . sqrt ( size )}) se_table = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "sample size" ) ax = se_table . plot ( marker = "o" , style = [ "-" , "--" ]) ax . set_title ( "Bigger samples, smaller standard error, with diminishing returns" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Sample size (orders)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Standard error of AOV (source monetary units)" ) plt . show () se_table . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } SE by simulation SD of orders / √n sample size 25 189.60 195.00 50 136.70 137.90 100 95.00 97.50 200 67.90 69.00 The two columns in the table above almost agree. The simulated SE follows a simple rule: standard error of a mean = standard deviation of the data ÷ √(sample size) Because of the square root, four times the data halves the SE . Going from 25 to 100 orders helps a lot; going from 1,000 to 4,000 costs four times as much for the same halving. That is why "just collect more data" has diminishing returns. In real work you have one sample, so you use the sample's standard deviation in the formula. That is what the next part does. Check your understanding 3 A survey of 400 customers gives an SE of 2 points. Roughly how many customers would you need for an SE of 1 point? Is it worth it if each response costs money?
docs.title: Part 3: Standard error, and why it shrinks with √n

docs.text: Now the real situation: you have one sample of 200 orders and no access to the population. You want a range of plausible values for the true AOV: a confidence interval (CI) . The bootstrap gets one by simulation, using only the sample: Treat your sample as a stand-in for the population. Draw a new sample of the same size from your sample, with replacement (some orders appear twice, some not at all). Compute its AOV. Repeat thousands of times. The middle 95% of those AOVs (the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile) is the bootstrap 95% percentile interval . Predict, then reveal The bootstrap never sees a single order outside your sample. Do you expect its interval to contain the true AOV? my_sample = rng . choice ( values , size = 200 , replace = False ) boot_means = np . array ([ rng . choice ( my_sample , size = len ( my_sample ), replace = True ) . mean () for _ in range ( 5000 )]) boot_low , boot_high = np . percentile ( boot_means , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( boot_means , bins = 50 ) ax . axvline ( boot_low , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "2.5th and 97.5th percentiles" ) ax . axvline ( boot_high , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . axvline ( true_mean , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV (normally unknown)" ) ax . set_title ( "5,000 bootstrap AOVs from one sample of 200 orders" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Bootstrap AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bootstrap samples" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Sample AOV: { my_sample . mean () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI: { boot_low : ,.2f } to { boot_high : ,.2f } " ) Sample AOV: 546.47 Bootstrap 95% CI: 414.72 to 704.65 The bootstrap works because the spread of AOVs within your sample's resamples imitates the spread you would see across real samples. It needs no formula, and it works for medians, ratios and differences just as well as for means.
docs.title: Part 4: Confidence intervals, bootstrap first

docs.text: For a mean there is also a shortcut. In a bell-shaped sampling distribution, about 95% of values lie within 1.96 standard errors of the centre, so: 95% CI = sample mean ± 1.96 × SE, with SE = sample standard deviation ÷ √n ( ddof=1 below tells numpy to use the sample standard deviation, which divides by n − 1 .) se = my_sample . std ( ddof = 1 ) / math . sqrt ( len ( my_sample )) formula_low = my_sample . mean () - 1.96 * se formula_high = my_sample . mean () + 1.96 * se pd . DataFrame ({ "low" : [ boot_low , formula_low ], "high" : [ boot_high , formula_high ], "contains true AOV" : [ boot_low <= true_mean <= boot_high , formula_low <= true_mean <= formula_high ], }, index = [ "Bootstrap percentile" , "Formula: mean ± 1.96 × SE" ]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } low high contains true AOV Bootstrap percentile 414.72 704.65 True Formula: mean ± 1.96 × SE 396.95 695.98 True The two intervals in the table above are close. For large samples they agree , because the bootstrap distribution is then close to the bell curve the formula assumes. They differ more when samples are small or the data are very skewed; then the bootstrap shows the lopsidedness and the formula does not. Check your understanding 4 Write one sentence for a manager that reports the AOV from this sample with its 95% interval. Use the words "between" and "orders", and avoid the word "probability".
docs.title: The formula interval

docs.text: A 95% interval does not mean "there is a 95% chance the true AOV is in this interval". The true AOV is fixed; this interval either contains it or not. The 95% describes the method : if you repeated the whole process many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true value. We can check that, because we know the true AOV. Predict, then reveal We draw 100 samples of 200 orders and build a formula interval from each. How many of the 100 intervals will contain the true AOV? def formula_ci ( sample ): se = sample . std ( ddof = 1 ) / math . sqrt ( len ( sample )) return sample . mean () - 1.96 * se , sample . mean () + 1.96 * se intervals = np . array ([ formula_ci ( rng . choice ( values , size = 200 , replace = False )) for _ in range ( 100 )]) covers = ( intervals [:, 0 ] <= true_mean ) & ( true_mean <= intervals [:, 1 ]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) for i , ( low , high ) in enumerate ( intervals ): ax . plot ([ low , high ], [ i , i ], color = "#2a78d6" if covers [ i ] else "#eb6834" , linewidth = 1.5 ) ax . axvline ( true_mean , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "True AOV" ) ax . set_title ( f " { covers . sum () } of 100 intervals contain the true AOV (orange = missed)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "95 % i nterval for AOV (source monetary units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sample number" ) ax . legend ( loc = "lower right" ) plt . show () Most lines cross the dashed true value; a few (orange) miss it, and from inside one sample you cannot tell which kind you have. That is the honest meaning of 95%. With many more repetitions we can measure how often the method succeeds for different sample sizes: rows = [] for size in [ 30 , 100 , 200 ]: hits = 0 for _ in range ( 2000 ): low , high = formula_ci ( rng . choice ( values , size = size , replace = False )) hits += low <= true_mean <= high rows . append ({ "sample size" : size , "share of intervals containing true AOV" : hits / 2000 }) coverage = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "sample size" ) coverage . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } share of intervals containing true AOV sample size 30 84.0% 100 89.1% 200 92.5% Very skewed data need bigger samples Read the table above. Superstore order values are extremely skewed (a few orders are huge), so with small samples the formula interval is a little too narrow and covers the true AOV less often than 95% . The bootstrap percentile interval has the same weakness. Coverage improves as the sample grows. With skewed money data, prefer large samples, and consider also reporting the median. Correct reading Wrong reading "We are 95% confident the true AOV is between a and b ": the method captures the truth 95% of the time "There is a 95% probability the true AOV is in this interval" A wider interval means less precision A wider interval means the AOV is higher or "more variable orders" only The interval is about the average , not individual orders "95% of orders are between a and b " Check your understanding 5 A report says "95% of our customers spend between 410 and 520." The number came from a 95% confidence interval for the mean. What is wrong with the sentence? Rewrite it.
docs.title: Part 5: What "95% confidence" means

docs.text: The marketing team tested a new checkout page . Comparing visitors who happened to see a new page with those who did not is risky: if the new page were shown mainly to returning desktop customers, it would look good even if it did nothing. An A/B test solves this with randomisation : Idea Meaning Control (A) Visitors who see the current page Treatment (B) Visitors who see the new page Random assignment A coin flip decides each visitor's group, so the groups are alike on average in everything else: device, mood, budget, even things we cannot measure Consequence A difference in outcomes larger than chance would produce can be attributed to the page. This is the one situation in this course where we may talk about cause About the data ab_test.csv is synthetic teaching data: every visitor and number was generated by the course. One row per visitor, randomly assigned to A or B over 28 days. Revenue is in neutral currency units . ab = load_marketing ( "ab_test.csv" ) print ( "Rows:" , len ( ab ), "| distinct visitors:" , ab [ "visitor_id" ] . nunique ()) print ( "Test days:" , ab [ "date" ] . min () . date (), "to" , ab [ "date" ] . max () . date ()) ab . head () Rows: 60000 | distinct visitors: 60000 Test days: 2025-03-03 to 2025-03-30 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitor_id date device variant converted revenue 0 V000038 2025-03-03 mobile A 0 0.00 1 V000076 2025-03-03 mobile A 0 0.00 2 V000110 2025-03-03 mobile A 0 0.00 3 V000131 2025-03-03 mobile A 0 0.00 4 V000139 2025-03-03 mobile B 0 0.00 Before reading any result, check the randomisation worked . Each group should get about half the visitors, and the device mix should be similar in A and B. balance = pd . crosstab ( ab [ "device" ], ab [ "variant" ], margins = True , margins_name = "All" ) balance [ "share in B" ] = ( balance [ "B" ] / balance [ "All" ]) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) balance .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } variant A B All share in B device desktop 11265 11385 22650 50.3% mobile 18608 18742 37350 50.2% All 29873 30127 60000 50.2% In the table above, about half of each device's visitors were assigned to B, so neither group got more mobile or desktop visitors. This is called a balance check (or sample ratio check). If one group had clearly more visitors than planned, you would investigate the assignment before trusting any result.
docs.title: Part 6: Experiments and why we randomise

docs.text: Conversion rate = visitors who bought ÷ visitors in the group. Revenue per visitor = revenue ÷ visitors, counting the zeros of visitors who did not buy. by_variant = ab . groupby ( "variant" ) . agg ( visitors = ( "visitor_id" , "count" ), buyers = ( "converted" , "sum" ), revenue = ( "revenue" , "sum" ), ) by_variant [ "conversion rate" ] = by_variant [ "buyers" ] / by_variant [ "visitors" ] by_variant [ "revenue per visitor" ] = by_variant [ "revenue" ] / by_variant [ "visitors" ] rate_a = by_variant . loc [ "A" , "conversion rate" ] rate_b = by_variant . loc [ "B" , "conversion rate" ] lift = rate_b - rate_a print ( f "Absolute lift: { lift * 100 : +.2f } percentage points" ) print ( f "Relative lift: { lift / rate_a : +.1% } " ) by_variant . assign ( revenue = by_variant [ "revenue" ] . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ), ** { "conversion rate" : by_variant [ "conversion rate" ] . map ( " {:.2%} " . format ), "revenue per visitor" : by_variant [ "revenue per visitor" ] . map ( " {:.2f} " . format )}, ) Absolute lift: +0.50 percentage points Relative lift: +15.8% .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitors buyers revenue conversion rate revenue per visitor variant A 29873 940 92,066 3.15% 3.08 B 30127 1098 105,280 3.64% 3.49 There are two ways to state the same lift, and mixing them up is a classic error: Lift Formula How to say it Absolute rate B − rate A " x percentage points higher" Relative (rate B − rate A) ÷ rate A " y percent higher than control" A move from 3.0% to 3.6% is 0.6 percentage points , or 20% higher . Always say which one you mean; relative lifts sound bigger. Check your understanding 6 A vendor promises "a 50% uplift in conversion!" on a page that converts at 2%. What conversion rate does that imply, and what extra question would you ask?
docs.title: Part 7: Conversion rate and lift

docs.text: The lift above comes from one sample of visitors. A different 60,000 visitors would give a different lift. So the lift needs an interval, just like the AOV did. Predict, then reveal Will the 95% interval for the lift include zero (no difference)? Write down your guess before running the cell. Bootstrap: resample visitors with replacement within each group , recompute both conversion rates and their difference, repeat. conv_a = ab . loc [ ab [ "variant" ] == "A" , "converted" ] . to_numpy () conv_b = ab . loc [ ab [ "variant" ] == "B" , "converted" ] . to_numpy () boot_lifts = np . array ([ rng . choice ( conv_b , size = len ( conv_b )) . mean () - rng . choice ( conv_a , size = len ( conv_a )) . mean () for _ in range ( 2000 ) ]) lift_low , lift_high = np . percentile ( boot_lifts , [ 2.5 , 97.5 ]) ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( boot_lifts * 100 , bins = 50 ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 1 , label = "No difference" ) ax . axvline ( lift_low * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "95% bootstrap interval" ) ax . axvline ( lift_high * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_title ( "Bootstrap lifts: conversion B minus conversion A" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Lift (percentage points)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bootstrap samples" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Bootstrap 95% CI for the lift: { lift_low * 100 : +.2f } to { lift_high * 100 : +.2f } percentage points" ) Bootstrap 95% CI for the lift: +0.20 to +0.77 percentage points Formula: the SE of a difference between two proportions combines the SE of each group: SE = √( rate A × (1 − rate A) ÷ visitors A + rate B × (1 − rate B) ÷ visitors B ) , and the interval is lift ± 1.96 × SE . n_a , n_b = len ( conv_a ), len ( conv_b ) se_lift = math . sqrt ( rate_a * ( 1 - rate_a ) / n_a + rate_b * ( 1 - rate_b ) / n_b ) pd . DataFrame ({ "low (points)" : [ lift_low * 100 , ( lift - 1.96 * se_lift ) * 100 ], "high (points)" : [ lift_high * 100 , ( lift + 1.96 * se_lift ) * 100 ], }, index = [ "Bootstrap" , "Formula" ]) . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } low (points) high (points) Bootstrap 0.20 0.77 Formula 0.21 0.79 With tens of thousands of visitors, the bootstrap and the formula agree closely. If the whole interval sits above zero, the data are hard to explain by chance alone; the interval also tells you how big the lift plausibly is, from its low end to its high end. Check your understanding 7 A lift's 95% interval runs from −0.1 to +0.9 percentage points. Can you say B is better? Can you say B makes no difference? What would you tell the manager?
docs.title: Part 8: A confidence interval for the lift

docs.text: A p-value answers one narrow question: if the new page made no difference at all , how often would chance alone produce a gap at least as large as the one we saw? We can answer it by simulation. If the page did nothing, the A and B labels are meaningless, so shuffling them should not matter. We: Shuffle the variant labels across all visitors (keeping group sizes). Recompute the difference in conversion rates. Repeat thousands of times: this is the "no difference" world. The p-value is the share of shuffles with a gap at least as large (in either direction) as the real one. Predict, then reveal In the shuffled world, where will the differences be centred? How many of 5,000 shuffles do you expect to beat the real lift? converted = ab [ "converted" ] . to_numpy () is_b = ( ab [ "variant" ] == "B" ) . to_numpy () shuffled_lifts = np . empty ( 5000 ) for i in range ( 5000 ): labels = rng . permutation ( is_b ) shuffled_lifts [ i ] = converted [ labels ] . mean () - converted [ ~ labels ] . mean () extreme = ( np . abs ( shuffled_lifts ) >= abs ( lift )) . sum () ax = plt . gca () ax . hist ( shuffled_lifts * 100 , bins = 50 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Shuffled labels (no real difference)" ) ax . axvline ( lift * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Observed lift" ) ax . axvline ( - lift * 100 , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = ":" ) ax . set_title ( "How big are lifts when the page makes no difference?" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Lift (percentage points)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of shuffles" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () print ( f "Shuffles with a gap at least as large: { extreme } of 5000" ) print ( f "Permutation p-value: about { max ( extreme , 1 ) / 5000 : .4f } " + ( " (an upper bound)" if extreme == 0 else "" )) Shuffles with a gap at least as large: 1 of 5000 Permutation p-value: about 0.0002 The grey histogram above is what pure chance produces. The observed lift sits far out in its tail, so very few shuffles (or none) reach it, and the p-value is small.
docs.title: Part 9: A p-value by shuffling (permutation test)

docs.text: There is also a formula (the two-proportion z-test ). It divides the lift by its standard error under the "no difference" assumption and reads the p-value from the bell curve. We wrap it in a function to reuse later; you do not need to memorise it. def compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors_a , buyers_b , visitors_b ): """Lift (B - A), its 95% interval and a two-sided p-value, by the normal formula.""" rate_a , rate_b = buyers_a / visitors_a , buyers_b / visitors_b lift = rate_b - rate_a se = math . sqrt ( rate_a * ( 1 - rate_a ) / visitors_a + rate_b * ( 1 - rate_b ) / visitors_b ) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) # "no difference" rate se_null = math . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) z = lift / se_null p_value = math . erfc ( abs ( z ) / math . sqrt ( 2 )) # two-sided, from the bell curve return { "lift" : lift , "low" : lift - 1.96 * se , "high" : lift + 1.96 * se , "z" : z , "p_value" : p_value } result = compare_rates ( conv_a . sum (), n_a , conv_b . sum (), n_b ) print ( f "Formula p-value: { result [ 'p_value' ] : .4f } (z = { result [ 'z' ] : .2f } )" ) Formula p-value: 0.0008 (z = 3.37) Compare the two p-values in the outputs above. They tell the same story: chance is a poor explanation for the gap. When only a handful of shuffles reach the observed gap, the permutation p-value is rough (one more or one fewer extreme shuffle changes it a lot); more shuffles would sharpen it. With large samples like this one, the formula is a good shortcut.
docs.title: The formula shortcut

docs.text: In plain language: "If the new page truly made no difference, a gap this large would happen by chance in about p of tests." A small p-value (by convention below 0.05) means chance is a poor explanation; we call the result statistically significant . Common misreading Why it is wrong "p is the probability that the page has no effect." p assumes no effect and asks how surprising the data are. It is not the probability of the assumption. "1 − p is the probability that B is better." Same mistake in reverse. "p < 0.05, so the effect is big and important." p mixes effect size with sample size. A tiny effect in a huge sample gets a tiny p. "p > 0.05, so there is no difference." Not significant means not shown , not "shown to be zero". Look at the interval. "p = 0.049 is a success and p = 0.051 a failure." 0.05 is a convention, not a cliff. Report the interval and the p-value. Practical significance asks whether the effect is big enough to matter for the business. Statistical significance only asks whether chance is a poor explanation. The confidence interval answers both: its position says whether zero is plausible, its ends say how big the effect could be. Predict, then reveal Two made-up tests. Test 1 has 5 million visitors per group and a true lift of 0.1 percentage points. Test 2 has 1,000 visitors per group and a true lift of 1 percentage point. Which one will be "statistically significant"? Which one matters more for the business? sim = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 21 ) tests = { "Test 1" : ( 5_000_000 , 0.030 , 0.031 ), # visitors per group, true rate A, true rate B "Test 2" : ( 1_000 , 0.030 , 0.040 )} rows = {} for name , ( visitors , true_a , true_b ) in tests . items (): buyers_a , buyers_b = sim . binomial ( visitors , true_a ), sim . binomial ( visitors , true_b ) r = compare_rates ( buyers_a , visitors , buyers_b , visitors ) rows [ name ] = { "visitors per group" : f " { visitors : , } " , "lift (points)" : f " { r [ 'lift' ] * 100 : +.2f } " , "95% CI (points)" : f " { r [ 'low' ] * 100 : +.2f } to { r [ 'high' ] * 100 : +.2f } " , "p-value" : f " { r [ 'p_value' ] : .4f } " if r [ "p_value" ] >= 0.0001 else "below 0.0001" } pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . T .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } visitors per group lift (points) 95% CI (points) p-value Test 1 5,000,000 +0.08 +0.06 to +0.10 below 0.0001 Test 2 1,000 +0.50 -1.03 to +2.03 0.5221 Read the table above. The huge test is clearly "significant", yet its lift is so small it may not pay for the change. The small test was built with a lift that would matter, but its interval is so wide that it cannot tell a worthwhile lift from zero, or even from a loss. Neither "significant" nor "not significant" is the whole story. Always report the interval, in the units the manager cares about. Check your understanding 8 Translate the checkout-page lift and its interval into "extra buyers per 10,000 visitors". Which number would you put in the headline for a manager, the p-value or this?
docs.title: Part 10: Reading a p-value, and practical versus statistical significance

docs.text: A 5% significance threshold means a false winner 5% of the time when there is no real effect , but only if you look once , at one result, decided in advance. Two everyday habits break that promise.
docs.title: Part 11: Peeking and multiple comparisons

docs.text: A colleague checks the test every day and stops the first day the p-value dips below 0.05. To see what that does, we make an A/A test : we shuffle the variant labels in the real data, so there is no real difference by construction, then follow the running result day by day. Predict, then reveal In A/A tests with no real difference, what share would end with a "winner" if you checked only on the last day? And if you checked every day and stopped at the first significant day? day = ( ab [ "date" ] - ab [ "date" ] . min ()) . dt . days . to_numpy () n_days = day . max () + 1 def daily_z ( labels ): """Running z statistic after each day of the test, for given B labels.""" buyers_b = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], weights = converted [ labels ], minlength = n_days )) visitors_b = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ labels ], minlength = n_days )) buyers_a = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], weights = converted [ ~ labels ], minlength = n_days )) visitors_a = np . cumsum ( np . bincount ( day [ ~ labels ], minlength = n_days )) pooled = ( buyers_a + buyers_b ) / ( visitors_a + visitors_b ) se_null = np . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / visitors_a + 1 / visitors_b )) return ( buyers_b / visitors_b - buyers_a / visitors_a ) / se_null aa_runs = np . array ([ daily_z ( rng . permutation ( is_b )) for _ in range ( 1000 )]) significant = np . abs ( aa_runs ) > 1.96 # |z| above 1.96 is the same as p below 0.05 print ( f "A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked once, on the last day: { significant [:, - 1 ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked every day: { significant . any ( axis = 1 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) ax = plt . gca () for run in aa_runs [: 40 ]: crosses = ( np . abs ( run ) > 1.96 ) . any () ax . plot ( range ( 1 , n_days + 1 ), run , color = "#2a78d6" if crosses else "#b8b6b0" , linewidth = 1.5 if crosses else 0.8 ) ax . axhline ( 1.96 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Significance threshold (p = 0.05)" ) ax . axhline ( - 1.96 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" ) ax . set_ylim ( - 3.5 , 3.5 ) ax . set_title ( "40 A/A tests: blue runs cross the threshold at least once by chance" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Day of the test" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Running z statistic (A/A, no real effect)" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked once, on the last day: 5.2% A/A tests with a 'winner' when checked every day: 27.1% Read the two shares above. Checked once, A/A tests produce a false winner about 5% of the time, as promised. Checked every day and stopped at the first dip below 0.05, the false-winner rate is several times higher, because a random walk that wanders long enough crosses the line by chance.
docs.title: Peeking

docs.text: Another colleague slices the test into 20 slices (2 devices × the first 10 days) and reports any slice where B "wins". Each slice has a 5% false-alarm chance, so with 20 slices a false alarm somewhere is likely: 1 − 0.95²⁰. slice_mask = day < 10 slice_key = day [ slice_mask ] * 2 + ( ab [ "device" ] . to_numpy ()[ slice_mask ] == "mobile" ) conv_s = converted [ slice_mask ] def slice_z ( labels ): """z statistic in each of the 20 device x day slices, for given B labels.""" lab = labels [ slice_mask ] vb = np . bincount ( slice_key [ lab ], minlength = 20 ) va = np . bincount ( slice_key [ ~ lab ], minlength = 20 ) bb = np . bincount ( slice_key [ lab ], weights = conv_s [ lab ], minlength = 20 ) ba = np . bincount ( slice_key [ ~ lab ], weights = conv_s [ ~ lab ], minlength = 20 ) pooled = ( ba + bb ) / ( va + vb ) se_null = np . sqrt ( pooled * ( 1 - pooled ) * ( 1 / va + 1 / vb )) return ( bb / vb - ba / va ) / se_null aa_slices = np . array ([ slice_z ( rng . permutation ( is_b )) for _ in range ( 1000 )]) print ( f "Chance of at least one false alarm in 20 slices, by the rule: { 1 - 0.95 ** 20 : .0% } " ) print ( f "Chance of at least one 'significant' slice, A/A simulation: { ( np . abs ( aa_slices ) > 1.96 ) . any ( axis = 1 ) . mean () : .0% } " ) Chance of at least one false alarm in 20 slices, by the rule: 64% Chance of at least one 'significant' slice, A/A simulation: 63% With no real effect at all, most A/A tests above still contain at least one "significant" slice. A slice that wins is a lead for a new test , not a finding. Rules that keep a test honest Before the test starts, write down the one primary measure , the sample size or duration , and the decision rule. Look at the result once , at the planned end. (There are methods for planned interim looks; they use stricter thresholds.) Treat subgroup and slice results as hypotheses . Name the few subgroups you care about in advance, and give each one its own interval. Report how many comparisons you made, not only the ones that "worked". Check your understanding 9 A team ran a test for three weeks, looked at 12 measures and found that "time on page" improved with p = 0.03. What would you ask before believing it?

DataFrame ({ "A" : [ rate_a * 100 , rev_a . mean ()], "B" : [ rate_b * 100 , rev_b . mean ()], "B − A" : [ lift * 100 , rev_b . mean () - rev_a . mean ()], "CI low" : [ lift_low * 100 , np . percentile ( boot_rpv , 2.5 )], "CI high" : [ lift_high * 100 , np . percentile ( boot_rpv , 97.5 )], }, index = [ "Conversion (%)" , "Revenue per visitor" ]) display ( summary . round ( 2 )) print ( f "The new checkout page converted { rate_b : .2% } of visitors against { rate_a : .2% } on the current page, " f "a lift of { lift * 100 : +.2f } percentage points (95% CI { lift_low * 100 : +.2f } to { lift_high * 100 : +.2f } ). " f "That is about { lift * 10000 : .0f } extra buyers per 10,000 visitors. " f "A gap this large would be very unlikely if the page made no difference (permutation p about { max ( extreme , 1 ) / 5000 : .4f } )." ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } A B B − A CI low CI high Conversion (%) 3.15 3.64 0.50 0.20 0.77 Revenue per visitor 3.08 3.49 0.41 0.09 0.74 The new checkout page converted 3.64% of visitors against 3.15% on the current page, a lift of +0.50 percentage points (95% CI +0.20 to +0.77). That is about 50 extra buyers per 10,000 visitors. A gap this large would be very unlikely if the page made no difference (permutation p about 0.0002). The printed sentence is the evidence a manager needs: what changed, by how much, how sure we are, and in business units. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ Finance partner: "I can take about a dozen lines into next month's expense review. I need a list I can defend: which department and account lines, why each one, and what to ask. And please make sure the numbers reconcile, last time a report double-counted the budget." About the data finance_actuals.csv and finance_budget.csv are synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional company's monthly management expense view for calendar 2025. No real company, person or supplier is described. Amounts are in neutral currency units . This is not a financial statement: there is no revenue, no balance sheet and no audit claim. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G5 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I6 Challenge Debugging and a recommendation C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Check the grain, keys and signs of a posting table and a budget table. Aggregate postings to the budget grain, then outer-join with an indicator. Reconcile the result to both sources. Compute variance, favourability and variance % correctly, including zero and unknown budgets. Rank exceptions by amount and by percentage, and explain the difference. Recognise a duplicate posting and its reversal behind a "favourable" month. Draw a variance chart whose colours are colour-blind-safe and labelled. Recommend review priorities with reasons and follow-up questions. Evidence you keep: a variance view, a reconciliation note and a short recommendation. docs.text: Join the actual cells to the budget one-to-one , keeping cells from both sides, and record where each came from. var = actual_cells . merge ( budget , on = KEY , how = "outer" , indicator = True , validate = "one_to_one" ) var [ "match" ] = var [ "_merge" ] . astype ( str ) . map ({ "both" : "actual and budget" , "left_only" : "actual only" , "right_only" : "budget only" }) var = var . drop ( columns = "_merge" ) var [ "postings" ] = var [ "postings" ] . fillna ( 0 ) . astype ( int ) var [ "actual" ] = var [ "actual" ] . fillna ( 0 ) # budget-only: no postings, so actual = 0 var [ "budget_status" ] = np . select ([ var [ "budget" ] . isna (), var [ "budget" ] == 0 ], [ "unknown budget" , "approved zero budget" ], default = "positive budget" ) var [ "variance" ] = var [ "actual" ] - var [ "budget" ] # NaN when the budget is unknown var [ "variance_pct" ] = np . where ( var [ "budget" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] / var [ "budget" ], np . nan ) var [ "direction" ] = np . select ([ var [ "budget" ] . isna (), var [ "variance" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] < 0 ], [ "not assessed (budget unknown)" , "unfavourable" , "favourable" ], default = "on budget" ) var . loc [( var [ "budget" ] == 0 ) & ( var [ "actual" ] > 0 ), "direction" ] = "unbudgeted spend against zero" pd . crosstab ( var [ "match" ], var [ "budget_status" ]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } budget_status approved zero budget positive budget unknown budget match actual and budget 1 424 0 actual only 0 0 6 budget only 2 5 0 Why fill actual with 0 but not budget ? A budget-only cell has no postings, so its spending really is 0 (once finance confirms the month's postings are complete). An actual-only cell has no budget row , so its budget is unknown . Filling it with 0 would invent an overspend.

docs.text: This function compares any variance table with the two sources. You will reuse it in the challenge. def reconcile ( table , label ): """Compare a variance table with the two source tables and print PASS or FAIL for each check.""" all_keys = pd . concat ([ actuals [ KEY ], budget [ KEY ]]) . drop_duplicates () checks = [ ( "One row per (month, department, account)" , not table . duplicated ( KEY ) . any ()), ( "Every key from either source is present" , len ( table ) == len ( all_keys )), ( "Actual total = signed posting total" , abs ( table [ "actual" ] . sum () - actuals [ "amount" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ( "Budget total = total of unique budget cells" , abs ( table [ "budget" ] . sum () - budget [ "budget" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ] print ( f "Reconciliation: { label } " ) print ( f " rows { len ( table ) } vs keys { len ( all_keys ) } " ) print ( f " actual { table [ 'actual' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs postings { actuals [ 'amount' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f " budget { table [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs budget cells { budget [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) for name , ok in checks : print ( f " { 'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL' } { name } " ) reconcile ( var , "my variance table" ) Reconciliation: my variance table rows 438 vs keys 438 actual 6,241,801.60 vs postings 6,241,801.60 budget 6,133,000.00 vs budget cells 6,133,000.00 PASS One row per (month, department, account) PASS Every key from either source is present PASS Actual total = signed posting total PASS Budget total = total of unique budget cells Copy the four PASS lines and the two totals into your evidence log. This is the start of your reconciliation note .

docs.text: Session 10 lecture: Finance: budget accountability ¶ Every month a finance partner compares what each department spent with what it was allowed to spend, and picks a handful of lines to question. This lecture shows how to build that comparison so the totals are right, the signs are read correctly, and the lines you flag are the ones that really deserve attention. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 9 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. From a random sample of 200 orders, the average order value is 450 with a 95% confidence interval from 400 to 500. Write one sentence for a manager that reports this correctly. You make your sample four times bigger. What happens to the standard error? An A/B test shows a lift of +0.4 percentage points with a 95% interval from −0.1 to +0.9. Can you say the new version is better? Can you say it makes no difference? A test gives p = 0.03. Say in plain words what that means, and give one common misreading. Why does checking a test every day and stopping on the first day p drops below 0.05 produce too many false winners? What you will be able to explain ¶ The grain of expense postings and of budget cells, and why they cannot be joined directly. How signs work in an expense ledger: expenses are positive , credits and reversals are negative . Why you aggregate first, then combine , and how an outer join with an indicator keeps every cell visible. The difference between an unknown budget , a budget with no spending and an approved zero budget . Variance = actual − budget , and why, for expenses, a positive variance is unfavourable . When a variance % exists, and why you never average percentages to get a total. How to judge materiality using both the amount and the percentage. Why a favourable month may only be a credit, reversal or timing effect. Which reconciliation checks prove that your comparison table adds up. This lecture builds on the grain ideas from Session 2 and the rate rules from Session 5 . In the Lab you build the full comparison yourself, debug a colleague's broken version and choose what the finance partner should review. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. Run the two cells below first: the finance data setup, then the cell that loads the two tables. # Finance data setup (synthetic). Ask your facilitator." ) return pd . read_csv ( io . Always add a legend too. FAVOURABLE , UNFAVOURABLE = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" actuals = load_finance ( "finance_actuals.csv" ) budget = load_finance ( "finance_budget.csv" ) print ( "Postings:" , len ( actuals ), "| budget cells:" , len ( budget )) Postings: 1378 | budget cells: 432 Part 1: The business decision ¶ Finance partner: "Every month I can review about a dozen budget lines with department heads. Which department and account lines should I put on the list, and why? I don't want to waste anyone's time on noise, and I don't want to miss a real problem." The decision is a short, defensible review list . To get there we need a comparison of actual spending with budget for every month, department and account, that we can trust to add up. About the data finance_actuals.csv and finance_budget.csv are synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional company's monthly management expense view for calendar 2025. No real company, person or supplier is described. Amounts are in neutral currency units . This is not a financial statement: there is no revenue, no balance sheet and no audit claim. Table One row is Key finance_actuals.csv One expense posting (an invoice, salary run, credit or reversal) posting_id finance_budget.csv One approved monthly budget cell ( month , department_id , account_id ) Part 2: Grain, keys and signs ¶ Before combining two tables, check what one row means in each and whether the keys really are unique. We also keep the department and account names next to their codes; the check below confirms each code has exactly one name, so the names can travel with the keys. KEY = [ "month" , "department_id" , "department" , "account_id" , "account" ] print ( "posting_id unique:" , actuals [ "posting_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Most budget rows for one (month, department, account):" , budget . groupby ( KEY ) . size () . max ()) print ( "Names per department code:" , actuals . groupby ( "department_id" )[ "department" ] . nunique () . max (), "| names per account code:" , actuals . groupby ( "account_id" )[ "account" ] . nunique () . max ()) print ( "Months:" , actuals [ "month" ] . min () . date (), "to" , actuals [ "month" ] . max () . date ()) actuals . head () posting_id unique: True Most budget rows for one (month, department, account): 1 Names per department code: 1 | names per account code: 1 Months: 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-01 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } posting_id posting_date month department_id department account_id account amount posting_type reference_posting_id description 0 P25-00001 2025-01-01 2025-01-01 D02 Marketing A200 Travel 534.24 expense Travel - Marketing 1 P25-00002 2025-01-01 2025-01-01 D06 Finance and Admin A300 Software subscriptions 254.84 expense Software subscriptions - Finance and Admin 2 P25-00003 2025-01-02 2025-01-01 D03 Operations A400 Facilities 9,148.20 expense Facilities - Operations 3 P25-00004 2025-01-02 2025-01-01 D05 People A300 Software subscriptions 1,350.20 expense Software subscriptions - People 4 P25-00005 2025-01-02 2025-01-01 D05 People A600 Training 2,036.12 expense Training - People Many postings fall into the same month, department and account. The budget has one row for each of those cells. So the two tables have different grains : postings are fine-grained, budgets are coarse. Signs ¶ In this ledger a positive amount is an expense. A negative amount is a credit (for example a supplier refunds an overcharge) or a reversal (an earlier posting is cancelled). A reversal also names the posting it cancels in reference_posting_id . Keep both rows in mind; we return to them in Part 8. Part 3: The join trap ¶ The quickest way to put actuals next to budgets is to join the posting table straight onto the budget table. Let us try it on one budget cell: Sales travel in May. Predict, then reveal There is one budget cell for Sales travel in May, and several postings. After joining postings to budget, then adding up the budget column, will you get the May budget, or something else? is_cell = lambda df : ( df [ "month" ] == "2025-05-01" ) & ( df [ "department" ] == "Sales" ) & ( df [ "account" ] == "Travel" ) one_budget = budget [ is_cell ( budget )] its_postings = actuals [ is_cell ( actuals )] joined = its_postings . merge ( one_budget , on = KEY ) print ( "Budget cells:" , len ( one_budget ), "| postings:" , len ( its_postings ), "| rows after the join:" , len ( joined )) print ( f "True May budget: { one_budget [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "'Budget' after the join: { joined [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) joined [[ "posting_id" , "amount" , "budget" ]] Budget cells: 1 | postings: 6 | rows after the join: 6 True May budget: 12,000.00 'Budget' after the join: 72,000.00 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } posting_id amount budget 0 P25-00484 2,123.44 12,000.00 1 P25-00487 1,492.03 12,000.00 2 P25-00501 6,818.31 12,000.00 3 P25-00538 952.07 12,000.00 4 P25-00552 6,500.00 12,000.00 5 P25-00553 6,500.00 12,000.00 The join copies the budget onto every posting, so adding up the budget column counts it once per posting. Nothing errors and nothing warns you. Now the whole year: naive = actuals . merge ( budget , on = KEY ) # postings joined straight to budgets matched_cells = budget . merge ( actuals [ KEY ] . drop_duplicates (), on = KEY ) # the same cells, each counted once print ( f "Budget after the naive join: { naive [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Budget of the same cells, counted once: { matched_cells [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Inflation factor: { naive [ 'budget' ] . sum () / matched_cells [ 'budget' ] . sum () : .2f } x" ) Budget after the naive join: 14,771,900.00 Budget of the same cells, counted once: 6,126,500.00 Inflation factor: 2.41x Read the output above. On this version of the data the naive join reports a budget several times too large, so every department looks massively under budget. Notice also that the naive join silently drops anything that does not match on both sides. The rule: aggregate first, then combine Bring both tables to the same grain before joining. Here that means adding up postings to one row per (month, department, account), then joining one-to-one to the budget cells. Part 4: Aggregate first, then an outer join with an indicator ¶ Step 1: add up the postings to the budget's grain. We also count the postings in each cell. actual_cells = actuals . groupby ( KEY , as_index = False ) . agg ( actual = ( "amount" , "sum" ), postings = ( "posting_id" , "count" )) print ( "Posting rows:" , len ( actuals ), "-> actual cells:" , len ( actual_cells )) actual_cells . head () Posting rows: 1378 -> actual cells: 431 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } month department_id department account_id account actual postings 0 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A100 Salaries and wages 85,470.10 2 1 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A200 Travel 6,843.41 6 2 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A300 Software subscriptions 3,767.03 2 3 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A400 Facilities 5,512.62 1 4 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A500 Professional services 2,071.17 3 Step 2: join to the budget with three safety features: Setting What it does how="outer" Keeps cells that appear on either side, not only on both indicator=True Adds a column _merge saying where each row came from validate="one_to_one" Stops with an error if either side has duplicate keys var = actual_cells . merge ( budget , on = KEY , how = "outer" , indicator = True , validate = "one_to_one" ) var [ "match" ] = var [ "_merge" ] . astype ( str ) . map ({ "both" : "actual and budget" , "left_only" : "actual only" , "right_only" : "budget only" }) var = var . drop ( columns = "_merge" ) var [ "match" ] . value_counts () match actual and budget 425 budget only 7 actual only 6 Name: count, dtype: int64 Most cells have both an actual and a budget. The two small groups are the interesting ones, and an inner join would have hidden both of them. Part 5: Unknown, missing and zero are different ¶ Situation What it means Actual Budget Variance Actual only Money was spent, but no budget cell exists the sum of postings unknown (not zero) unknown Budget only A budget was approved, nobody posted anything 0, once we accept the postings are complete the budget 0 − budget Approved zero budget The budget is explicitly 0 the sum of postings 0 the actual; no % An unknown budget must never be filled with 0: that would turn "we don't know" into "this was not allowed", and the cell would look like a large overspend. Part 6: Variance and favourability ¶ variance = actual − budget For an expense , spending more than budget is bad news for the company, so: Variance Meaning for an expense Word to use positive spent more than budget unfavourable (overspend) negative spent less than budget favourable (underspend) unknown budget unknown not assessed (For revenue the rule flips: earning more than budget is favourable. Never reuse an expense colour rule on a revenue chart.) variance % = variance ÷ budget , only when the budget is above zero . With a zero budget the division is undefined; we label the cell "unbudgeted spend against zero" instead of inventing a percentage. var [ "variance" ] = var [ "actual" ] - var [ "budget" ] # NaN when the budget is unknown var [ "variance_pct" ] = np . where ( var [ "budget" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] / var [ "budget" ], np . nan ) var [ "direction" ] = np . select ( [ var [ "budget" ] . isna (), var [ "variance" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] < 0 ], [ "not assessed (budget unknown)" , "unfavourable" , "favourable" ], default = "on budget" , ) var . loc [( var [ "budget" ] == 0 ) & ( var [ "actual" ] > 0 ), "direction" ] = "unbudgeted spend against zero" var [ "direction" ] . value_counts () direction unfavourable 232 favourable 197 not assessed (budget unknown) 6 on budget 2 unbudgeted spend against zero 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 Predict, then reveal Look again at the joined May Sales travel row. Is its variance favourable or unfavourable? Is its variance % small, medium or large? may = var . loc [ is_cell ( var ), [ "month" , "department" , "account" , "actual" , "budget" , "variance" , "variance_pct" , "direction" ]] may . assign ( variance_pct = may [ "variance_pct" ] . map ( " {:+.0%} " . format )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } month department account actual budget variance variance_pct direction 145 2025-05-01 Sales Travel 24,385.85 12,000.00 12,385.85 +103% unfavourable Check your understanding 3 A colleague colours every negative variance red "because negative numbers are bad". On an expense report, what will that chart tell the reader, and why is it wrong? Part 7: Reconciliation checks ¶ A comparison table is only useful if it still adds up to its sources. Run these checks every time you build one, and keep the output as evidence. def reconcile ( table , label ): """Compare a variance table with the two source tables and print PASS or FAIL for each check.""" all_keys = pd . concat ([ actuals [ KEY ], budget [ KEY ]]) . drop_duplicates () checks = [ ( "One row per (month, department, account)" , not table . duplicated ( KEY ) . any ()), ( "Every key from either source is present" , len ( table ) == len ( all_keys )), ( "Actual total = signed posting total" , abs ( table [ "actual" ] . sum () - actuals [ "amount" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ( "Budget total = total of unique budget cells" , abs ( table [ "budget" ] . sum () - budget [ "budget" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ] print ( f "Reconciliation: { label } " ) print ( f " actual { table [ 'actual' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs postings { actuals [ 'amount' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f " budget { table [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs budget cells { budget [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) for name , ok in checks : print ( f " { 'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL' } { name } " ) reconcile ( var , "aggregate first, then outer join" ) Reconciliation: aggregate first, then outer join actual 6,241,801.60 vs postings 6,241,801.60 budget 6,133,000.00 vs budget cells 6,133,000.00 PASS One row per (month, department, account) PASS Every key from either source is present PASS Actual total = signed posting total PASS Budget total = total of unique budget cells All four checks pass. Notice that .sum() skips the unknown budgets, so the budget total is the total of the cells that exist . Unknown is not added as zero; it is simply not there. Check your understanding 4 Which of the four checks would have caught the naive join from Part 3? Which would catch an inner join? Part 8: Materiality, using amount and percentage ¶ Neither number alone tells you what matters: A large amount can be a small % of a very large budget (salaries). A large % can be a tiny amount on a small budget. A common review rule uses both. The thresholds are business choices agreed with finance, not statistics. Here: flag a cell if the variance is at least 5,000 currency units either way, or at least 25% of budget and at least 1,000 currency units. Averaging monthly percentages is closer only because months have similar budgets; it is still the wrong method. Rules for a total variance % Add up actual and budget over the comparable scope (cells with a known budget). Compute the % from those totals. docs.text: Every month a finance partner compares what each department spent with what it was allowed to spend, and picks a handful of lines to question. This lecture shows how to build that comparison so the totals are right, the signs are read correctly, and the lines you flag are the ones that really deserve attention. docs.text: Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 9 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. From a random sample of 200 orders, the average order value is 450 with a 95% confidence interval from 400 to 500. Write one sentence for a manager that reports this correctly. You make your sample four times bigger. What happens to the standard error? An A/B test shows a lift of +0.4 percentage points with a 95% interval from −0.1 to +0.9. Can you say the new version is better? Can you say it makes no difference? A test gives p = 0.03. Say in plain words what that means, and give one common misreading. Why does checking a test every day and stopping on the first day p drops below 0.05 produce too many false winners?

docs.text: The grain of expense postings and of budget cells, and why they cannot be joined directly. How signs work in an expense ledger: expenses are positive , credits and reversals are negative . Why you aggregate first, then combine , and how an outer join with an indicator keeps every cell visible. The difference between an unknown budget , a budget with no spending and an approved zero budget . Variance = actual − budget , and why, for expenses, a positive variance is unfavourable . When a variance % exists, and why you never average percentages to get a total. How to judge materiality using both the amount and the percentage. Why a favourable month may only be a credit, reversal or timing effect. Which reconciliation checks prove that your comparison table adds up. This lecture builds on the grain ideas from Session 2 and the rate rules from Session 5 . In the Lab you build the full comparison yourself, debug a colleague's broken version and choose what the finance partner should review. docs.text: Finance partner: "Every month I can review about a dozen budget lines with department heads. Which department and account lines should I put on the list, and why? I don't want to waste anyone's time on noise, and I don't want to miss a real problem." The decision is a short, defensible review list . To get there we need a comparison of actual spending with budget for every month, department and account, that we can trust to add up. About the data finance_actuals.csv and finance_budget.csv are synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional company's monthly management expense view for calendar 2025. No real company, person or supplier is described. Amounts are in neutral currency units . This is not a financial statement: there is no revenue, no balance sheet and no audit claim. docs.text: The quickest way to put actuals next to budgets is to join the posting table straight onto the budget table. Let us try it on one budget cell: Sales travel in May. Predict, then reveal There is one budget cell for Sales travel in May, and several postings. After joining postings to budget, then adding up the budget column, will you get the May budget, or something else? is_cell = lambda df : ( df [ "month" ] == "2025-05-01" ) & ( df [ "department" ] == "Sales" ) & ( df [ "account" ] == "Travel" ) one_budget = budget [ is_cell ( budget )] its_postings = actuals [ is_cell ( actuals )] joined = its_postings . merge ( one_budget , on = KEY ) print ( "Budget cells:" , len ( one_budget ), "| postings:" , len ( its_postings ), "| rows after the join:" , len ( joined )) print ( f "True May budget: { one_budget [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "'Budget' after the join: { joined [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) joined [[ "posting_id" , "amount" , "budget" ]] Budget cells: 1 | postings: 6 | rows after the join: 6 True May budget: 12,000.00 'Budget' after the join: 72,000.00 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } posting_id amount budget 0 P25-00484 2,123.44 12,000.00 1 P25-00487 1,492.03 12,000.00 2 P25-00501 6,818.31 12,000.00 3 P25-00538 952.07 12,000.00 4 P25-00552 6,500.00 12,000.00 5 P25-00553 6,500.00 12,000.00 The join copies the budget onto every posting, so adding up the budget column counts it once per posting. Nothing errors and nothing warns you. Now the whole year: naive = actuals . merge ( budget , on = KEY ) # postings joined straight to budgets matched_cells = budget . merge ( actuals [ KEY ] . drop_duplicates (), on = KEY ) # the same cells, each counted once print ( f "Budget after the naive join: { naive [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Budget of the same cells, counted once: { matched_cells [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f "Inflation factor: { naive [ 'budget' ] . sum () / matched_cells [ 'budget' ] . sum () : .2f } x" ) Budget after the naive join: 14,771,900.00 Budget of the same cells, counted once: 6,126,500.00 Inflation factor: 2.41x Read the output above. On this version of the data the naive join reports a budget several times too large, so every department looks massively under budget. Notice also that the naive join silently drops anything that does not match on both sides. The rule: aggregate first, then combine Bring both tables to the same grain before joining. Here that means adding up postings to one row per (month, department, account), then joining one-to-one to the budget cells.

We also count the postings in each cell. actual_cells = actuals . groupby ( KEY , as_index = False ) . agg ( actual = ( "amount" , "sum" ), postings = ( "posting_id" , "count" )) print ( "Posting rows:" , len ( actuals ), "-> actual cells:" , len ( actual_cells )) actual_cells . head () Posting rows: 1378 -> actual cells: 431 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } month department_id department account_id account actual postings 0 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A100 Salaries and wages 85,470.10 2 1 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A200 Travel 6,843.41 6 2 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A300 Software subscriptions 3,767.03 2 3 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A400 Facilities 5,512.62 1 4 2025-01-01 D01 Sales A500 Professional services 2,071.17 3 Step 2: join to the budget with three safety features: Setting What it does how="outer" Keeps cells that appear on either side, not only on both indicator=True Adds a column _merge saying where each row came from validate="one_to_one" Stops with an error if either side has duplicate keys var = actual_cells . merge ( budget , on = KEY , how = "outer" , indicator = True , validate = "one_to_one" ) var [ "match" ] = var [ "_merge" ] . astype ( str ) . map ({ "both" : "actual and budget" , "left_only" : "actual only" , "right_only" : "budget only" }) var = var . drop ( columns = "_merge" ) var [ "match" ] . value_counts () match actual and budget 425 budget only 7 actual only 6 Name: count, dtype: int64 Most cells have both an actual and a budget. The two small groups are the interesting ones, and an inner join would have hidden both of them.

docs.text: variance = actual − budget For an expense , spending more than budget is bad news for the company, so: Variance Meaning for an expense Word to use positive spent more than budget unfavourable (overspend) negative spent less than budget favourable (underspend) unknown budget unknown not assessed (For revenue the rule flips: earning more than budget is favourable. Never reuse an expense colour rule on a revenue chart.) variance % = variance ÷ budget , only when the budget is above zero . With a zero budget the division is undefined; we label the cell "unbudgeted spend against zero" instead of inventing a percentage. var [ "variance" ] = var [ "actual" ] - var [ "budget" ] # NaN when the budget is unknown var [ "variance_pct" ] = np . where ( var [ "budget" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] / var [ "budget" ], np . nan ) var [ "direction" ] = np . select ( [ var [ "budget" ] . isna (), var [ "variance" ] > 0 , var [ "variance" ] < 0 ], [ "not assessed (budget unknown)" , "unfavourable" , "favourable" ], default = "on budget" , ) var . loc [( var [ "budget" ] == 0 ) & ( var [ "actual" ] > 0 ), "direction" ] = "unbudgeted spend against zero" var [ "direction" ] . value_counts () direction unfavourable 232 favourable 197 not assessed (budget unknown) 6 on budget 2 unbudgeted spend against zero 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 Predict, then reveal Look again at the joined May Sales travel row. docs.text: A comparison table is only useful if it still adds up to its sources. Run these checks every time you build one, and keep the output as evidence. def reconcile ( table , label ): """Compare a variance table with the two source tables and print PASS or FAIL for each check.""" all_keys = pd . concat ([ actuals [ KEY ], budget [ KEY ]]) . drop_duplicates () checks = [ ( "One row per (month, department, account)" , not table . duplicated ( KEY ) . any ()), ( "Every key from either source is present" , len ( table ) == len ( all_keys )), ( "Actual total = signed posting total" , abs ( table [ "actual" ] . sum () - actuals [ "amount" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ( "Budget total = total of unique budget cells" , abs ( table [ "budget" ] . sum () - budget [ "budget" ] . sum ()) < 0.005 ), ] print ( f "Reconciliation: { label } " ) print ( f " actual { table [ 'actual' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs postings { actuals [ 'amount' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) print ( f " budget { table [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } vs budget cells { budget [ 'budget' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " ) for name , ok in checks : print ( f " { 'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL' } { name } " ) reconcile ( var , "aggregate first, then outer join" ) Reconciliation: aggregate first, then outer join actual 6,241,801.60 vs postings 6,241,801.60 budget 6,133,000.00 vs budget cells 6,133,000.00 PASS One row per (month, department, account) PASS Every key from either source is present PASS Actual total = signed posting total PASS Budget total = total of unique budget cells All four checks pass. Notice that .sum() skips the unknown budgets, so the budget total is the total of the cells that exist . Unknown is not added as zero; it is simply not there. Check your understanding 4 Which of the four checks would have caught the naive join from Part 3? Which would catch an inner join?

docs.text: Neither number alone tells you what matters: A large amount can be a small % of a very large budget (salaries). A large % can be a tiny amount on a small budget. A common review rule uses both. The thresholds are business choices agreed with finance, not statistics. Here: flag a cell if the variance is at least 5,000 currency units either way, or at least 25% of budget and at least 1,000 currency units. AMOUNT_LIMIT = 5000 PCT_LIMIT = 0.25 MIN_AMOUNT_FOR_PCT = 1000 big_amount = var [ "variance" ] . abs () >= AMOUNT_LIMIT big_pct = ( var [ "variance_pct" ] . abs () >= PCT_LIMIT ) & ( var [ "variance" ] . abs () >= MIN_AMOUNT_FOR_PCT ) var [ "review_flag" ] = np . select ([ big_amount & big_pct , big_amount , big_pct ], [ "amount and %" , "amount" , "%" ], default = "" ) flagged = var [ var [ "review_flag" ] != "" ] print ( "Cells flagged:" , len ( flagged ), "of" , len ( var )) known = var . dropna ( subset = [ "variance_pct" ]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) ax . scatter ( known [ "variance_pct" ] * 100 , known [ "variance" ], s = 14 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Not flagged" ) # Purple, green and black here mark review flags, not favourability (blue and orange are kept for that). for flag , colour , marker in [( "amount" , "#7a5195" , "o" ), ( "%" , "#1baf7a" , "s" ), ( "amount and %" , "black" , "D" )]: part = known [ known [ "review_flag" ] == flag ] ax . scatter ( part [ "variance_pct" ] * 100 , part [ "variance" ], s = 36 , color = colour , marker = marker , label = f "Flagged: { flag } " ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "Monthly cells: variance in currency units against variance %" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Variance % o f budget (right = over budget)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Variance (currency units)" ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . show () Cells flagged: 17 of 438 Read the chart above. Salary cells sit high or low on the vertical axis but close to zero %; small training or travel cells can sit far to the right with modest amounts. Each flagged group needs a different follow-up question. docs.text: What is the company's overall variance %? Three colleagues give three answers. Predict, then reveal Will "the average of all the cells' variance %" be close to the variance % computed from total actual and total budget? comparable = var [ var [ "budget_status" ] != "unknown budget" ] # cells with a known budget (including zero) unknown = var [ var [ "budget_status" ] == "unknown budget" ] total_actual = comparable [ "actual" ] . sum () total_budget = comparable [ "budget" ] . sum () monthly = comparable . groupby ( "month" )[[ "actual" , "budget" ]] . sum () print ( f "Comparable scope: actual { total_actual : ,.2f } | budget { total_budget : ,.2f } | " f "variance { total_actual - total_budget : +,.2f } " ) print ( f " Variance % from totals (correct): { ( total_actual - total_budget ) / total_budget : +.1% } " ) print ( f " Average of the 12 monthly %: { (( monthly [ 'actual' ] - monthly [ 'budget' ]) / monthly [ 'budget' ]) . mean () : +.1% } " ) print ( f " Average of every cell's %: { comparable [ 'variance_pct' ] . mean () : +.1% } " ) print ( f "Reported separately, actuals with unknown budget: { unknown [ 'actual' ] . sum () : ,.2f } " f "( { ', ' . join ( sorted ( unknown [ 'account' ] . unique ())) } , { len ( unknown ) } cells)" ) Comparable scope: actual 6,208,423.43 | budget 6,133,000.00 | variance +75,423.43 Variance % from totals (correct): +1.2% Average of the 12 monthly %: +1.2% Average of every cell's %: -0.2% Reported separately, actuals with unknown budget: 33,378.17 (Cloud hosting, 6 cells) Averaging cell percentages gives a tiny training budget the same weight as a large salary budget, so a few small cells drag the "average" far from the truth. Averaging monthly percentages is closer only because months have similar budgets; it is still the wrong method. Rules for a total variance % Add up actual and budget over the comparable scope (cells with a known budget). Compute the % from those totals. Report the unknown-budget actuals separately , with their amount. Never treat their budget as zero, and never leave them out silently.

docs.text: Question Method Trap to avoid What is one row? Check keys: posting_id ; (month, department, account) Assuming two tables share a grain How do I combine actuals and budgets? Aggregate postings first, then outer join with indicator and validate Joining postings to budgets (budget inflation); inner joins (lost cells) What if a budget is missing? Label it unknown ; report its actuals separately Filling unknown budgets with 0 Is a variance good or bad? Expense: positive = unfavourable Colouring every negative number red When does a % exist? Only when budget > 0 Dividing by zero budgets; 100% for budget-only lines without comment What is the total %? docs.text: Session 11 lab: Are deliveries on time? ¶ Build an on-time rate that counts every shipment that was due, including the ones still stuck in transit. Then compare carriers and warehouses fairly, describe delivery times and the backlog, fix three broken dashboards and recommend one process for the operations manager to investigate. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ Operations manager: "Customers are complaining about late deliveries, and December felt terrible. I can afford one improvement project next quarter. Tell me which carrier or warehouse process to investigate first, what the evidence is, and what else we would need to check before we blame anyone." Your answer must rest on numbers the manager can trust: the right denominator, visible volumes, a view of the late work still open, and comparisons that are not distorted by mix or by small groups. About the data shipments.csv (operations-v1) is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional retailer's outbound shipments dispatched in 2025, from three fictional warehouses with three fictional carriers. One row per shipment . It is a snapshot at the end of 31 December 2025 (the cutoff ): a blank delivered_date means "not delivered by the cutoff", not "never". How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G4 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I6 Challenge Debugging and a recommendation C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Check a snapshot's keys, statuses and date order before measuring anything. Build the due, not-yet-due and unknown-promise populations and reconcile them to the total. Calculate an on-time rate whose denominator includes overdue shipments still pending. Compare carriers and warehouses as ratios of counts, with due volumes and carrier mix visible. Describe completed-shipment lead times with mean, median and 90th percentile. Measure the overdue backlog and its age. Find and fix three common service-dashboard bugs. Recommend one process investigation, with its evidence and its limits. Evidence you keep: a carrier comparison, a lead-time distribution, a backlog summary and a short recommendation. Before you start ¶ Read the Session 11 lecture . Re-read the weighted-rate and Simpson's paradox parts of the Session 5 lecture . Run both setup cells. # Operations data setup (synthetic). Run this cell first. # Downloads the course's synthetic shipment data from GitHub and checks it is the exact version this course uses. import hashlib import io import os import urllib.request import pandas as pd OPERATIONS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Aayush181509/AnalyticsLecture/main/data/synthetic/operations-v1/" OPERATIONS_SHA256 = { "shipments.csv" : "7b5c0860beb2a16ba4f84a3dd0b5bdf9d88e968b720c6541f1dcb7d688c75687" } OPERATIONS_DIR = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_OPERATIONS_DIR" , "" ) CUTOFF = pd . G3 (Core): The on-time rate, overall ¶ On-time rate = on-time due shipments ÷ all due shipments, including those still pending. on_time = due [ "on_time" ] . sum () pending_due = due [ "pending" ] . sum () on_time_rate = on_time / len ( due ) print ( f "Due shipments: { len ( due ) } " ) print ( f " delivered on time: { on_time } " ) print ( f " delivered late: { ( due [ 'delivered_date' ] . notna () & ~ due [ 'on_time' ]) . sum () } " ) print ( f " still pending (overdue/today): { pending_due } " ) print ( f "On-time rate: { on_time } / { len ( due ) } = { on_time_rate : .1% } " ) print () delivered_only = due [ due [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] print ( f "Delivered-only rate (wrong): { delivered_only [ 'on_time' ] . mean () : .1% } from { len ( delivered_only ) } shipments" ) Due shipments: 5742 delivered on time: 4700 delivered late: 885 still pending (overdue/today): 157 On-time rate: 4700 / 5742 = 81.9% Delivered-only rate (wrong): 84.2% from 5585 shipments Write the result as a sentence in your evidence log, with the numerator, the denominator and what was excluded: "As of 31 December 2025, ___% of the ___ shipments due by then were delivered on time; ___ still pending are counted as late. ___ shipments promised for January and ___ with no recorded promise are not included." docs.text: Build an on-time rate that counts every shipment that was due, including the ones still stuck in transit. Then compare carriers and warehouses fairly, describe delivery times and the backlog, fix three broken dashboards and recommend one process for the operations manager to investigate. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive .
docs.title: Session 11 lab: Are deliveries on time?

docs.text: Operations manager: "Customers are complaining about late deliveries, and December felt terrible. I can afford one improvement project next quarter. Tell me which carrier or warehouse process to investigate first, what the evidence is, and what else we would need to check before we blame anyone." Your answer must rest on numbers the manager can trust: the right denominator, visible volumes, a view of the late work still open, and comparisons that are not distorted by mix or by small groups. About the data shipments.csv (operations-v1) is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional retailer's outbound shipments dispatched in 2025, from three fictional warehouses with three fictional carriers. One row per shipment . It is a snapshot at the end of 31 December 2025 (the cutoff ): a blank delivered_date means "not delivered by the cutoff", not "never".

docs.text: Check a snapshot's keys, statuses and date order before measuring anything. Build the due, not-yet-due and unknown-promise populations and reconcile them to the total. Calculate an on-time rate whose denominator includes overdue shipments still pending. Compare carriers and warehouses as ratios of counts, with due volumes and carrier mix visible. Describe completed-shipment lead times with mean, median and 90th percentile. Measure the overdue backlog and its age. Find and fix three common service-dashboard bugs. Recommend one process investigation, with its evidence and its limits. Evidence you keep: a carrier comparison, a lead-time distribution, a backlog summary and a short recommendation.

docs.text: shipment_id is unique; statuses agree with blank and known delivery dates; impossible date orders are zero. Due + not yet due + unknown promise = eligible shipments; plus canceled = all shipments. The on-time denominator includes due shipments still pending; not-yet-due shipments are excluded even if delivered. Unknown promise dates are excluded with their count stated . Every rate is a ratio of counts, with its due count shown; empty groups show "n/a". Lead times are labelled "completed shipments", with the count, and Express and Standard are kept apart. Days past due are at least 0, and due-today pending shipments are counted as late. Carrier and warehouse comparisons show the carrier mix, and small groups have intervals. Service measures count shipments, not orders.

docs.text: Session 11 lecture: Operations: service performance ¶ "How many deliveries arrive on time?" sounds like the easiest question in operations. It is easy to get wrong: shipments that have not arrived yet quietly drop out, early deliveries for next month sneak in, and a carrier's bad week hides inside a warehouse average. This lecture builds an on-time rate that a manager can trust, then looks at delivery times, the backlog of late work and fair comparisons between carriers and warehouses. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 10 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. A cost line had a budget of 10,000 and actual spending of 9,000. What is the variance in currency units? Is it favourable or unfavourable? Why do finance teams label variances "favourable" or "unfavourable" instead of relying only on the plus or minus sign? The budget table has one row per department per month; the actuals table has one row per invoice. In what order would you aggregate and join them, and why? After a join, the total budget is three times what finance expected. What is the most likely cause, and how would you check it? Line X is 40% over a small budget; line Y is 3% over a very large one. Which do you look at first, and what number helps you decide? What you will be able to explain ¶ How event dates and a cutoff turn a stream of shipments into a snapshot, and what each status means at that moment. Why the grain is the shipment, not the order, when one order can be split. Which shipments belong in the due population , and why not-yet-due and unknown-promise shipments stay out of the on-time rate. Why an on-time rate built on delivered shipments only overstates service (survivorship). How to describe lead time for completed shipments: distribution, mean versus median, percentiles and tails, box plots. How to measure the backlog : days past due and how old the late work is. How to compare carriers and warehouses fairly : ratios of counts, visible volumes, carrier mix , and honest uncertainty for small groups. This lecture reuses ideas from earlier sessions: weighted rates and Simpson's paradox ( Session 5 ), distributions and percentiles ( Session 4 ), trends ( Session 7 ) and intervals for rates ( Session 9 ). In the Lab you build the same measures yourself, fix three broken dashboards and recommend one process to investigate.
