Why Canceled No Nothing to deliver Promise unknown No, but count it and say so We cannot judge it; hiding the count hides a data problem Promised after the cutoff No ("not yet due"), even if already delivered Its deadline has not arrived; it is still workload Promised on or before the cutoff Yes ("due"), delivered or not The deadline has passed; an undelivered one is a failure Due and delivered on or before the promise Yes, and in the numerator On time The function below applies these rules. A second person averages the twelve monthly rates instead. Will either equal the overall rate from Part 5? by_month = service_table ( s . assign ( promised_month = s [ "promised_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" )), "promised_month" ) print ( f "Ratio of counts (all due shipments): { on_time_rate : .1% } <- right" ) print ( f "Mean of the three carrier percentages: { by_carrier [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } <- wrong method" ) print ( f "Mean of the twelve monthly percentages: { by_month [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } <- wrong method" ) Ratio of counts (all due shipments): 81.9% <- right Mean of the three carrier percentages: 82.0% <- wrong method Mean of the twelve monthly percentages: 83.9% <- wrong method The average of percentages gives every group the same weight, however many shipments it carried. With these three carriers it happens to land close to the right answer, which is luck, not a reason to use it. With months it does not: the busiest months at the end of the year were also the worst, and the simple average gives them no more weight than a quiet month, so it overstates the year. The overall rate must weight each group by its due volume, which is exactly what adding up the counts does. This is the weighted-rate rule from Session 5 : add the numerators, add the denominators, then divide. Before blaming it, ask what it ships with . Warehouses do not choose carriers at random. Predict, then reveal If the worst-looking warehouse sends most of its parcels with the weakest carrier, what will its rates look like within each carrier? wc = service_table ( s , [ "warehouse" , "carrier" ]) rates = wc [ "on_time_rate" ] . unstack ( "carrier" ) mix = wc [ "due" ] . unstack ( "carrier" ) mix_share = mix . div ( mix . sum ( axis = 1 ), axis = 0 ) print ( "On-time rate, warehouse × carrier:" ) display ( rates . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) print ( "Due shipments, warehouse × carrier:" ) display ( mix ) print ( "Carrier mix: share of each warehouse's due shipments" ) display ( mix_share . map ( " {:.0%} " . format )) On-time rate, warehouse × carrier: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 72.4% 85.5% 86.6% North hub 75.1% 85.1% 87.0% South hub 74.5% 85.8% 85.3% Due shipments, warehouse × carrier: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 605 518 967 North hub 454 502 1239 South hub 1000 239 218 Carrier mix: share of each warehouse's due shipments .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 29% 25% 46% North hub 21% 23% 56% South hub 69% 16% 15% Read the three tables together. Within each carrier, the warehouses have similar on-time rates. The warehouse that looks worst overall sends a much larger share of its shipments with the weakest carrier. Its overall rate is low mainly because of its carrier mix , not because its own process is worse. This is the same mechanism as Simpson's paradox in Session 5 : an overall comparison that is driven by different mixes across groups. One way to make the comparison fair is to ask: what would each warehouse score if it had the company's overall carrier mix? company_mix = mix . sum () / mix . sum () . sum () # share of all due shipments by carrier mix_adjusted = ( rates * company_mix ) . sum ( axis = 1 ) # each warehouse's carrier rates, company weights pd . DataFrame ({ "actual on-time rate" : by_warehouse [ "on_time_rate" ], "with the company's carrier mix" : mix_adjusted , }) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } actual on-time rate with the company's carrier mix warehouse Central hub 82.2% 81.3% North hub 84.1% 82.3% South hub 78.0% 81.5% With the same carrier mix, the warehouses are close together. So the first investigation is probably not that warehouse's packing process: it is the carrier it relies on, or the reason it relies on that carrier (location, contracts, the routes it serves). Part of the answer needs evidence the data do not hold, which is the right thing to say to the manager. Check your understanding 6 A director says: "The worst warehouse is the problem; let's retrain its staff." Using the tables above, write two sentences that explain why that may be the wrong project. Part 10: Small groups and uncertainty ¶ Some warehouse × carrier cells have far fewer due shipments than others. As in Session 9 , a rate from a few hundred shipments wobbles more than one from a few thousand. An approximate 95% interval for a rate is rate ± 1.96 × √(rate × (1 − rate) ÷ due) . Strictly, these shipments are not a random sample, but the interval is a useful guide to how much a rate could move by chance from one period to the next. Treat any gap smaller than the intervals as "not shown". wc_ci = wc . copy () half_width = 1.96 * np . sqrt ( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] * ( 1 - wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ]) / wc_ci [ "due" ]) wc_ci [ "low" ], wc_ci [ "high" ] = wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] - half_width , wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] + half_width wc_ci = wc_ci . sort_values ( "on_time_rate" ) labels = [ f " { w } × { c } ( { n } due)" for ( w , c ), n in zip ( wc_ci . index , wc_ci [ "due" ])] ax = plt . gca () ax . errorbar ( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] * 100 , range ( len ( wc_ci )), xerr = [( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] - wc_ci [ "low" ]) * 100 , ( wc_ci [ "high" ] - wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ]) * 100 ], fmt = "o" , capsize = 4 ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( len ( wc_ci )), labels ) ax . set_title ( "On-time rate by warehouse × carrier, with approximate 95 % i ntervals" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "On-time rate (%)" ) plt . show () Read the chart above. Groups with fewer due shipments have wider bars. Cells for the same carrier overlap across warehouses, while the gap between the weakest carrier and the others is larger than the bars. That is the pattern that justifies a carrier-focused investigation, rather than a warehouse one. Check your understanding 7 A cell with 40 due shipments has an on-time rate 8 points below the rest. Would you put it at the top of your report? What would you do instead? Part 11: Worked case: the monthly trend and the December disruption ¶ The manager "felt" December was terrible. We build the monthly on-time rate by promised month (the month the deadline fell in), correctly and with the delivered-only shortcut, and show the due volume underneath. due = s [ s [ "population" ] == "due" ] . assign ( promised_month = lambda d : d [ "promised_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" )) monthly = due . groupby ( "promised_month" ) . agg ( due = ( "on_time" , "size" ), on_time = ( "on_time" , "sum" ), pending = ( "pending" , "sum" )) monthly [ "correct rate" ] = monthly [ "on_time" ] / monthly [ "due" ] delivered_m = due [ due [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] . groupby ( "promised_month" )[ "on_time" ] . agg ([ "sum" , "size" ]) monthly [ "delivered-only rate" ] = delivered_m [ "sum" ] / delivered_m [ "size" ] fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 6 ), sharex = True , gridspec_kw = { "height_ratios" : [ 2 , 1 ]}) x = monthly . index . to_timestamp () ax1 . plot ( x , monthly [ "correct rate" ] * 100 , marker = "o" , label = "Correct: all due shipments" ) ax1 . plot ( x , monthly [ "delivered-only rate" ] * 100 , marker = "o" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Wrong: delivered only" ) ax1 . set_title ( "On-time rate by promised month, 2025" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "On-time rate (%)" ) ax1 . legend ( loc = "lower left" ) ax2 . bar ( x , monthly [ "due" ], width = 20 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Due shipments" ) ax2 . bar ( x , monthly [ "pending" ], width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" , label = "Of which still pending" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Shipments" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Promised month" ) ax2 . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () monthly . tail ( 3 ) . assign ( ** { c : monthly [ c ] . tail ( 3 ) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) for c in [ "correct rate" , "delivered-only rate" ]}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due on_time pending correct rate delivered-only rate promised_month 2025-10 403 359 0 89.1% 89.1% 2025-11 627 474 0 75.6% 75.6% 2025-12 790 437 157 55.3% 69.0% Read the chart from top to bottom: For most of the year the two lines are identical : by the cutoff, every shipment promised before December had been delivered, so the filter removed nothing. In the last two months, due volume rises (the peak season) and the rate falls. In December the lines split. Many December shipments are still pending at the cutoff; the delivered-only line drops them and reports a much milder decline than the correct line. So the manager's feeling was right, and the delivered-only dashboard would have understated the disruption at exactly the moment it mattered. One honest caveat: December's correct rate is a snapshot . Some of those pending shipments will be delivered in January, all of them late, so the December rate cannot go up, but the lead-time picture for December is still incomplete. The manager-ready summary: dec = monthly . iloc [ - 1 ] worst_carrier = by_carrier [ "on_time_rate" ] . idxmin () print ( f "As of 31 December 2025, { on_time_rate : .1% } of the { len ( s [ s [ 'population' ] == 'due' ]) } shipments due in 2025 " f "were delivered on time ( { populations [ 'not yet due' ] } not yet due and { populations [ 'unknown promise' ] } " f "with no recorded promise are excluded). December was the worst month: { dec [ 'correct rate' ] : .1% } of " f " { dec [ 'due' ] : .0f } due shipments, with { dec [ 'pending' ] : .0f } still pending; a delivered-only report would " f "have shown { dec [ 'delivered-only rate' ] : .1% } . { worst_carrier } has the lowest on-time rate of the three " f "carriers ( { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'on_time_rate' ] : .1% } of { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'due' ] } due) " f "and the largest overdue backlog ( { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'pending' ] } pending)." ) As of 31 December 2025, 81.9% of the 5742 shipments due in 2025 were delivered on time (99 not yet due and 12 with no recorded promise are excluded). December was the worst month: 55.3% of 790 due shipments, with 157 still pending; a delivered-only report would have shown 69.0%. ParcelOne has the lowest on-time rate of the three carriers (74.0% of 2059 due) and the largest overdue backlog (129 pending). Before recommending "investigate the carrier", you would want evidence the data do not hold: whether the carrier serves harder routes or regions, when the warehouse actually handed parcels over (a late handover is the warehouse's delay, not the carrier's), whether the December peak exceeded agreed volumes, and whether the delivery scans are reliable. docs.text: "How many deliveries arrive on time?" sounds like the easiest question in operations. It is easy to get wrong: shipments that have not arrived yet quietly drop out, early deliveries for next month sneak in, and a carrier's bad week hides inside a warehouse average. This lecture builds an on-time rate that a manager can trust, then looks at delivery times, the backlog of late work and fair comparisons between carriers and warehouses. What is the variance in currency units? Is it favourable or unfavourable? Why do finance teams label variances "favourable" or "unfavourable" instead of relying only on the plus or minus sign? The budget table has one row per department per month; the actuals table has one row per invoice. In what order would you aggregate and join them, and why? After a join, the total budget is three times what finance expected. What is the most likely cause, and how would you check it? Line X is 40% over a small budget; line Y is 3% over a very large one. Which do you look at first, and what number helps you decide?

docs.text: How event dates and a cutoff turn a stream of shipments into a snapshot, and what each status means at that moment. Why the grain is the shipment, not the order, when one order can be split. Which shipments belong in the due population , and why not-yet-due and unknown-promise shipments stay out of the on-time rate. Why an on-time rate built on delivered shipments only overstates service (survivorship). How to describe lead time for completed shipments: distribution, mean versus median, percentiles and tails, box plots. How to measure the backlog : days past due and how old the late work is. How to compare carriers and warehouses fairly : ratios of counts, visible volumes, carrier mix , and honest uncertainty for small groups. This lecture reuses ideas from earlier sessions: weighted rates and Simpson's paradox ( Session 5 ), distributions and percentiles ( Session 4 ), trends ( Session 7 ) and intervals for rates ( Session 9 ). In the Lab you build the same measures yourself, fix three broken dashboards and recommend one process to investigate. docs.text: Operations manager: "Customers are complaining about late deliveries, and December felt terrible. I can afford one improvement project next quarter. Tell me which carrier or warehouse process to investigate first, and how sure you are." The manager is not asking for a pretty chart. They need to choose one thing to investigate , so the analysis must: The manager needs So we measure How reliable is delivery overall? The on-time rate, with the right numerator and denominator Where is reliability worst? On-time rate by carrier and warehouse, with volumes How bad is the late work right now? The backlog of overdue shipments and how old it is How long do deliveries take? Lead-time distribution, not only its average Is a difference real or just mix or noise? Mix-aware comparisons and intervals for small groups About the data shipments.csv (operations-v1) is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: a fictional retailer's outbound shipments dispatched in 2025, with three fictional warehouses and three fictional carriers. It is a snapshot taken at the end of 31 December 2025 , the cutoff . Dates are calendar days.
docs.title: Part 1: The decision

docs.text: Each shipment has up to three event dates : Date Meaning Can it be blank? dispatch_date The day it left the warehouse No: every row was dispatched by the cutoff promised_date The day delivery was promised to the customer Yes, for a few rows: the promise was not recorded (a data-quality problem) delivered_date The day it was delivered Yes: not delivered by the cutoff , or canceled A blank delivered_date does not mean "never". It means " not yet, as far as we knew on 31 December ". Some of those shipments will arrive in January. Data like this, where the outcome is unknown at the snapshot, is called censored : we only know the delivery takes at least this long. shipments = load_shipments () print ( "Rows:" , len ( shipments ), "| columns:" , list ( shipments . columns )) shipments [[ "shipment_id" , "order_id" , "carrier" , "dispatch_date" , "promised_date" , "delivered_date" , "status" ]] . head () Rows: 5893 | columns: ['shipment_id', 'order_id', 'warehouse_id', 'warehouse', 'carrier_id', 'carrier', 'service', 'dispatch_date', 'promised_date', 'delivered_date', 'status'] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } shipment_id order_id carrier dispatch_date promised_date delivered_date status 0 SHP-00001 ORD-00001 ParcelOne 2025-01-01 2025-01-03 2025-01-03 delivered 1 SHP-00002 ORD-00002 SwiftRoute 2025-01-01 2025-01-06 2025-01-04 delivered 2 SHP-00003 ORD-00003 ParcelOne 2025-01-01 2025-01-06 2025-01-05 delivered 3 SHP-00004 ORD-00004 SwiftRoute 2025-01-01 2025-01-06 2025-01-18 delivered 4 SHP-00005 ORD-00005 Regional Express 2025-01-01 2025-01-06 2025-01-04 delivered First check what the status column says, and whether it agrees with the dates. status_check = pd . crosstab ( shipments [ "status" ], [ shipments [ "delivered_date" ] . notna () . map ({ True : "delivered date known" , False : "delivered date blank" })], margins = True , margins_name = "All" , ) status_check .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } delivered_date delivered date blank delivered date known All status canceled 40 0 40 delivered 0 5603 5603 in_transit 250 0 250 All 290 5603 5893 In the table above, every delivered shipment has a delivery date and every in_transit or canceled shipment has none. That agreement is worth checking every time: if they disagreed, you would have to decide which one to trust before measuring anything. Next, date order . Nothing can be delivered before it is dispatched, and nothing in a 31 December snapshot can be delivered after 31 December. checks = { "delivered before dispatch" : ( shipments [ "delivered_date" ] < shipments [ "dispatch_date" ]) . sum (), "promised before dispatch" : ( shipments [ "promised_date" ] < shipments [ "dispatch_date" ]) . sum (), "dispatched after the cutoff" : ( shipments [ "dispatch_date" ] > CUTOFF ) . sum (), "delivered after the cutoff" : ( shipments [ "delivered_date" ] > CUTOFF ) . sum (), "promised after the cutoff (not yet due)" : ( shipments [ "promised_date" ] > CUTOFF ) . sum (), "promise date missing" : shipments [ "promised_date" ] . isna () . sum (), } pd . Series ( checks , name = "rows" ) delivered before dispatch 0 promised before dispatch 0 dispatched after the cutoff 0 delivered after the cutoff 0 promised after the cutoff (not yet due) 99 promise date missing 12 Name: rows, dtype: int64 Read the counts above. The first four are impossible events and should be zero. The last two are not errors : some promises fall in January (the customer was told "you will have it on 2 January"), and a few promise dates were never recorded. Both groups need special treatment in Part 4. Check your understanding 1 A shipment has status in_transit and was promised for 28 December. Is it late? Will it always be late? What would you need to know to answer the second question?

docs.text: A customer order can be split into more than one shipment (for example, one item ships from another warehouse). The carrier delivers shipments, not orders. print ( "Unique shipment_id:" , shipments [ "shipment_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Unique order_id: " , shipments [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print () print ( "Shipments per order:" ) shipments . groupby ( "order_id" ) . size () . value_counts () . sort_index () . rename_axis ( "shipments in the order" ) . rename ( "orders" ) Unique shipment_id: True Unique order_id: False Shipments per order: shipments in the order 1 4507 2 693 Name: orders, dtype: int64 So shipment_id is the key (one row each) and order_id repeats. One split order can have one part on time and one part late. If you count orders , you have to invent a rule ("an order is on time if its first part is?"), and the denominator no longer matches the carrier's work. Count shipments for service measures. You will see what goes wrong when someone counts orders in the lab.
docs.title: Part 3: The grain is the shipment

docs.text: Before touching 5,000 rows, we work through eight made-up shipments by hand. Each one is a different situation you will meet in real data. fixture = pd . DataFrame ({ "shipment_id" : [ "A" , "B" , "C" , "D" , "E" , "F" , "G" , "H" ], "situation" : [ "on time" , "late" , "overdue, still pending" , "due today, still pending" , "not yet due, delivered early" , "unknown promise" , "canceled" , "delivered on the promise day" ], "status" : [ "delivered" , "delivered" , "in_transit" , "in_transit" , "delivered" , "delivered" , "canceled" , "delivered" ], "dispatch_date" : [ "2025-12-05" , "2025-12-05" , "2025-12-15" , "2025-12-26" , "2025-12-28" , "2025-12-08" , "2025-12-22" , "2025-12-26" ], "promised_date" : [ "2025-12-10" , "2025-12-10" , "2025-12-20" , "2025-12-31" , "2026-01-02" , None , "2025-12-27" , "2025-12-31" ], "delivered_date" : [ "2025-12-09" , "2025-12-14" , None , None , "2025-12-30" , "2025-12-12" , None , "2025-12-31" ], }) for col in [ "dispatch_date" , "promised_date" , "delivered_date" ]: fixture [ col ] = pd . to_datetime ( fixture [ col ]) fixture .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } shipment_id situation status dispatch_date promised_date delivered_date 0 A on time delivered 2025-12-05 2025-12-10 2025-12-09 1 B late delivered 2025-12-05 2025-12-10 2025-12-14 2 C overdue, still pending in_transit 2025-12-15 2025-12-20 NaT 3 D due today, still pending in_transit 2025-12-26 2025-12-31 NaT 4 E not yet due, delivered early delivered 2025-12-28 2026-01-02 2025-12-30 5 F unknown promise delivered 2025-12-08 NaT 2025-12-12 6 G canceled canceled 2025-12-22 2025-12-27 NaT 7 H delivered on the promise day delivered 2025-12-26 2025-12-31 2025-12-31 Predict, then reveal The cutoff is the end of 31 December 2025. For each row, decide: is it in the due population (promised on or before the cutoff, not canceled)? If it is, was it on time (delivered on or before the promise)? Then write down the numerator (on-time due shipments) and the denominator (all due shipments) before you run the next cell. The rules, from the data's metric contract: Situation In the on-time denominator? Why Canceled No Nothing to deliver Promise unknown No, but count it and say so We cannot judge it; hiding the count hides a data problem Promised after the cutoff No ("not yet due"), even if already delivered Its deadline has not arrived; it is still workload Promised on or before the cutoff Yes ("due"), delivered or not The deadline has passed; an undelivered one is a failure Due and delivered on or before the promise Yes, and in the numerator On time The function below applies these rules. We reuse it on the real data. def add_service_columns ( df , cutoff = CUTOFF ): """Label each shipment's population at the cutoff and add on-time, pending and lead-time columns.""" out = df . copy () out [ "population" ] = np . select ( [ out [ "status" ] == "canceled" , out [ "promised_date" ] . isna (), out [ "promised_date" ] > cutoff ], [ "canceled" , "unknown promise" , "not yet due" ], default = "due" , ) delivered = out [ "delivered_date" ] . notna () out [ "on_time" ] = delivered & ( out [ "delivered_date" ] <= out [ "promised_date" ]) out [ "pending" ] = ~ delivered & ( out [ "status" ] != "canceled" ) # Days past due: only for due shipments still pending; at least 0 (due today = 0). overdue = ( out [ "population" ] == "due" ) & out [ "pending" ] out [ "days_past_due" ] = ( cutoff - out [ "promised_date" ]) . dt . days . clip ( lower = 0 ) . where ( overdue ) # Lead time: completed (delivered) shipments only; blank otherwise. out [ "lead_days" ] = ( out [ "delivered_date" ] - out [ "dispatch_date" ]) . dt . days return out fx = add_service_columns ( fixture ) fx [[ "shipment_id" , "situation" , "population" , "on_time" , "pending" , "days_past_due" , "lead_days" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } shipment_id situation population on_time pending days_past_due lead_days 0 A on time due True False NaN 4.00 1 B late due False False NaN 9.00 2 C overdue, still pending due False True 11.00 NaN 3 D due today, still pending due False True 0.00 NaN 4 E not yet due, delivered early not yet due True False NaN 2.00 5 F unknown promise unknown promise False False NaN 4.00 6 G canceled canceled False False NaN NaN 7 H delivered on the promise day due True False NaN 5.00 due_fx = fx [ fx [ "population" ] == "due" ] print ( "Due shipments (denominator): " , len ( due_fx ), "->" , list ( due_fx [ "shipment_id" ])) print ( "On time among due (numerator): " , due_fx [ "on_time" ] . sum (), "->" , list ( due_fx . loc [ due_fx [ "on_time" ], "shipment_id" ])) print ( f "On-time rate: { due_fx [ 'on_time' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) print () delivered_fx = due_fx [ due_fx [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] print ( f "'Delivered only' rate (wrong): { delivered_fx [ 'on_time' ] . mean () : .0% } from { len ( delivered_fx ) } shipments" ) print ( "Excluded and reported:" , fx . loc [ fx [ "population" ] != "due" , "population" ] . value_counts () . to_dict ()) Due shipments (denominator): 5 -> ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'H'] On time among due (numerator): 2 -> ['A', 'H'] On-time rate: 40% 'Delivered only' rate (wrong): 67% from 3 shipments Excluded and reported: {'not yet due': 1, 'unknown promise': 1, 'canceled': 1} Compare the output with your prediction. Three details trip people up: C and D have not arrived, so they are in the denominator and not in the numerator. D was due today and is still pending: it is a failure at the snapshot , with 0 days past due. E arrived early, but its deadline is in January. Counting it now would let next month's easy wins flatter this month's score. H was delivered on the promise day. "On or before" means it is on time; check the boundary every time you write a comparison ( <= , not < ). docs.text: Now the real data. First label every shipment and reconcile the populations: every shipment must land in exactly one group, and the groups must add back to the total. s = add_service_columns ( shipments ) populations = s [ "population" ] . value_counts () . reindex ([ "due" , "not yet due" , "unknown promise" , "canceled" ]) display ( populations . rename ( "shipments" ) . to_frame ()) print ( "Groups add up to all shipments:" , populations . sum () == len ( s )) eligible = s [ s [ "population" ] != "canceled" ] print ( "Eligible (not canceled):" , len ( eligible ), "= due + not yet due + unknown promise:" , populations [[ "due" , "not yet due" , "unknown promise" ]] . sum () == len ( eligible )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } shipments population due 5742 not yet due 99 unknown promise 12 canceled 40 Groups add up to all shipments: True Eligible (not canceled): 5853 = due + not yet due + unknown promise: True Inside the due population, some shipments were delivered and some are still pending: due = s [ s [ "population" ] == "due" ] due_breakdown = pd . Series ({ "delivered on time" : ( due [ "on_time" ]) . sum (), "delivered late" : ( due [ "delivered_date" ] . notna () & ~ due [ "on_time" ]) . sum (), "still pending (overdue or due today)" : due [ "pending" ] . sum (), }, name = "due shipments" ) display ( due_breakdown . to_frame ()) on_time_rate = due [ "on_time" ] . sum () / len ( due ) print ( f "On-time rate = { due [ 'on_time' ] . sum () } on-time due shipments / { len ( due ) } due shipments = { on_time_rate : .1% } " ) print ( f "Not counted in the rate: { populations [ 'not yet due' ] } not yet due, " f " { populations [ 'unknown promise' ] } with an unknown promise date (reported, not hidden)." ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due shipments delivered on time 4700 delivered late 885 still pending (overdue or due today) 157 On-time rate = 4700 on-time due shipments / 5742 due shipments = 81.9% Not counted in the rate: 99 not yet due, 12 with an unknown promise date (reported, not hidden). That printed sentence is the format to use with a manager: the rate and its numerator and denominator, and what was left out and why. Zero denominators If a group has no due shipments (a new carrier, a quiet week), its on-time rate is not available , never 0% or 100%. pandas gives NaN when you divide 0 by 0; show it as "n/a" with the count of 0.
docs.title: Part 5: The due population and the on-time rate

docs.text: Many dashboards start with a filter status == "delivered" , because only delivered rows have a delivery date to compare. That one filter removes every overdue shipment that is still stuck: the worst cases disappear. Predict, then reveal Will the delivered-only rate be higher or lower than the correct rate? By a lot or a little? delivered_due = due [ due [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] delivered_only_rate = delivered_due [ "on_time" ] . mean () comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "on time" : [ due [ "on_time" ] . sum (), delivered_due [ "on_time" ] . sum ()], "denominator" : [ len ( due ), len ( delivered_due )], "on-time rate" : [ on_time_rate , delivered_only_rate ], }, index = [ "Correct: all due shipments" , "Wrong: delivered only" ]) display ( comparison . assign ( ** { "on-time rate" : comparison [ "on-time rate" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )})) print ( f "Shipments that vanish with the filter: { len ( due ) - len ( delivered_due ) } (all of them failures)" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } on time denominator on-time rate Correct: all due shipments 4700 5742 81.9% Wrong: delivered only 4700 5585 84.2% Shipments that vanish with the filter: 157 (all of them failures) The numerator is the same in both rows; only the denominator shrinks. This is survivorship : by looking only at shipments that "survived" to delivery, you lose exactly the ones that failed worst. The gap grows when things go badly, because that is when more shipments are stuck. In other words, the wrong method looks best exactly when the operation is worst . Part 11 shows this month by month. Check your understanding 3 A carrier stops delivering entirely for the last week of the year. What happens to its delivered-only on-time rate for that week? What happens to the correct rate?
docs.title: Part 6: Why "delivered only" overstates service

docs.text: The on-time rate is a yes/no measure. Lead time (delivered date − dispatch date, in calendar days) shows how long deliveries take. It exists only for completed shipments, so always say so and give the count. Predict, then reveal Lead times cannot be negative, most deliveries take a few days, and a few take weeks. Will the mean be above, below or equal to the median? completed = s [ s [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] lead_summary = completed . groupby ( "service" )[ "lead_days" ] . agg ( completed = "count" , mean = "mean" , median = "median" , p75 = lambda x : x . quantile ( 0.75 ), p90 = lambda x : x . quantile ( 0.90 ), p95 = lambda x : x . quantile ( 0.95 ), max = "max" , ) display ( lead_summary ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 ), sharey = False ) for ax , ( service , part ) in zip ( axes , completed . groupby ( "service" )): bins = np . arange ( 0 , part [ "lead_days" ] . max () + 2 ) - 0.5 ax . hist ( part [ "lead_days" ], bins = bins ) ax . axvline ( part [ "lead_days" ] . mean (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Mean" ) ax . axvline ( part [ "lead_days" ] . median (), color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Median" ) ax . set_title ( f " { service } : completed shipments only" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Lead time (calendar days)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Shipments" ) ax . legend () fig . tight_layout () plt . show () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } completed mean median p75 p90 p95 max service Express 1200 3.08 2.00 3.00 4.00 12.00 24.00 Standard 4403 4.90 4.00 4.00 6.00 15.00 26.00 Read the charts and table above: The distributions are right-skewed : a tall peak at a few days and a long thin tail of slow deliveries. The tail pulls the mean above the median . The median says "a typical delivery"; the mean is pushed up by the stragglers. Percentiles describe the tail directly. "90% of Standard deliveries arrive within p90 days" is a promise a manager can check against the contract; the mean is not. Express and Standard have different promises (2 and 5 days), so never pool them into one lead-time average: a change in the share of Express would move the average even if no delivery got faster.

docs.text: A box plot shows the same distribution compactly, which is handy for comparing many groups side by side. The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile, the line inside is the median, and the dots are unusually slow (or fast) deliveries. standard = completed [ completed [ "service" ] == "Standard" ] carriers = sorted ( standard [ "carrier" ] . unique ()) ax = plt . gca () ax . boxplot ([ standard . loc [ standard [ "carrier" ] == c , "lead_days" ] for c in carriers ], flierprops = { "marker" : "." , "markersize" : 4 , "alpha" : 0.5 }) ax . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , len ( carriers ) + 1 ), carriers ) ax . axhline ( 5 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Standard promise: 5 days" ) ax . set_title ( "Standard lead time by carrier, completed shipments" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Lead time (calendar days)" ) ax . legend ( loc = "upper right" ) plt . show ()

docs.text: Lead time is measured only for shipments that arrived. The shipments still pending at the cutoff are, by definition, the ones that are taking a long time, and they are missing from the chart. So completed-only lead time is optimistic , the same survivorship problem as Part 6. The pending shipments are not useless: we know they have taken at least this long so far. pending_due = s [( s [ "population" ] == "due" ) & s [ "pending" ]] age_so_far = ( CUTOFF - pending_due [ "dispatch_date" ]) . dt . days print ( f "Completed shipments in the lead-time chart: { len ( completed ) } " ) print ( f "Due shipments still pending, not in the chart: { len ( pending_due ) } " ) print ( f "Their time since dispatch so far: median { age_so_far . median () : .0f } days, max { age_so_far . max () } days (and counting)" ) Completed shipments in the lead-time chart: 5603 Due shipments still pending, not in the chart: 157 Their time since dispatch so far: median 11 days, max 24 days (and counting) Check your understanding 4 Your report says "median Standard lead time: x days (completed shipments)". A manager asks why you added "(completed shipments)". Explain in one sentence, and say which direction the true figure probably lies.
docs.title: What completed-only lead time leaves out

docs.text: The on-time rate looks back. The backlog looks at today: how many due shipments are still pending, and how late they already are. Days past due = cutoff − promised date , for due shipments still pending, never below 0. A shipment promised for the cutoff day and still pending has 0 days past due, but it is still a failure at the snapshot. bucket_edges = [ - 1 , 0 , 3 , 7 , 14 , 10_000 ] bucket_names = [ "0 (due today)" , "1–3" , "4–7" , "8–14" , "15+" ] pending_due = pending_due . assign ( age_band = pd . cut ( pending_due [ "days_past_due" ], bucket_edges , labels = bucket_names )) backlog = pd . crosstab ( pending_due [ "carrier" ], pending_due [ "age_band" ], margins = True , margins_name = "All" ) display ( backlog ) ax = backlog . drop ( index = "All" , columns = "All" ) . T . plot ( kind = "bar" , stacked = True , rot = 0 ) ax . set_title ( "Overdue pending shipments at the cutoff, by days past due" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Days past due" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Shipments" ) plt . show () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } age_band 0 (due today) 1–3 4–7 8–14 15+ All carrier ParcelOne 6 30 37 35 21 129 Regional Express 2 3 3 0 0 8 SwiftRoute 5 6 4 3 2 20 All 13 39 44 38 23 157 Read the table and chart above. A backlog report answers three questions: how many (size), how old (age bands, or median and maximum days past due) and whose (carrier, warehouse). A backlog concentrated in one carrier's old bands is a different problem from a large but fresh backlog spread across everyone, which might just be a busy final week. Check your understanding 5 Two carriers each have 20 overdue pending shipments. For one, all are 1–3 days past due; for the other, half are more than 14 days past due. Which needs a phone call first, and what would you ask?

Part 9: Comparing carriers and warehouses fairly

docs.text: def service_table ( df , by ): """On-time rate as a ratio of counts for each group, with the due count visible.""" due_rows = df [ df [ "population" ] == "due" ] t = due_rows . groupby ( by ) . agg ( due = ( "on_time" , "size" ), on_time = ( "on_time" , "sum" ), pending = ( "pending" , "sum" )) t [ "on_time_rate" ] = t [ "on_time" ] / t [ "due" ] . where ( t [ "due" ] > 0 ) # n/a when nothing is due return t by_carrier = service_table ( s , "carrier" ) by_carrier . assign ( on_time_rate = by_carrier [ "on_time_rate" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due on_time pending on_time_rate carrier ParcelOne 2059 1524 129 74.0% Regional Express 1259 1075 8 85.4% SwiftRoute 2424 2101 20 86.7% Predict, then reveal Someone averages the three carrier rates above to get "the company's on-time rate". A second person averages the twelve monthly rates instead. Will either equal the overall rate from Part 5? by_month = service_table ( s . assign ( promised_month = s [ "promised_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" )), "promised_month" ) print ( f "Ratio of counts (all due shipments): { on_time_rate : .1% } <- right" ) print ( f "Mean of the three carrier percentages: { by_carrier [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } <- wrong method" ) print ( f "Mean of the twelve monthly percentages: { by_month [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } <- wrong method" ) Ratio of counts (all due shipments): 81.9% <- right Mean of the three carrier percentages: 82.0% <- wrong method Mean of the twelve monthly percentages: 83.9% <- wrong method The average of percentages gives every group the same weight, however many shipments it carried. With these three carriers it happens to land close to the right answer, which is luck, not a reason to use it. With months it does not: the busiest months at the end of the year were also the worst, and the simple average gives them no more weight than a quiet month, so it overstates the year. The overall rate must weight each group by its due volume, which is exactly what adding up the counts does. This is the weighted-rate rule from Session 5 : add the numerators, add the denominators, then divide.
docs.title: Ratios of counts, with the counts visible

docs.text: by_warehouse = service_table ( s , "warehouse" ) by_warehouse . assign ( on_time_rate = by_warehouse [ "on_time_rate" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due on_time pending on_time_rate warehouse Central hub 2090 1718 49 82.2% North hub 2195 1846 49 84.1% South hub 1457 1136 59 78.0% One warehouse looks clearly worse than the others. Before blaming it, ask what it ships with . Warehouses do not choose carriers at random. Predict, then reveal If the worst-looking warehouse sends most of its parcels with the weakest carrier, what will its rates look like within each carrier? wc = service_table ( s , [ "warehouse" , "carrier" ]) rates = wc [ "on_time_rate" ] . unstack ( "carrier" ) mix = wc [ "due" ] . unstack ( "carrier" ) mix_share = mix . div ( mix . sum ( axis = 1 ), axis = 0 ) print ( "On-time rate, warehouse × carrier:" ) display ( rates . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) print ( "Due shipments, warehouse × carrier:" ) display ( mix ) print ( "Carrier mix: share of each warehouse's due shipments" ) display ( mix_share . map ( " {:.0%} " . format )) On-time rate, warehouse × carrier: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 72.4% 85.5% 86.6% North hub 75.1% 85.1% 87.0% South hub 74.5% 85.8% 85.3% Due shipments, warehouse × carrier: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 605 518 967 North hub 454 502 1239 South hub 1000 239 218 Carrier mix: share of each warehouse's due shipments .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carrier ParcelOne Regional Express SwiftRoute warehouse Central hub 29% 25% 46% North hub 21% 23% 56% South hub 69% 16% 15% Read the three tables together. Within each carrier, the warehouses have similar on-time rates. The warehouse that looks worst overall sends a much larger share of its shipments with the weakest carrier. Its overall rate is low mainly because of its carrier mix , not because its own process is worse. This is the same mechanism as Simpson's paradox in Session 5 : an overall comparison that is driven by different mixes across groups. One way to make the comparison fair is to ask: what would each warehouse score if it had the company's overall carrier mix? company_mix = mix . sum () / mix . sum () . sum () # share of all due shipments by carrier mix_adjusted = ( rates * company_mix ) . sum ( axis = 1 ) # each warehouse's carrier rates, company weights pd . DataFrame ({ "actual on-time rate" : by_warehouse [ "on_time_rate" ], "with the company's carrier mix" : mix_adjusted , }) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } actual on-time rate with the company's carrier mix warehouse Central hub 82.2% 81.3% North hub 84.1% 82.3% South hub 78.0% 81.5% With the same carrier mix, the warehouses are close together. So the first investigation is probably not that warehouse's packing process: it is the carrier it relies on, or the reason it relies on that carrier (location, contracts, the routes it serves). Part of the answer needs evidence the data do not hold, which is the right thing to say to the manager. Check your understanding 6 A director says: "The worst warehouse is the problem; let's retrain its staff." Using the tables above, write two sentences that explain why that may be the wrong project.
docs.title: Warehouses, and the carrier mix

docs.text: Some warehouse × carrier cells have far fewer due shipments than others. As in Session 9 , a rate from a few hundred shipments wobbles more than one from a few thousand. An approximate 95% interval for a rate is rate ± 1.96 × √(rate × (1 − rate) ÷ due) . Strictly, these shipments are not a random sample, but the interval is a useful guide to how much a rate could move by chance from one period to the next. Treat any gap smaller than the intervals as "not shown". wc_ci = wc . copy () half_width = 1.96 * np . sqrt ( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] * ( 1 - wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ]) / wc_ci [ "due" ]) wc_ci [ "low" ], wc_ci [ "high" ] = wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] - half_width , wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] + half_width wc_ci = wc_ci . sort_values ( "on_time_rate" ) labels = [ f " { w } × { c } ( { n } due)" for ( w , c ), n in zip ( wc_ci . index , wc_ci [ "due" ])] ax = plt . gca () ax . errorbar ( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] * 100 , range ( len ( wc_ci )), xerr = [( wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ] - wc_ci [ "low" ]) * 100 , ( wc_ci [ "high" ] - wc_ci [ "on_time_rate" ]) * 100 ], fmt = "o" , capsize = 4 ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( len ( wc_ci )), labels ) ax . set_title ( "On-time rate by warehouse × carrier, with approximate 95 % i ntervals" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "On-time rate (%)" ) plt . show () Read the chart above. Groups with fewer due shipments have wider bars. Cells for the same carrier overlap across warehouses, while the gap between the weakest carrier and the others is larger than the bars. That is the pattern that justifies a carrier-focused investigation, rather than a warehouse one. Check your understanding 7 A cell with 40 due shipments has an on-time rate 8 points below the rest. Would you put it at the top of your report? What would you do instead?

docs.text: The manager "felt" December was terrible. We build the monthly on-time rate by promised month (the month the deadline fell in), correctly and with the delivered-only shortcut, and show the due volume underneath. due = s [ s [ "population" ] == "due" ] . assign ( promised_month = lambda d : d [ "promised_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" )) monthly = due . groupby ( "promised_month" ) . agg ( due = ( "on_time" , "size" ), on_time = ( "on_time" , "sum" ), pending = ( "pending" , "sum" )) monthly [ "correct rate" ] = monthly [ "on_time" ] / monthly [ "due" ] delivered_m = due [ due [ "delivered_date" ] . notna ()] . groupby ( "promised_month" )[ "on_time" ] . agg ([ "sum" , "size" ]) monthly [ "delivered-only rate" ] = delivered_m [ "sum" ] / delivered_m [ "size" ] fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 6 ), sharex = True , gridspec_kw = { "height_ratios" : [ 2 , 1 ]}) x = monthly . index . to_timestamp () ax1 . plot ( x , monthly [ "correct rate" ] * 100 , marker = "o" , label = "Correct: all due shipments" ) ax1 . plot ( x , monthly [ "delivered-only rate" ] * 100 , marker = "o" , linestyle = "--" , label = "Wrong: delivered only" ) ax1 . set_title ( "On-time rate by promised month, 2025" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "On-time rate (%)" ) ax1 . legend ( loc = "lower left" ) ax2 . bar ( x , monthly [ "due" ], width = 20 , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Due shipments" ) ax2 . bar ( x , monthly [ "pending" ], width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" , label = "Of which still pending" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Shipments" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Promised month" ) ax2 . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () monthly . tail ( 3 ) . assign ( ** { c : monthly [ c ] . tail ( 3 ) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) for c in [ "correct rate" , "delivered-only rate" ]}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due on_time pending correct rate delivered-only rate promised_month 2025-10 403 359 0 89.1% 89.1% 2025-11 627 474 0 75.6% 75.6% 2025-12 790 437 157 55.3% 69.0% Read the chart from top to bottom: For most of the year the two lines are identical : by the cutoff, every shipment promised before December had been delivered, so the filter removed nothing. In the last two months, due volume rises (the peak season) and the rate falls. In December the lines split. Many December shipments are still pending at the cutoff; the delivered-only line drops them and reports a much milder decline than the correct line. So the manager's feeling was right, and the delivered-only dashboard would have understated the disruption at exactly the moment it mattered. One honest caveat: December's correct rate is a snapshot . Some of those pending shipments will be delivered in January, all of them late, so the December rate cannot go up, but the lead-time picture for December is still incomplete. The manager-ready summary: dec = monthly . iloc [ - 1 ] worst_carrier = by_carrier [ "on_time_rate" ] . idxmin () print ( f "As of 31 December 2025, { on_time_rate : .1% } of the { len ( s [ s [ 'population' ] == 'due' ]) } shipments due in 2025 " f "were delivered on time ( { populations [ 'not yet due' ] } not yet due and { populations [ 'unknown promise' ] } " f "with no recorded promise are excluded). December was the worst month: { dec [ 'correct rate' ] : .1% } of " f " { dec [ 'due' ] : .0f } due shipments, with { dec [ 'pending' ] : .0f } still pending; a delivered-only report would " f "have shown { dec [ 'delivered-only rate' ] : .1% } . { worst_carrier } has the lowest on-time rate of the three " f "carriers ( { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'on_time_rate' ] : .1% } of { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'due' ] } due) " f "and the largest overdue backlog ( { by_carrier . loc [ worst_carrier , 'pending' ] } pending)." ) As of 31 December 2025, 81.9% of the 5742 shipments due in 2025 were delivered on time (99 not yet due and 12 with no recorded promise are excluded). December was the worst month: 55.3% of 790 due shipments, with 157 still pending; a delivered-only report would have shown 69.0%. ParcelOne has the lowest on-time rate of the three carriers (74.0% of 2059 due) and the largest overdue backlog (129 pending). Before recommending "investigate the carrier", you would want evidence the data do not hold: whether the carrier serves harder routes or regions, when the warehouse actually handed parcels over (a late handover is the warehouse's delay, not the carrier's), whether the December peak exceeded agreed volumes, and whether the delivery scans are reliable. You list these in the lab's recommendation.

docs.text: Answer these at the start of the next lecture, which opens the marketing case : comparing campaigns. Write short answers. A campaign had 10,000 visits, 800 add-to-carts and 200 purchases. What is the visit-to-purchase conversion rate? What is the cart-to-purchase rate? Campaign A converted 2% of 1,000 visitors; campaign B converted 4% of 100 visitors. A colleague says the two campaigns together converted 3%. What is the right combined rate, and what rule from today does it use? A campaign spent 5,000 currency units and brought 100 purchases worth 20,000 in revenue. What is the cost per acquisition (CPA)? What is the return on ad spend (ROAS)? A customer saw a social media ad on Monday, searched for the brand on Thursday and bought. Under "last click" attribution, which channel gets the credit? What does that rule miss? Campaign X has a higher conversion rate than campaign Y, but X was shown only to returning customers. Can you conclude that X's ads are better? What kind of evidence would let you say so?

docs.text: Session 12 lab: Which campaigns deserve the budget? ¶ Build a campaign scorecard that adds up, find the rows where a rate cannot exist, catch a channel ranking that a small campaign has flipped, debug three broken ROAS analyses, and turn what you find into a controlled test the marketing lead can approve. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ Marketing lead: "Next quarter's budget is fixed. I want to move some money towards the campaigns that work best, but I can only defend a change I can measure. Which campaigns deserve a controlled budget change , and how would we know if it worked?" Your job is to give her a scorecard she can trust, an honest reading of it, and one test proposal. Not a new budget split. About the data marketing_daily.csv is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: one row per day of 2025 × paid campaign , describing no real company, brand or platform. Money is in neutral currency units . Each purchase is credited to exactly one campaign on the same day; there is no touchpoint history and no organic traffic. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G4 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I4 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Check a campaign-day table's key, completeness and funnel order before computing any rate. Compute CTR, conversion rate, CPC, CPA and ROAS as ratios of sums at any level, and reconcile them to the company total. Treat zero denominators as "not available" and report review cases instead of hiding them. Explain why the mean of campaign rates and the weighted rate rank channels differently. Build a CPA and ROAS scorecard that keeps volumes visible. Separate attributed revenue from incremental revenue, and propose a controlled test with a success metric and guardrails. Evidence you keep: your campaign scorecard, a short explanation of the weighted-rate result, and a test proposal. Before you start ¶ Read the Session 12 lecture . Re-read the weighted-rate part of the Session 5 lecture and the A/B test parts of the Session 9 lecture . docs.text: Marketing lead: "Next quarter's budget is fixed. I want to move some money towards the campaigns that work best, but I can only defend a change I can measure. Which campaigns deserve a controlled budget change , and how would we know if it worked?" Your job is to give her a scorecard she can trust, an honest reading of it, and one test proposal. Not a new budget split. About the data marketing_daily.csv is synthetic teaching data generated by the course: one row per day of 2025 × paid campaign , describing no real company, brand or platform. Money is in neutral currency units . Each purchase is credited to exactly one campaign on the same day; there is no touchpoint history and no organic traffic.

docs.text: Session 12 lecture: Marketing: campaign evaluation ¶ Marketing dashboards are full of rates: click-through, conversion, cost per acquisition, return on ad spend. This lecture shows how to calculate them so they add up, how a small campaign can make a whole channel look better than it is, and why "this campaign earned the most revenue per unit of spend" is not the same as "give it more money". Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 11 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. To measure on-time delivery for last month, which shipments belong in the denominator: the ones delivered last month, or the ones due last month? Why does it matter? Some shipments that were due last month have still not arrived. A colleague drops them because "they have no delivery date yet". What happens to the on-time rate, and why is that misleading? Lead times are skewed: most shipments take a few days, a few take weeks. Which would you report as the "typical" lead time, the mean or the median? What extra number would you add? Two carriers have on-time rates of 95% and 90%. What else must you know before you call the first one better? What you will be able to explain ¶ The decision a campaign review supports, and why its answer is usually "test this", not "move all the money". The marketing funnel (impressions → clicks → sessions → conversions) and the grain of a campaign-day table. Five funnel rates, CTR, conversion rate, CPC, CPA and ROAS , each calculated as a ratio of sums . What to do when a denominator is zero , and which rows are review cases . Why the mean of campaign rates can rank channels in the wrong order, while the weighted rate does not. What attributed revenue can and cannot tell you, and why ROAS is neither profit nor proof that the spend caused the sales. How to turn a promising comparison into a controlled test of a budget change. This lecture builds on Metrics and KPIs (weighted rates), Correlation and regression (confounding) and Sampling, uncertainty and experiments (A/B tests). Stage Column One unit is… Media cost spend currency units paid to show the ads that day Shown impressions one time an ad or email was shown Clicked clicks one click on it Visited sessions one website visit that started from a click Bought conversions one session that ended in a purchase (one order per purchasing session) Value attributed_revenue the value of those orders, before returns Grain: one row per calendar day × campaign . The key is ( date , campaign_id ). A row is not a person: one shopper who clicks on three days is counted on three rows, and nothing in the table links them. Predict, then reveal If every campaign has a row for every day of 2025, how many rows should there be? Check your answer against the "Rows" line in Part 1, then run the checks below. key_unique = not daily . duplicated ([ "date" , "campaign_id" ]) . any () expected_rows = daily [ "date" ] . nunique () * daily [ "campaign_id" ] . nunique () funnel_ok = ( ( daily [ "impressions" ] >= daily [ "clicks" ]) & ( daily [ "clicks" ] >= daily [ "sessions" ]) & ( daily [ "sessions" ] >= daily [ "conversions" ]) & ( daily [ "conversions" ] >= 0 ) ) print ( "Key (date, campaign_id) unique:" , key_unique ) print ( "Rows:" , len ( daily ), "| days x campaigns:" , expected_rows ) print ( "Rows breaking the funnel order:" , ( ~ funnel_ok ) . sum ()) print ( "Rows with negative spend or revenue:" , (( daily [ "spend" ] < 0 ) | ( daily [ "attributed_revenue" ] < 0 )) . sum ()) Key (date, campaign_id) unique: True Rows: 2555 | days x campaigns: 2555 Rows breaking the funnel order: 0 Rows with negative spend or revenue: 0 All four checks pass in the output above, so we can trust the structure. If a row had more sessions than clicks, you would stop and ask why (a tracking change? a join that duplicated rows?) before computing a single rate. The funnel narrows sharply at each stage. Part 6: Weighted rate versus the mean of campaign rates ¶ The marketing lead asks for conversion rate by channel . Two channels, Search and Social, have two campaigns each. There are two ways to get a channel's rate: Method How Problem Mean of campaign rates compute each campaign's rate, then average them gives a tiny campaign the same vote as a huge one Weighted rate (ratio of sums) add the channel's conversions and sessions, then divide none: it is the channel's actual rate Predict, then reveal Look back at the scorecard in Part 5. Social has one big campaign with a low conversion rate (SOC-01, a broad audience) and one small campaign with a very high rate (SOC-02, past visitors). On the mean of campaign rates , will Social beat Search? On the weighted rate ? campaign_rate = by_campaign [ "conv_rate" ] . groupby ( "channel" ) . mean () channel = add_rates ( daily . groupby ( "channel" )[ COUNTS ] . sum ()) compare = pd . For channels with a single campaign, the two methods agree. For Social they do not: the mean of campaign rates lifts Social above Search, while the weighted rate puts it well below. The mean of rates treats SOC-02 and SOC-01 as equals, so the small campaign's high rate drags the "Social" figure up. The weighted rate gives each session one vote, so SOC-01's large volume dominates, as it does in the real business. The rule To combine rates across campaigns, days, regions or anything else, add the numerators and the denominators, then divide . A mean of rates answers a different question ("what does a typical campaign look like?"), which is rarely what a manager means by "the channel's rate". There is a second lesson in SOC-02's name: it targets past visitors , people who already know the shop. Such campaigns usually convert well because their audience was already likely to buy. That leads to the next part. Check your understanding 4 A regional manager averages the conversion rates of her ten stores' websites and reports it as "the region's conversion rate". When would that number be close to the true regional rate, and when would it be far off? Part 7: Attribution, and what ROAS does not tell you ¶ attributed_revenue is revenue credited to a campaign. In this data the rule is simple: each purchase belongs to exactly one campaign, on the same day. Real attribution is messier, and the simple rule hides questions the table cannot answer. The table can tell you The table cannot tell you How much revenue was credited to each campaign Whether the buyer saw other campaigns first (there is no touchpoint history) Cost per credited purchase (CPA) Whether the buyer would have bought anyway, without the ad Revenue credited per unit of spend (ROAS) Sales from people who came on their own (there is no organic traffic) Trends in these numbers over time Whether last-click or any multi-touch rule would credit the same campaign So this table cannot prove a last-click or multi-touch claim, and it cannot measure incrementality : the sales that happened because of the campaign and would not have happened without it. ROAS is not profit ¶ ROAS divides revenue by media spend only. It ignores: Product cost : a ROAS of 3 means little if the products cost 80% of their price to make or buy. Returns : attributed revenue is counted before returns. Other costs : agency fees, creative production, discounts and staff time. ROAS is not causal lift ¶ A high ROAS says "a lot of revenue was credited here", not "the spend caused this revenue". A campaign aimed at past visitors can show a high ROAS while adding few extra sales, because many of those people were going to buy anyway. Predict, then reveal In a previous session we saw that spend and revenue both rise late in the year. If you compared ROAS in the busiest months with ROAS earlier in the year, could you tell how much of the change came from the budget and how much from the season? weekly = daily . set_index ( "date" ) . resample ( "W-SUN" )[[ "spend" , "conversions" ]] . sum () # weeks ending on Sunday weekly = weekly . loc [ "2025-01-12" : "2025-12-28" ] # complete Monday-to-Sunday weeks only fig , ax1 = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) ax1 . plot ( weekly . index , weekly [ "spend" ], color = "#2a78d6" , label = "Spend" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Weekly spend (currency units)" , color = "#2a78d6" ) ax2 = ax1 . twinx () ax2 . plot ( weekly . index , weekly [ "conversions" ], color = "#eb6834" , label = "Conversions" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Weekly conversions" , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . grid ( False ) ax1 . set_title ( "Spend and conversions rise together at the end of the year" ) plt . show () Both lines climb in the last months of the year. Budgets went up and shoppers were in a buying mood at the same time, so a before/after comparison would give the budget credit for the season. This is the confounding you met in Session 8: season drives both spend and sales. Check your understanding 5 A colleague says: "SOC-02's ROAS is many times SOC-01's, so every unit we move from SOC-01 to SOC-02 earns that many times more." Name two separate reasons this may be false. Part 8: From comparison to experiment ¶ Everything so far is an observational comparison : we looked at what happened. It can point to candidates, but it cannot say what more (or less) money would do. For that, Session 9's tool is the right one: a controlled test . Design How it works for a budget change Watch out for Holdout Randomly keep a share of the target audience from seeing the campaign; compare their purchases with those who see it Needs a platform that can hold people out; small effects need big groups Geo split Randomly pick some regions to get the extra budget and some to stay as they are; compare sales, not attributed revenue Regions differ; pick matched pairs and compare change from before Time switching Alternate the budget on and off week by week Seasons and holidays; carry-over from earlier weeks A test proposal answers six questions before it starts: Change: what exactly changes (for example "raise campaign X's daily budget by a fifth")? Design: who or which regions get the change, chosen at random? Primary metric: one number decided in advance, ideally total conversions or revenue in the test group, not attributed revenue. Guardrails: numbers that must not get worse (CPA, return rate, unsubscribes, complaints). Duration: long enough for enough conversions and at least whole weeks; avoid big holidays unless they are the point. Decision rule: what result leads to "scale up", "keep as is" or "stop", including the uncertainty interval from Session 9. Check your understanding 6 Why should the primary metric be total conversions in the test regions rather than revenue attributed to the campaign? Part 9: Worked case — a scorecard the lead can use ¶ We combine everything into one scorecard. It keeps volumes next to rates , keeps blanks as "n/a", flags Email as not comparable, and sorts by conversions so the campaigns that move the business are at the top. scorecard = by_campaign [[ "spend" , "conversions" , "attributed_revenue" , "conv_rate" , "CPA" , "ROAS" ]] . copy () scorecard [ "share of conversions" ] = scorecard [ "conversions" ] / scorecard [ "conversions" ] . sum () scorecard [ "note" ] = "" scorecard . loc [ scorecard . index . get_level_values ( "channel" ) == "Email" , "note" ] = "near-zero media cost: ROAS not comparable" scorecard = scorecard . sort_values ( "conversions" , ascending = False ) show ( scorecard ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } spend conversions attributed_revenue conv_rate CPA ROAS share of conversions note channel campaign_id Search SRCH-01 362,654.08 24,629 2,897,731.90 3.62% 14.72 7.99 44.11% SRCH-02 256,844.20 15,308 1,589,252.73 3.14% 16.78 6.19 27.41% Social SOC-01 433,453.56 6,408 595,049.96 1.15% 67.64 1.37 11.48% Email EML-01 15,426.37 4,378 451,164.11 2.17% 3.52 29.25 7.84% near-zero media cost: ROAS not comparable Social SOC-02 24,001.47 2,850 315,601.00 6.29% 8.42 13.15 5.10% Display DISP-01 207,555.98 1,518 132,218.98 0.84% 136.73 0.64 2.72% Video VID-01 169,989.92 748 68,082.75 1.08% 227.26 0.40 1.34% paid = scorecard . drop ( "Email" , level = "channel" ) . reset_index () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( paid [ "spend" ], paid [ "ROAS" ], s = paid [ "conversions" ] / 40 , alpha = 0.6 , color = "#2a78d6" ) for _ , row in paid . iterrows (): ax . annotate ( row [ "campaign_id" ], ( row [ "spend" ], row [ "ROAS" ]), textcoords = "offset points" , xytext = ( 8 , 4 ), fontsize = 9 ) ax . axhline ( 1 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 , linestyle = ":" ) ax . text ( ax . get_xlim ()[ 0 ], 1.1 , " ROAS = 1 (revenue equals media cost)" , ha = "left" , va = "bottom" , fontsize = 8 ) ax . set_title ( "Paid campaigns: attributed ROAS against spend (bubble = conversions)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Spend in 2025 (currency units)" ) ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( " {x:,.0f} " ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Attributed ROAS" ) plt . show () How to read the chart: campaigns at the top right are efficient and large ; at the top left, efficient but small ; at the bottom right, large but expensive . The dotted line marks where credited revenue only just equals media cost. Remember it is not a profit line: product cost and returns are missing. A recommendation built from this scorecard, in the form the lead asked for: What the data show: name the campaigns that combine high volume with a low CPA, and the large campaigns whose ROAS is close to or below 1, using the numbers in the scorecard. What they do not show: attributed revenue is not incremental; Email and past-visitor campaigns may get credit for buyers who would have bought anyway; ROAS is before product cost and returns. What to do: test one bounded budget change on one candidate (design, primary metric, guardrails, duration and decision rule), rather than reallocating the whole budget. Summary ¶ Question Tool Trap to avoid Can I trust the table? Key, completeness and funnel-order checks Computing rates before checking the grain What is the rate for a campaign, channel or year? Ratio of sums ( add_rates ) Averaging or adding rates What if the denominator is zero? safe_div : blank, "not available" Showing 0 or infinity; deleting review cases Which channel converts best? Weighted rate with volumes shown Mean of campaign rates (the SOC-02 effect) Which campaign is most efficient? CPA and ROAS with spend and conversions Ranking a tiny-cost campaign (Email) first Did the spend cause the sales? A controlled test (holdout, geo split) Treating attributed revenue or ROAS as incremental Is it profitable? Needs product cost, returns, other costs Reading ROAS as profit Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture, which opens the HR case : headcount and staff turnover. You do not need any HR knowledge; use common sense. Write short answers. A team had 40 people on 1 January and 44 on 31 December. Does that mean only 4 people joined during the year? Explain. Headcount can be counted on one day, or averaged over a period. Why might the two differ for a shop that hires many seasonal staff? 6 people left a team during the year. Is the turnover rate 6 ÷ (headcount today)? What would be a fairer denominator, and why? A department of 5 people lost 2 people; a department of 200 lost 30. Which has the higher turnover rate, and which number would you trust more? Why might an HR report hide numbers for groups with only two or three people? docs.text: Marketing dashboards are full of rates: click-through, conversion, cost per acquisition, return on ad spend. This lecture shows how to calculate them so they add up, how a small campaign can make a whole channel look better than it is, and why "this campaign earned the most revenue per unit of spend" is not the same as "give it more money". docs.text: Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 11 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. To measure on-time delivery for last month, which shipments belong in the denominator: the ones delivered last month, or the ones due last month? Why does it matter? Some shipments that were due last month have still not arrived. A colleague drops them because "they have no delivery date yet". What happens to the on-time rate, and why is that misleading? Lead times are skewed: most shipments take a few days, a few take weeks. Which would you report as the "typical" lead time, the mean or the median? What extra number would you add? Two carriers have on-time rates of 95% and 90%. What else must you know before you call the first one better?

docs.text: The decision a campaign review supports, and why its answer is usually "test this", not "move all the money". The marketing funnel (impressions → clicks → sessions → conversions) and the grain of a campaign-day table. Five funnel rates, CTR, conversion rate, CPC, CPA and ROAS , each calculated as a ratio of sums . What to do when a denominator is zero , and which rows are review cases . Why the mean of campaign rates can rank channels in the wrong order, while the weighted rate does not. What attributed revenue can and cannot tell you, and why ROAS is neither profit nor proof that the spend caused the sales. How to turn a promising comparison into a controlled test of a budget change. This lecture builds on Metrics and KPIs (weighted rates), Correlation and regression (confounding) and Sampling, uncertainty and experiments (A/B tests). In the Lab you build the campaign scorecard yourself and write a test proposal. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. docs.text: Marketing lead: "Next quarter's budget is fixed. I want to move some money towards the campaigns that work best, but I can only defend a change I can measure. Which campaigns deserve a controlled budget change , and how would we know if it worked?" Notice what the lead is not asking. She does not want a ranking to copy into next quarter's plan. She wants a short list of candidates and a way to test them. That shapes the whole analysis: Step Question for this case Question Which campaigns are efficient and big enough to matter? Understanding What does one row mean? What does "conversion" and "revenue" mean here? Preparation Are the keys unique? Do the funnel counts make sense? Where are the zero denominators? docs.text: Every paid campaign pushes people down the same funnel . Each stage is a count, and each count can only be as large as the one before it. Stage Column One unit is… Media cost spend currency units paid to show the ads that day Shown impressions one time an ad or email was shown Clicked clicks one click on it Visited sessions one website visit that started from a click Bought conversions one session that ended in a purchase (one order per purchasing session) Value attributed_revenue the value of those orders, before returns Grain: one row per calendar day × campaign . The key is ( date , campaign_id ). A row is not a person: one shopper who clicks on three days is counted on three rows, and nothing in the table links them. Predict, then reveal If every campaign has a row for every day of 2025, how many rows should there be? Check your answer against the "Rows" line in Part 1, then run the checks below. key_unique = not daily . duplicated ([ "date" , "campaign_id" ]) . any () expected_rows = daily [ "date" ] . nunique () * daily [ "campaign_id" ] . nunique () funnel_ok = ( ( daily [ "impressions" ] >= daily [ "clicks" ]) & ( daily [ "clicks" ] >= daily [ "sessions" ]) & ( daily [ "sessions" ] >= daily [ "conversions" ]) & ( daily [ "conversions" ] >= 0 ) ) print ( "Key (date, campaign_id) unique:" , key_unique ) print ( "Rows:" , len ( daily ), "| days x campaigns:" , expected_rows ) print ( "Rows breaking the funnel order:" , ( ~ funnel_ok ) . sum ()) print ( "Rows with negative spend or revenue:" , (( daily [ "spend" ] < 0 ) | ( daily [ "attributed_revenue" ] < 0 )) . sum ()) Key (date, campaign_id) unique: True Rows: 2555 | days x campaigns: 2555 Rows breaking the funnel order: 0 Rows with negative spend or revenue: 0 All four checks pass in the output above, so we can trust the structure. If a row had more sessions than clicks, you would stop and ask why (a tracking change? a join that duplicated rows?) before computing a single rate. The funnel narrows sharply at each stage. A log scale lets you see every stage on one chart: stages = [ "impressions" , "clicks" , "sessions" , "conversions" ] company = daily [ stages ] . sum () ax = company . plot . barh ( logx = True , color = "#2a78d6" ) ax . invert_yaxis () ax . set_title ( "2025 company funnel: each stage is a fraction of the one before" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Count for the year (log scale)" ) for i , value in enumerate ( company ): ax . text ( value , i , f " { value : ,.0f } " , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show ()

docs.text: Each rate divides one funnel count by another. The rule from Session 5 applies everywhere: add up the numerator, add up the denominator, then divide . Never add up or average rates. Rate Formula Read it as Better when CTR (click-through rate) clicks ÷ impressions share of showings that got a click higher Conversion rate conversions ÷ sessions share of visits that bought higher CPC (cost per click) spend ÷ clicks currency units paid per click lower CPA (cost per acquisition) spend ÷ conversions currency units paid per purchase lower ROAS (return on ad spend) attributed revenue ÷ spend revenue credited per unit of spend higher The helper add_rates() from the setup cell does exactly this to any table of summed counts.
