Three things to notice: Every value has its unit and comparison inside it: "a share of a total", "this month versus the rest of the year", "how many of how many". The check column names something you actually did in code, not "looks right". The limitation column is never empty. A claim without a limitation is a claim nobody has questioned yet. Predict, then reveal Register row E4 reports the return on ad spend (ROAS) for all campaigns together as a ratio of sums . Would the mean of the individual campaign ROAS values be higher or lower? Which campaign would pull it? print ( f "Ratio of sums (correct): { roas_all : .2f } " ) print ( f "Mean of the campaign ROAS: { campaigns [ 'roas' ] . mean () : .2f } <- gives a tiny-budget campaign equal weight" ) campaigns . sort_values ( "roas" , ascending = False ) . round ( 2 ) Ratio of sums (correct): 4.12 Mean of the campaign ROAS: 8.43 <- gives a tiny-budget campaign equal weight .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } spend attributed_revenue roas campaign_id EML-01 15,426.37 451,164.11 29.25 SOC-02 24,001.47 315,601.00 13.15 SRCH-01 362,654.08 2,897,731.90 7.99 SRCH-02 256,844.20 1,589,252.73 6.19 SOC-01 433,453.56 595,049.96 1.37 DISP-01 207,555.98 132,218.98 0.64 VID-01 169,989.92 68,082.75 0.40 The mean of campaign ratios is pulled up by a campaign with almost no media cost (Email): it gets the same weight as campaigns spending hundreds of times more. This is the weighted-rate rule from Session 5 again, and it is exactly the kind of check the register's check column should record. Check your understanding 2 A register row reads: claim "Warehouse staffing is a problem", value "high", check "chart looks bad", limitation blank. Rewrite the four columns so that a reviewer could verify them.
docs.title: Part 4: The evidence register

docs.text: When analysts want "one table", the tempting move is to join everything on whatever columns look shared: a month, an order ID, a department name. Across these five datasets every such join is false. Looks shared Why it is not a key Month Many rows per month on both sides: a month join multiplies rows order_id Superstore and operations both have one, but they are different fictional businesses Department "Operations" Finance and HR both have one, but they are separate fictional organisations Revenue Superstore Sales and marketing attributed revenue measure different things in different contexts Predict, then reveal Someone joins the 2025 Superstore order lines to the marketing campaign-days on month , "so we can see sales and spend together". How many rows will the result have, and what will happen to the Sales total? retail_2025 = orders [ orders [ "order_date" ] . dt . year == 2025 ] mk = marketing . assign ( order_month = marketing [ "date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp ()) bad = retail_2025 . merge ( mk [[ "order_month" , "campaign_id" , "spend" ]], on = "order_month" ) # a false join print ( f "Order lines before the join: { len ( retail_2025 ) : , } " ) print ( f "Rows after the join: { len ( bad ) : , } " ) print ( f "Sales before the join: { retail_2025 [ 'sales' ] . sum () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "'Sales' after the join: { bad [ 'sales' ] . sum () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Order IDs found in both Superstore and operations: " f " { len ( set ( orders [ 'order_id' ]) & set ( shipments [ 'order_id' ])) } " ) Order lines before the join: 2,634 Rows after the join: 562,051 Sales before the join: 613,934 'Sales' after the join: 131,112,132 Order IDs found in both Superstore and operations: 0 Each order line was repeated once for every campaign-day in its month, so Sales was multiplied many times over. This is the many-to-many join from Session 3 and the duplicated-budget trap from Session 10 , at a much larger scale. And the order IDs that look shared have no values in common at all: they come from different fictional businesses. The second false combination is adding revenues . Marketing's attributed revenue is a synthetic allocation of purchases to campaigns in a fictional marketing context. It is not extra retail revenue, and it is not a part of Superstore Sales either. pd . DataFrame ({ "2025 total" : [ retail_m [ "sales" ] . sum (), marketing_m [ "attributed_revenue" ] . sum ()], "units" : [ "source monetary units" , "currency units" ], "what it measures" : [ "Sales on order lines of a fictitious store" , "Purchase value allocated to campaigns, synthetic" ], }, index = [ "Superstore Sales" , "Marketing attributed revenue" ]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } 2025 total units what it measures Superstore Sales 613,933.58 source monetary units Sales on order lines of a fictitious store Marketing attributed revenue 6,049,101.43 currency units Purchase value allocated to campaigns, synthetic The two totals above are in different units , from different fictional contexts , measuring different things . Adding them gives a number that describes nothing. Even inside one real company, campaign-attributed revenue would be a subset of total revenue (the same sales seen through a marketing lens), so adding it would count those sales twice.
docs.title: Part 5: Combining evidence without false joins

docs.text: You may still want to look at the domains together, for example to describe the shape of a year. The safe way is: Build each monthly table separately (Part 3). Align them on the same calendar months (2025 only, the period every dataset covers). Keep each measure in its own units and its own panel. Do not add, divide or correlate across them as if they were one system. Say in the title or caption that they are separate contexts . pd.concat with axis=1 lines the tables up by their month index. There is one row per month on each side , so nothing is multiplied; the assert checks that. side_by_side = pd . concat ({ "Retail Sales (source units)" : retail_m [ "sales" ], "Marketing spend (currency units)" : marketing_m [ "spend" ], "Operations on-time rate" : operations_m [ "on_time_rate" ], "HR Operations headcount (closing)" : hr_ops_m [ "closing" ], }, axis = 1 ) side_by_side . index = side_by_side . index . strftime ( "%Y-%m" ) assert len ( side_by_side ) == 12 and side_by_side . index . is_unique , "expected exactly one row per month" assert side_by_side . notna () . all () . all (), "a month is missing in one of the domains" side_by_side . assign ( ** { "Operations on-time rate" : side_by_side [ "Operations on-time rate" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Retail Sales (source units) Marketing spend (currency units) Operations on-time rate HR Operations headcount (closing) 2025-01 18,830.33 114,433.76 87.1% 157 2025-02 22,978.82 104,709.05 87.2% 154 2025-03 53,031.07 113,242.09 88.7% 153 2025-04 38,829.16 109,540.31 89.6% 156 2025-05 57,042.84 111,622.34 87.0% 155 2025-06 40,937.15 114,021.19 85.9% 180 2025-07 40,300.50 113,586.15 87.9% 192 2025-08 31,716.81 115,309.19 86.8% 184 2025-09 73,521.66 106,980.40 86.9% 175 2025-10 59,831.00 130,248.75 89.1% 168 2025-11 79,411.97 159,504.47 75.6% 154 2025-12 97,502.28 176,727.88 55.3% 151 fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 6.5 ), sharex = True ) panels = [ ( "Retail Sales (source units)" , "Superstore: Sales by order month" , "Source monetary units" , 1 ), ( "Marketing spend (currency units)" , "Marketing: media spend" , "Currency units" , 1 ), ( "Operations on-time rate" , "Operations: on-time rate by promised month" , " % o f due shipments" , 100 ), ( "HR Operations headcount (closing)" , "HR: Operations team headcount" , "Employees at month end" , 1 ), ] x = np . arange ( 12 ) for ax , ( col , title , ylabel , scale ) in zip ( axes . flat , panels ): ax . plot ( x , side_by_side [ col ] * scale , marker = "o" , markersize = 4 , color = "#2a78d6" ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_ylabel ( ylabel ) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , None ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xticks ( x , [ m [ 5 :] for m in side_by_side . index ]) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month of 2025" ) fig . suptitle ( "Four separate fictional contexts on one calendar: compare shapes, not causes" , fontweight = "bold" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" ) fig . text ( 0.01 , - 0.01 , "Each panel comes from a different dataset with its own units. No rows are linked across panels." , fontsize = 8 , color = "#555555" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Each panel answers a question about its own context. Retail Sales and marketing spend both rise late in the year; the on-time rate falls at the end of the year; the Operations team grew in mid-year and then shrank. Predict, then reveal Compute the correlation between monthly marketing spend and the monthly on-time rate. These come from different fictional organisations . What value do you expect? side_by_side . corr () . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Retail Sales (source units) Marketing spend (currency units) Operations on-time rate HR Operations headcount (closing) Retail Sales (source units) 1.00 0.76 -0.72 -0.25 Marketing spend (currency units) 0.76 1.00 -0.91 -0.34 Operations on-time rate -0.72 -0.91 1.00 0.35 HR Operations headcount (closing) -0.25 -0.34 0.35 1.00 The correlations in the table above are strong, including between marketing spend and the on-time rate, which come from datasets that have nothing to do with each other . Why? Several series share a calendar pattern : activity builds towards the end of the year. Any two series with a year-end bump will correlate, whatever their source. This is a common trend , a kind of confounding from Session 8 . There are only 12 points . With so few, strong correlations appear easily by chance. No mechanism connects them: no shared orders, staff or shipments. So co-movement across separate contexts is not evidence of a link . Within one real company you would still need a mechanism, shared keys and a design (such as an experiment) before claiming that one series drives another. Check your understanding 3 A draft capstone says: "When marketing spend went up, deliveries got worse (correlation −0.9), so marketing overloaded the warehouse." Give three reasons this sentence cannot be supported with these datasets.
docs.title: The honest alternative: side by side on a common calendar

docs.text: The register says what is true . A decision also needs what matters . A simple, transparent tool is a weighted scoring table : List the options (A to D from Part 2). Choose a few criteria that matter to the decision-maker, and write down what a high score means. Score each option on each criterion from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong), with a reason that points to the register. Give each criterion a weight (weights add up to 1) and compute the weighted score. Test whether the ranking survives reasonable changes in the weights. Criterion 5 means Evidence it rests on Size of problem Large gap affecting many customers or a lot of money Register values Strength of evidence Clean contract, checks passed, few caveats Register checks and limitations Cost (5 = cheap) Little money or effort to act Judgement; ask the owner Speed to effect Results visible within the quarter Judgement Urgency Waiting makes it clearly worse Trend in the register period Scores are judgements, not data The table makes judgement visible so others can disagree with a specific number. It does not make judgement objective. Always show the reasons next to the scores. scores = pd . DataFrame ({ "size" : [ 5 , 4 , 3 , 2 ], "evidence" : [ 4 , 3 , 2 , 5 ], "cost" : [ 3 , 3 , 5 , 4 ], "speed" : [ 4 , 2 , 5 , 3 ], "urgency" : [ 5 , 4 , 2 , 2 ], }, index = [ "A: carrier and peak capacity" , "B: Operations retention" , "C: marketing budget shift" , "D: software contracts" ]) reasons = { "A: carrier and peak capacity" : "E2: large December drop on many shipments; clean due-population contract" , "B: Operations retention" : "E3: high turnover, but causes unknown and effect slow" , "C: marketing budget shift" : "E4: cheap and fast, but attribution is not incremental" , "D: software contracts" : "E5: well-measured overspend, but a small share of spend" , } weights = pd . Series ({ "size" : 0.30 , "evidence" : 0.25 , "cost" : 0.15 , "speed" : 0.15 , "urgency" : 0.15 }) assert abs ( weights . sum () - 1 ) < 1e-9 , "weights must add up to 1" result = scores . assign ( weighted = scores @ weights , reason = pd . Series ( reasons )) . sort_values ( "weighted" , ascending = False ) result .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } size evidence cost speed urgency weighted reason A: carrier and peak capacity 5 4 3 4 5 4.30 E2: large December drop on many shipments; cle... B: Operations retention 4 3 3 2 4 3.30 E3: high turnover, but causes unknown and effe... D: software contracts 2 5 4 3 2 3.20 E5: well-measured overspend, but a small share... C: marketing budget shift 3 2 5 5 2 3.20 E4: cheap and fast, but attribution is not inc... Option A has the highest weighted score with these weights. But someone in the room will say "evidence should count for more" or "cost is what really matters". Before you present a ranking, test it. Predict, then reveal If you give cost twice its weight (and scale the others down so the weights still add to 1), does option A stay first? def rerank ( scores , weights , criterion , factor ): """Multiply one criterion's weight by `factor`, renormalise to 1, and return the winner and its margin.""" w = weights . copy () w [ criterion ] *= factor w = w / w . sum () total = ( scores @ w ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) return { "criterion" : criterion , "weight now" : round ( w [ criterion ], 2 ), "winner" : total . index [ 0 ], "margin over 2nd" : round ( total . iloc [ 0 ] - total . iloc [ 1 ], 2 )} one_at_a_time = pd . DataFrame ([ rerank ( scores , weights , c , f ) for c in weights . index for f in ( 0.5 , 2.0 )]) one_at_a_time .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } criterion weight now winner margin over 2nd 0 size 0.18 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.76 1 size 0.46 A: carrier and peak capacity 1.00 2 evidence 0.14 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.97 3 evidence 0.40 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.68 4 cost 0.08 A: carrier and peak capacity 1.08 5 cost 0.26 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.70 6 speed 0.08 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.92 7 speed 0.26 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.83 8 urgency 0.08 A: carrier and peak capacity 0.95 9 urgency 0.26 A: carrier and peak capacity 1.00 The table above changes one weight at a time, halving or doubling it. A second, broader test draws thousands of random weight sets and counts how often each option comes first. The generator is seeded , so everyone gets the same result. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 15 ) random_weights = rng . dirichlet ( np . ones ( len ( weights )), size = 2000 ) # 2,000 weight sets, each adding to 1 totals = scores . to_numpy () @ random_weights . T # one column of totals per weight set winners = pd . Series ( scores . index [ totals . argmax ( axis = 0 )]) share_first = winners . value_counts ( normalize = True ) . reindex ( scores . index , fill_value = 0 ) ax = plt . gca () ax . barh ( share_first . index , share_first * 100 , color = [ "#eb6834" ] + [ "#b8b6b0" ] * 3 ) ax . invert_yaxis () ax . set_title ( "How often each option ranks first under 2,000 random weight sets" ) ax . set_xlabel ( " % o f weight sets in which the option ranks first" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Option" ) plt . show () share_first . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) . to_frame ( "ranked first" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } ranked first A: carrier and peak capacity 78% B: Operations retention 0% C: marketing budget shift 16% D: software contracts 6% How to read the two tests: If the winner stays the same when you halve or double any single weight, and wins in most random weight sets, the recommendation is robust to weighting . Say so in one sentence. If the winner flips, the decision depends on values , not data. Show the decision-maker which weight matters and let them choose: "If cost matters most, D; otherwise A." Neither test checks the scores themselves. A wrong score is a wrong input, whatever the weights. Peer review (Part 8) is where scores get challenged. Check your understanding 4 Option A wins in most random weight sets. A colleague says, "So A is the right decision with that probability." What is wrong with this reading?
docs.title: Part 6: Trade-off analysis

docs.text: The validation pack is what lets a reviewer trust your numbers without redoing the whole project. It has three parts: Part Contents Why Data versions Dataset name, file, SHA-256 checksum, rows, as-of date Proves which exact data produced the numbers Reconciliations Totals and counts that must agree, written as assert checks Catches joins, filters and dropped rows Reproducibility A notebook that runs from top to bottom in a fresh session, with fixed seeds and library versions Anyone gets the same numbers The setup cells already checked each file's SHA-256 when it was loaded: a mismatch would have printed a warning. The cell below records the versions explicitly, and adds a short fingerprint of each loaded table so you can tell later whether a table changed after loading. def source_sha256 ( local_dir , url , name ): """SHA-256 of a source file, read the same way as its setup cell reads it.""" if local_dir : with open ( os . path . join ( local_dir , name ), "rb" ) as f : return hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () return hashlib . sha256 ( urllib . request . urlopen ( url + name ) . read ()) . hexdigest () def fingerprint ( df ): """First 12 characters of the SHA-256 of the table's CSV text: changes if any value changes.""" return hashlib . sha256 ( df . to_csv ( index = False ) . encode ()) . hexdigest ()[: 12 ] versions = pd . docs.text: A peer review is not a vote on whether the work is good. It is a structured test of the evidence, done by someone who did not build it. Step Reviewer does Author does 1. Read the decision Restate the decision and recommendation in one sentence Confirm or correct the restatement 2. Pick one critical number Choose the number the recommendation depends on most and recompute it from the raw data, without looking at the author's code Provide the register row and the data version 3. Test one competing explanation Name one other reason the pattern could appear, and look for evidence for or against it Say whether the briefing already addresses it 4. Hunt for false links Check for joins across datasets, added revenues, mixed units and causal verbs Fix or withdraw any claim that fails 5. Check the limitations Is every register row's limitation specific? Is anything important missing? Add missing limits 6. Write the feedback One strength , one critical issue , one next action Record the response in a revision log Rules that keep peer review useful: Be specific: "the December rate excludes pending shipments" helps; "check your numbers" does not. Critique the evidence , not the person. If the reviewer cannot reproduce the critical number, the claim is not yet verified , however good the chart looks.

docs.text: Question Tool Trap to avoid What must a capstone show? One decision, three or more domains, all five in the portfolio A tour of "insights" with no decision How do I record evidence? Evidence register: claim, source, metric, grain, period, value, check, limitation Values typed by hand; blank limitations How do I combine datasets? Aggregate inside each dataset, then place side by side on a common calendar Joining rows on month, order ID or department name Can I add revenues across domains? No: keep each measure in its own units and context Adding attributed revenue to retail Sales Do moving-together series show a link? No: common trends and 12 points make correlation cheap Causal words for co-movement How do I weigh options? Weighted scoring with reasons and a weight-sensitivity test Hidden judgement presented as data How does a reviewer trust it? Validation pack: versions, reconciliations, reproducible notebook "It looks right" as a check

Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ Operations director: "I have ten minutes before the leadership meeting. Tell me what you want me to approve, why, how sure you are, and what we will watch afterwards. If they ask me a hard question, I need to be able to answer it." About the data shipments.csv is synthetic teaching data generated by the course for a fictional retailer, with fictional warehouses and carriers. The cutoff is 2025-12-31. In the independent tasks you switch to your own capstone, which may use other course datasets; keep each finding in its own context. docs.text: Extract the few facts an executive needs from a longer analysis, each with its context. Write a one-page brief with the recommendation first. Design one summary figure with a so-what title, a highlighted comparison and intervals. Structure your own briefing and prepare answers to the questions you expect. Critique a briefing with the rubric, with specific comments. Turn feedback into a prioritised revision plan. Answer challenge questions with evidence, honest uncertainty and clear limits. docs.text: Session 16 lecture: Executive briefings ¶ An analysis only changes a decision if the people who decide understand it, trust it and remember it. This lecture is about that last step: putting the recommendation first, giving every number its context and its uncertainty, designing one figure that carries the message, and answering hard questions with evidence rather than confidence. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer these questions on the Session 15 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. Name four of the eight columns of an evidence register, and say why the limitation column should never be empty. Why is joining Superstore order lines to marketing campaign-days on month wrong? What happens to the Sales total? Superstore Sales and marketing attributed revenue are both "revenue". Give two reasons you cannot add them. Two monthly series from separate datasets have a correlation of −0.9. What can you conclude, and why? In a trade-off table, what does a weight-sensitivity test check, and what does it not check? What are the three parts of a validation pack? What you will be able to explain ¶ Why executives need the recommendation first , and how the pyramid principle organises a briefing. How to write so-what titles that state the message instead of the topic. How to give a number its context : denominator, period, comparison, unit and sensible rounding. How to present uncertainty honestly with ranges, confidence intervals and stated assumptions. How to design one summary figure that carries the main message. What fits on one page or in three to five slides , and what belongs in an appendix. How to handle challenge : "How do you know?", "What would change your mind?" and other hard questions. The common failure modes of analytical presentations, and the feedback rubric used to review briefings. This lecture builds on storytelling from the Session 14 lecture and Storytelling with data , and on confidence intervals from the Session 9 lecture . The running example is the operations case from Session 11 . In the Lab you turn an analysis into a one-page brief, prepare your own briefing, critique a peer's with the rubric and plan a revision. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. warehouses and carriers are fictional. The cutoff is 2025-12-31. The briefing examples below are about this operations context only. Part 1: Recommendation first ¶ Analysts are trained to tell the story in the order they did the work: data, method, findings, and finally the recommendation. Executives need the reverse order, because their scarce resource is attention and their job is the decision. Analyst's natural order Executive order 1. Background and data 1. Recommendation and the decision you need 2. Method 2. Two or three reasons , each with its key number 3. Findings 3. Trade-offs , risks and uncertainty 4. Caveats 4. Next steps : owner, measure, review date 5. Recommendation (if time) 5. Appendix: method, definitions, checks The pyramid principle (from Barbara Minto's consulting work) gives the structure: one governing message at the top, a few supporting arguments below it, and evidence under each argument. A listener who stops after the first sentence still has the answer; one who keeps listening gets the reasons, then the evidence. Predict, then reveal Using the Session 11 analysis, what would you put at the top of the pyramid for the operations manager? Write one sentence before running the next cell. by_carrier_dec = due [ due [ "promised_month" ] == "2025-12-01" ] . groupby ( "carrier" )[ "on_time" ] . agg ([ "size" , "mean" ]) worst = by_carrier_dec [ "mean" ] . idxmin () pyramid = { "Governing message" : f "Review { worst } 's peak-season performance before next year's peak: December promises were " f "kept far less often than in the rest of the year." , "Reason 1" : f "December on-time rate { december [ 'rate' ] : .0% } of { int ( december [ 'due' ]) } due shipments, " f "against { jan_oct_rate : .0% } for January to October." , "Reason 2" : f " { worst } kept { by_carrier_dec . loc [ worst , 'mean' ] : .0% } of its { int ( by_carrier_dec . loc [ worst , 'size' ]) } " f "December promises; the other carriers did better." , "Reason 3" : f " { monthly [ 'due' ] . idxmax () : %B } had the most due shipments of the year ( { monthly [ 'due' ] . max () } ), " f "so the failure hit the most customers." , } for level , text in pyramid . items (): indent = "" if level == "Governing message" else " " print ( f " { indent }{ level } : { text } " ) Governing message: Review ParcelOne's peak-season performance before next year's peak: December promises were kept far less often than in the rest of the year. Reason 1: December on-time rate 55% of 790 due shipments, against 88% for January to October. Reason 2: ParcelOne kept 24% of its 288 December promises; the other carriers did better. Reason 3: December had the most due shipments of the year (790), so the failure hit the most customers. The governing message above is an action , not a finding, and it is specific: who, what, by when. Each reason carries one number with its comparison. The evidence for each reason (definitions, checks, the carrier mix) goes in the appendix, ready for questions. Check your understanding 1 A briefing opens with "Today I will walk you through our data sources and cleaning steps." Rewrite the first sentence for an executive audience, using the operations case. Part 2: So-what titles ¶ Every slide or figure title should state the message , so a reader who only reads titles still gets the argument. Topic title (what the chart is about) So-what title (what the reader should conclude) On-time rate by month, 2025 December promises were missed far more often than in any other month On-time rate by carrier One carrier accounts for most of December's missed promises Due shipments by month The busiest month was also the least reliable one Data quality checks Every shipment is accounted for; those with unknown promise dates are excluded and listed Good so-what titles are full sentences , use the reader's words , and are true for the whole chart , not just its most dramatic point. Because the title states a number-based claim, build it from the data so it can never drift from the chart. best_month = monthly [ "rate" ] . idxmax () . strftime ( "%B" ) title = ( f "December's on-time rate ( { december [ 'rate' ] : .0% } ) was the lowest of 2025; " f "the best month was { best_month } ( { monthly [ 'rate' ] . max () : .0% } )" ) print ( title ) December's on-time rate (55%) was the lowest of 2025; the best month was April (90%) Part 3: Numbers with context ¶ A bare number cannot be judged. "60%" is good news for a coin toss and terrible news for delivery promises. Every number in a briefing needs: Context Question it answers Example of the missing piece Denominator Out of how many? "...of n due shipments" Period When, and up to which cutoff? "...promised in December 2025, as of 31 December" Comparison Compared with what? "...against the January to October rate" Unit and definition Measured how? "on time = delivered on or before the promised date" Sensible rounding How precise is it really? "62%" not "61.8421%" Predict, then reveal Which of the two sentences printed below will an operations director remember and act on? Which one could be misread? def in_context ( k , n , label , period , comparison_rate , comparison_label ): """A rate written with its denominator, period and comparison, rounded for speech.""" rate = k / n gap = ( rate - comparison_rate ) * 100 return ( f " { label } : { rate : .0% } ( { k : , } of { n : , } ) { period } , " f " { abs ( gap ) : .0f } percentage points { 'below' if gap < 0 else 'above' } { comparison_label } ( { comparison_rate : .0% } )." ) print ( "Bare: " , f "On-time rate: { december [ 'rate' ] : .4% } " ) print ( "In context: " , in_context ( int ( december [ "on_time" ]), int ( december [ "due" ]), "On-time deliveries" , "for shipments promised in December 2025" , jan_oct_rate , "January to October" )) Bare: On-time rate: 55.3165% In context: On-time deliveries: 55% (437 of 790) for shipments promised in December 2025, 32 percentage points below January to October (88%). The second sentence above can be repeated in a corridor and still be right. Notice two details: A difference between two percentages is in percentage points , not percent. "From 80% to 60%" is a fall of 20 percentage points , which is a fall of 25% in relative terms . Say which one you mean. Four decimal places suggest a precision nobody needs. Round for speech; keep the exact figure in the appendix. Check your understanding 2 A slide says "Returns up 50%!". List three pieces of context you need before you can judge whether this matters. Part 4: Presenting uncertainty honestly ¶ Executives make decisions under uncertainty all the time. What they need from you is an honest statement of how sure you are, in plain words. Ranges and confidence intervals ¶ In Session 9 you built confidence intervals for a sample mean and an A/B lift. Here every December shipment is in the data, so what is uncertain? The useful question is: "Could a month like this happen by chance in a process that is really running at its normal rate?" Treating December's shipments as one draw from the ongoing delivery process, a 95% interval shows the range of rates consistent with what we saw. For a rate p from n cases, the formula interval is p ± 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n) . The bootstrap from Session 9 gives a check by simulation. def rate_ci ( k , n , z = 1.96 ): """Rate with a normal-approximation 95% interval (fine when n is large and p not near 0 or 1).""" p = k / n half = z * np . sqrt ( p * ( 1 - p ) / n ) return p , p - half , p + half rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 16 ) dec_outcomes = due . loc [ due [ "promised_month" ] == "2025-12-01" , "on_time" ] . to_numpy () boot = np . array ([ rng . choice ( dec_outcomes , size = len ( dec_outcomes ), replace = True ) . mean () for _ in range ( 5000 )]) p , low , high = rate_ci ( int ( december [ "on_time" ]), int ( december [ "due" ])) pd . DataFrame ({ "estimate" : [ p , p ], "95 % lo w" : [ low , np . percentile ( boot , 2.5 )], "95 % hi gh" : [ high , np . percentile ( boot , 97.5 )], }, index = [ "Formula" , "Bootstrap (5,000 resamples, seed 16)" ]) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimate 95% low 95% high Formula 55.3% 51.8% 58.8% Bootstrap (5,000 resamples, seed 16) 55.3% 51.8% 58.7% The two methods in the table above agree closely, as they should with several hundred shipments. Now the comparison the briefing actually makes: December against January to October. Predict, then reveal Will the 95% interval for the difference between December and January–October include zero? p1 , n1 = december [ "rate" ], int ( december [ "due" ]) p0 , n0 = jan_oct_rate , int ( jan_oct [ "due" ] . sum ()) diff = p1 - p0 half = 1.96 * np . sqrt ( p1 * ( 1 - p1 ) / n1 + p0 * ( 1 - p0 ) / n0 ) print ( f "December minus Jan-Oct: { diff * 100 : +.1f } points, 95% interval { ( diff - half ) * 100 : +.1f } to { ( diff + half ) * 100 : +.1f } points" ) December minus Jan-Oct: -32.3 points, 95% interval -35.9 to -28.7 points The whole interval above is far from zero: December's drop is much too large to be chance variation at this volume. That is the statistical part. The business part is separate: the drop is also large in practical terms , because it affected the busiest month. Report both, in plain words. Say Avoid "December's rate was between about [low] and [high], far below the rate of earlier months." "There is a 95% probability that the true rate is in this interval." "The drop is too large to be explained by month-to-month chance." "The result is statistically significant" (with no size or meaning) "We assume December's shipments reflect the process as it ran in that month." Leaving the assumption unstated "This shows when and where promises failed, not why ." "ParcelOne caused the December failure." State your assumptions ¶ Every briefing rests on choices. List the ones that could change the answer, briefly, in the appendix: Definitions : on time means delivered on or before the promised date; pending due shipments count as failures. Population : canceled shipments and shipments with unknown promise dates are excluded and listed. Period and cutoff : promised months of 2025; data as of 31 December 2025. Uncertainty model : shipments treated as independent draws, which is optimistic if failures cluster (one bad truck delays many parcels). Real uncertainty is probably wider than the interval. Check your understanding 3 An executive asks: "Every December shipment is in the data. Why do you need an interval at all?" Answer in two sentences. Part 5: One summary figure ¶ If the audience remembers one picture, make it the right one. A good summary figure: Has a so-what title built from the data. Shows the comparison that carries the message (December against the rest of the year). Shows uncertainty where it matters (a band or error bars). Highlights the key point with colour and greys out the context. Has labelled axes with units , and a caption with the definition, source and cutoff. ci = pd . DataFrame ([ rate_ci ( k , n ) for k , n in zip ( monthly [ "on_time" ], monthly [ "due" ])], columns = [ "rate" , "low" , "high" ], index = monthly . index ) x = np . arange ( len ( monthly )) colours = [ "#eb6834" if m . month == 12 else "#b8b6b0" for m in monthly . index ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) ax . bar ( x , ci [ "rate" ] * 100 , color = colours ) ax . errorbar ( x , ci [ "rate" ] * 100 , yerr = [( ci [ "rate" ] - ci [ "low" ]) * 100 , ( ci [ "high" ] - ci [ "rate" ]) * 100 ], fmt = "none" , ecolor = "black" , elinewidth = 1 , capsize = 3 ) ax . axhline ( jan_oct_rate * 100 , color = "#2a78d6" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 1.5 , label = f "January-October: { jan_oct_rate : .0% } " ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 , loc = "lower left" ) ax . set_xticks ( x , monthly . index . strftime ( "%b" )) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) ax . set_title ( f "December promises were kept far less often: { december [ 'rate' ] : .0% } on time " f "vs { jan_oct_rate : .0% } earlier in 2025" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Promised month, 2025" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "On-time rate ( % o f due shipments)" ) fig . text ( 0.01 , - 0.02 , "On time = delivered on or before the promised date; pending due shipments count as late. " "Black bars: 95 % i ntervals. Synthetic operations-v1 data, cutoff 2025-12-31." , fontsize = 8 , color = "#555555" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Compare the figure above with a default chart of twelve equal bars. The orange bar, the dashed reference line and the title do the work; the intervals show that the earlier months are steady and December is clearly different. Everything else is grey. Check your understanding 4 A colleague wants to add carrier, warehouse and service lines to this figure "so it is complete". What would you say, and where would that detail go instead? Part 6: One page, or three to five slides ¶ Briefings are short by design. Two common formats: One-page brief Three-to-five-slide briefing Title = the recommendation as a sentence Slide 1 : the decision needed and your recommendation Recommendation in two or three sentences, with owner and timing Slide 2 : the one summary figure, with a so-what title Why : two or three findings, each with its number in context Slide 3 : trade-offs between the options, and why this one Trade-offs and risks Slide 4 : uncertainty, limits and what would change your mind Uncertainty and limits Slide 5 : next steps: owner, monitoring measure, review date Next steps and monitoring measure Appendix : definitions, checks, data versions, detailed tables For the capstone, the recommended flow is: decision requested → two or three evidence-backed findings → the cross-domain trade-off → recommended action and owner → monitoring measure and review period → limits and next evidence. Aim for about six minutes of talking and two minutes of questions. Keep metric definitions, checks and detailed slices in the appendix. Part 7: Handling questions and challenge ¶ Questions are not attacks; they are the audience testing whether to trust you . Prepare for the predictable ones. Question What a good answer contains "How do you know?" The definition, the check you ran and the data version: "on-time due shipments ÷ all due shipments; populations reconcile; operations-v1, cutoff 31 December" "What would change your mind?" Specific evidence: "If next month's ParcelOne rate returned to its earlier level with the same volume, the problem was a one-off" "Compared with what?" The baseline and why you chose it "Is this the cause?" Honest scope: "This shows where and when; to show why, we need..." "What happens if we wait?" The cost of delay, with its uncertainty "Why not option X instead?" The trade-off table and the weight-sensitivity result A question you cannot answer "I don't know. I can find out by [specific analysis] by [date]." Never guess a number The best preparation is an appendix of ready answers : small tables that answer the predictable follow-ups. For example, "Is it just one carrier?": due [ "period" ] = np . where ( due [ "promised_month" ] >= "2025-11-01" , "Nov-Dec" , "Jan-Oct" ) answer = due . groupby ([ "carrier" , "period" ])[ "on_time" ] . agg ( due = "size" , rate = "mean" ) . unstack ( "period" ) answer . columns = [ f " { measure } { period } " for measure , period in answer . columns ] answer [[ "due Jan-Oct" , "rate Jan-Oct" , "due Nov-Dec" , "rate Nov-Dec" ]] . assign ( ** { c : lambda t , c = c : t [ c ] . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) for c in [ "rate Jan-Oct" , "rate Nov-Dec" ]}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due Jan-Oct rate Jan-Oct due Nov-Dec rate Nov-Dec carrier ParcelOne 1546 84% 513 44% Regional Express 947 89% 312 73% SwiftRoute 1832 90% 592 77% The table above lets you answer in one breath: every carrier's rate fell in the peak, but one fell much further. That is a more honest answer than either "yes, it is one carrier" or "no, it is everyone". Check your understanding 5 An executive says: "Your numbers are wrong; our December was fine." Describe, in three steps, how you would respond without becoming defensive. Part 8: Common failure modes ¶ Failure What it looks like Fix Burying the lead The recommendation appears on the last slide Recommendation in the first sentence Data dump Twelve charts "for completeness" One summary figure; the rest in the appendix Naked numbers "60%" with no denominator, period or comparison Number + denominator + period + comparison False precision "61.8421%" Round for speech; exact figures in the appendix Hidden uncertainty A single number presented as certain A range and the main assumptions Causal overreach "X caused Y" from descriptive data or co-movement Say what the data show, and what would show causes False links Findings from separate datasets presented as one story Keep each finding in its own context Defensive answers Arguing with the questioner Acknowledge, show the evidence, offer a follow-up No ask Ends with "any questions?" End with the decision you need and the next step Part 9: The feedback rubric ¶ Briefings and capstones are reviewed with a rubric of criteria and four levels. This working rubric is for feedback , so you know what strong work looks like; it is not an official grade. It includes a criterion for statistical reasoning : whether uncertainty, correlation versus causation and the choice of summaries are handled well. Criterion 4: strong 3: sound 2: developing 1: limited Decision framing and metric contracts Decision bounded; every metric's grain, period, filters and missing-value rule explicit Clear decision; minor gaps in definitions Broad decision or one important definition missing No actionable decision; definitions missing Preparation and analytical correctness Grain and joins preserved; calculations reproducible Core results correct; small non-critical issues A join, date or denominator issue affects a result Core results cannot be trusted Validation and reproducibility Versions, reconciliations, hand checks and corrected bugs complete Critical checks done; minor gaps Checks mostly visual or incomplete Little usable validation Statistical reasoning Uncertainty quantified and explained; association kept separate from causation; right summary for each distribution Uncertainty and causation handled with small gaps Uncertainty ignored or one causal overclaim Repeated overclaims; misleading summaries Visual communication One clear summary figure; so-what titles; labelled units; accessible colours Clear figures with small labelling issues A misleading encoding or missing context Charts misrepresent the evidence Recommendation, synthesis and limitations Prioritised action with owner and monitoring; trade-offs and limits explicit; three or more domains without false links Feasible action; synthesis and limits present Action weakly linked to evidence; superficial synthesis Unsupported recommendation; major overclaim Executive briefing Recommendation first; numbers in context; answers challenge with evidence Clear briefing; competent answers Overlong or unclear; weak answers Cannot explain key results or assumptions The cell below turns the rubric into a scoring table. Each criterion has a weight; a criterion scores weight × level ÷ 4 , so all level-4 scores give 100. The weights are a teaching proposal to show how a rubric combines criteria; your facilitator will tell you how feedback is used in your course. rubric = pd . DataFrame ({ "weight" : [ 15 , 20 , 15 , 15 , 10 , 15 , 10 ], }, index = [ "Decision framing and metric contracts" , "Preparation and analytical correctness" , "Validation and reproducibility" , "Statistical reasoning" , "Visual communication" , "Recommendation, synthesis and limitations" , "Executive briefing" ]) assert rubric [ "weight" ] . sum () == 100 example_levels = [ 3 , 4 , 3 , 2 , 3 , 3 , 4 ] # an illustrative peer's levels, 1-4 scored = rubric . assign ( level = example_levels , points = lambda t : t [ "weight" ] * t [ "level" ] / 4 ) print ( f "Total: { scored [ 'points' ] . sum () : .1f } of 100. Lowest-level criterion: { scored [ 'level' ] . idxmin () } " ) scored Total: 78.8 of 100. Lowest-level criterion: Statistical reasoning .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weight level points Decision framing and metric contracts 15 3 11.25 Preparation and analytical correctness 20 4 20.00 Validation and reproducibility 15 3 11.25 Statistical reasoning 15 2 7.50 Visual communication 10 3 7.50 Recommendation, synthesis and limitations 15 3 11.25 Executive briefing 10 4 10.00 Read the scored table above the way a reviewer would: the total matters less than the lowest criterion , because that is where the next revision should start. A materially wrong critical number is never "averaged away": it must be corrected before the recommendation can be treated as verified. Part 10: Reflection and next steps ¶ Over the Python sessions you have moved through the whole analytics workflow: Stage What you can now do Question Turn a request into a decision, population, period and measure Data Check grain, keys, types and missing values; clean and log changes Measure Define metrics with contracts; use ratios of sums; avoid the classic traps Describe and relate Summarise distributions, trends and relationships, and know what correlation cannot show Quantify uncertainty Build confidence intervals and read an A/B test honestly Apply Analyse retail, finance, operations, marketing and HR cases under their contracts Communicate Build dashboards, write so-what titles, brief executives and handle challenge What comes next: the Tableau section. The course continues by rebuilding key analyses in Tableau, using the same datasets and the same metric contracts. Everything in this lecture carries over: a Tableau dashboard needs the same so-what titles, context and honesty about uncertainty. See the course roadmap . Reflection ¶ Answer these for yourself; your lab's course reflection builds on them. Which one trap from the course (for example, the mean of rates, the current-headcount denominator, dropped pending shipments, a false join) are you most likely to meet at work? How will you spot it? Which check will you now run on every analysis before you share it? Think of a decision at your own workplace. What would its evidence register contain, and which domain would be hardest to measure? What would you do differently if you started your capstone again? Summary ¶ Question Tool Trap to avoid What do I say first? The recommendation, as an action Opening with data and method How do I organise the argument? Pyramid: message → reasons → evidence A chronological story of the work What goes in a title? A so-what sentence built from the data A topic label How do I state a number? Denominator, period, comparison, unit, rounding Naked numbers; false precision How sure am I? A range or interval, plus assumptions, in plain words Hiding uncertainty; "95% probability" wording How do I handle challenge? Prepared appendix answers; "what would change my mind" Guessing, arguing, or causal overreach How is a briefing judged? A rubric with levels, including statistical reasoning Treating a total as more important than the weakest criterion Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you: Turn a provided operations analysis into a one-page brief and a single summary figure. Prepare your own capstone briefing: structure, figure and an anticipated-questions table. Critique a peer's briefing with the rubric, and write a revision plan. Challenge: answer three tough executive questions in writing, with evidence. Finish with an exit ticket and a course reflection. Open the Session 16 lab .

docs.text: An analysis only changes a decision if the people who decide understand it, trust it and remember it. This lecture is about that last step: putting the recommendation first, giving every number its context and its uncertainty, designing one figure that carries the message, and answering hard questions with evidence rather than confidence. How to handle challenge : "How do you know?", "What would change your mind?" and other hard questions. docs.text: Analysts are trained to tell the story in the order they did the work: data, method, findings, and finally the recommendation. Executives need the reverse order, because their scarce resource is attention and their job is the decision. Analyst's natural order Executive order 1. Background and data 1. Recommendation and the decision you need 2. Method 2. Two or three reasons , each with its key number 3. Findings 3. Trade-offs , risks and uncertainty 4. Caveats 4. Next steps : owner, measure, review date 5. Recommendation (if time) 5. Appendix: method, definitions, checks The pyramid principle (from Barbara Minto's consulting work) gives the structure: one governing message at the top, a few supporting arguments below it, and evidence under each argument. A listener who stops after the first sentence still has the answer; one who keeps listening gets the reasons, then the evidence. Predict, then reveal Using the Session 11 analysis, what would you put at the top of the pyramid for the operations manager? Write one sentence before running the next cell. by_carrier_dec = due [ due [ "promised_month" ] == "2025-12-01" ] . groupby ( "carrier" )[ "on_time" ] . agg ([ "size" , "mean" ]) worst = by_carrier_dec [ "mean" ] . idxmin () pyramid = { "Governing message" : f "Review { worst } 's peak-season performance before next year's peak: December promises were " f "kept far less often than in the rest of the year." , "Reason 1" : f "December on-time rate { december [ 'rate' ] : .0% } of { int ( december [ 'due' ]) } due shipments, " f "against { jan_oct_rate : .0% } for January to October." , "Reason 2" : f " { worst } kept { by_carrier_dec . loc [ worst , 'mean' ] : .0% } of its { int ( by_carrier_dec . loc [ worst , 'size' ]) } " f "December promises; the other carriers did better." , "Reason 3" : f " { monthly [ 'due' ] . idxmax () : %B } had the most due shipments of the year ( { monthly [ 'due' ] . max () } ), " f "so the failure hit the most customers." , } for level , text in pyramid . items (): indent = "" if level == "Governing message" else " " print ( f " { indent }{ level } : { text } " ) Governing message: Review ParcelOne's peak-season performance before next year's peak: December promises were kept far less often than in the rest of the year. Reason 1: December on-time rate 55% of 790 due shipments, against 88% for January to October. Reason 2: ParcelOne kept 24% of its 288 December promises; the other carriers did better. Reason 3: December had the most due shipments of the year (790), so the failure hit the most customers. The governing message above is an action , not a finding, and it is specific: who, what, by when. Each reason carries one number with its comparison. The evidence for each reason (definitions, checks, the carrier mix) goes in the appendix, ready for questions. docs.text: A bare number cannot be judged. "60%" is good news for a coin toss and terrible news for delivery promises. Every number in a briefing needs: Context Question it answers Example of the missing piece Denominator Out of how many? "...of n due shipments" Period When, and up to which cutoff? "...promised in December 2025, as of 31 December" Comparison Compared with what? "...against the January to October rate" Unit and definition Measured how? "on time = delivered on or before the promised date" Sensible rounding How precise is it really? "62%" not "61.8421%" Predict, then reveal Which of the two sentences printed below will an operations director remember and act on? Which one could be misread? def in_context ( k , n , label , period , comparison_rate , comparison_label ): """A rate written with its denominator, period and comparison, rounded for speech.""" rate = k / n gap = ( rate - comparison_rate ) * 100 return ( f " { label } : { rate : .0% } ( { k : , } of { n : , } ) { period } , " f " { abs ( gap ) : .0f } percentage points { 'below' if gap < 0 else 'above' } { comparison_label } ( { comparison_rate : .0% } )." ) print ( "Bare: " , f "On-time rate: { december [ 'rate' ] : .4% } " ) print ( "In context: " , in_context ( int ( december [ "on_time" ]), int ( december [ "due" ]), "On-time deliveries" , "for shipments promised in December 2025" , jan_oct_rate , "January to October" )) Bare: On-time rate: 55.3165% In context: On-time deliveries: 55% (437 of 790) for shipments promised in December 2025, 32 percentage points below January to October (88%). The second sentence above can be repeated in a corridor and still be right. Notice two details: A difference between two percentages is in percentage points , not percent. "From 80% to 60%" is a fall of 20 percentage points , which is a fall of 25% in relative terms . Say which one you mean. Four decimal places suggest a precision nobody needs. Round for speech; keep the exact figure in the appendix. Check your understanding 2 A slide says "Returns up 50%!". List three pieces of context you need before you can judge whether this matters.
docs.title: Part 3: Numbers with context

docs.text: Executives make decisions under uncertainty all the time. What they need from you is an honest statement of how sure you are, in plain words.
docs.title: Part 4: Presenting uncertainty honestly

docs.text: In Session 9 you built confidence intervals for a sample mean and an A/B lift. Here every December shipment is in the data, so what is uncertain? The useful question is: "Could a month like this happen by chance in a process that is really running at its normal rate?" Treating December's shipments as one draw from the ongoing delivery process, a 95% interval shows the range of rates consistent with what we saw. For a rate p from n cases, the formula interval is p ± 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n) . The bootstrap from Session 9 gives a check by simulation. def rate_ci ( k , n , z = 1.96 ): """Rate with a normal-approximation 95% interval (fine when n is large and p not near 0 or 1).""" p = k / n half = z * np . sqrt ( p * ( 1 - p ) / n ) return p , p - half , p + half rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 16 ) dec_outcomes = due . loc [ due [ "promised_month" ] == "2025-12-01" , "on_time" ] . to_numpy () boot = np . array ([ rng . choice ( dec_outcomes , size = len ( dec_outcomes ), replace = True ) . mean () for _ in range ( 5000 )]) p , low , high = rate_ci ( int ( december [ "on_time" ]), int ( december [ "due" ])) pd . DataFrame ({ "estimate" : [ p , p ], "95 % lo w" : [ low , np . percentile ( boot , 2.5 )], "95 % hi gh" : [ high , np . percentile ( boot , 97.5 )], }, index = [ "Formula" , "Bootstrap (5,000 resamples, seed 16)" ]) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimate 95% low 95% high Formula 55.3% 51.8% 58.8% Bootstrap (5,000 resamples, seed 16) 55.3% 51.8% 58.7% The two methods in the table above agree closely, as they should with several hundred shipments. Now the comparison the briefing actually makes: December against January to October. Predict, then reveal Will the 95% interval for the difference between December and January–October include zero? p1 , n1 = december [ "rate" ], int ( december [ "due" ]) p0 , n0 = jan_oct_rate , int ( jan_oct [ "due" ] . sum ()) diff = p1 - p0 half = 1.96 * np . sqrt ( p1 * ( 1 - p1 ) / n1 + p0 * ( 1 - p0 ) / n0 ) print ( f "December minus Jan-Oct: { diff * 100 : +.1f } points, 95% interval { ( diff - half ) * 100 : +.1f } to { ( diff + half ) * 100 : +.1f } points" ) December minus Jan-Oct: -32.3 points, 95% interval -35.9 to -28.7 points The whole interval above is far from zero: December's drop is much too large to be chance variation at this volume. That is the statistical part. The business part is separate: the drop is also large in practical terms , because it affected the busiest month. Report both, in plain words. Say Avoid "December's rate was between about [low] and [high], far below the rate of earlier months." "There is a 95% probability that the true rate is in this interval." "The drop is too large to be explained by month-to-month chance." "The result is statistically significant" (with no size or meaning) "We assume December's shipments reflect the process as it ran in that month." Leaving the assumption unstated "This shows when and where promises failed, not why ." "ParcelOne caused the December failure."
docs.title: Ranges and confidence intervals

docs.text: Every briefing rests on choices. List the ones that could change the answer, briefly, in the appendix: Definitions : on time means delivered on or before the promised date; pending due shipments count as failures. Population : canceled shipments and shipments with unknown promise dates are excluded and listed. Period and cutoff : promised months of 2025; data as of 31 December 2025. Uncertainty model : shipments treated as independent draws, which is optimistic if failures cluster (one bad truck delays many parcels). Real uncertainty is probably wider than the interval. Check your understanding 3 An executive asks: "Every December shipment is in the data. Why do you need an interval at all?" Answer in two sentences.
docs.title: State your assumptions

docs.text: If the audience remembers one picture, make it the right one. A good summary figure: Has a so-what title built from the data. Shows the comparison that carries the message (December against the rest of the year). Shows uncertainty where it matters (a band or error bars). Highlights the key point with colour and greys out the context. Has labelled axes with units , and a caption with the definition, source and cutoff. ci = pd . DataFrame ([ rate_ci ( k , n ) for k , n in zip ( monthly [ "on_time" ], monthly [ "due" ])], columns = [ "rate" , "low" , "high" ], index = monthly . index ) x = np . arange ( len ( monthly )) colours = [ "#eb6834" if m . month == 12 else "#b8b6b0" for m in monthly . index ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) ax . bar ( x , ci [ "rate" ] * 100 , color = colours ) ax . errorbar ( x , ci [ "rate" ] * 100 , yerr = [( ci [ "rate" ] - ci [ "low" ]) * 100 , ( ci [ "high" ] - ci [ "rate" ]) * 100 ], fmt = "none" , ecolor = "black" , elinewidth = 1 , capsize = 3 ) ax . axhline ( jan_oct_rate * 100 , color = "#2a78d6" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 1.5 , label = f "January-October: { jan_oct_rate : .0% } " ) ax . legend ( fontsize = 8 , loc = "lower left" ) ax . set_xticks ( x , monthly . index . strftime ( "%b" )) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) ax . set_title ( f "December promises were kept far less often: { december [ 'rate' ] : .0% } on time " f "vs { jan_oct_rate : .0% } earlier in 2025" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Promised month, 2025" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "On-time rate ( % o f due shipments)" ) fig . text ( 0.01 , - 0.02 , "On time = delivered on or before the promised date; pending due shipments count as late. " "Black bars: 95 % i ntervals. Synthetic operations-v1 data, cutoff 2025-12-31." , fontsize = 8 , color = "#555555" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Compare the figure above with a default chart of twelve equal bars. The orange bar, the dashed reference line and the title do the work; the intervals show that the earlier months are steady and December is clearly different. Everything else is grey. Check your understanding 4 A colleague wants to add carrier, warehouse and service lines to this figure "so it is complete". What would you say, and where would that detail go instead?
docs.title: Part 5: One summary figure

docs.text: Briefings are short by design. Two common formats: One-page brief Three-to-five-slide briefing Title = the recommendation as a sentence Slide 1 : the decision needed and your recommendation Recommendation in two or three sentences, with owner and timing Slide 2 : the one summary figure, with a so-what title Why : two or three findings, each with its number in context Slide 3 : trade-offs between the options, and why this one Trade-offs and risks Slide 4 : uncertainty, limits and what would change your mind Uncertainty and limits Slide 5 : next steps: owner, monitoring measure, review date Next steps and monitoring measure Appendix : definitions, checks, data versions, detailed tables For the capstone, the recommended flow is: decision requested → two or three evidence-backed findings → the cross-domain trade-off → recommended action and owner → monitoring measure and review period → limits and next evidence. Aim for about six minutes of talking and two minutes of questions. Keep metric definitions, checks and detailed slices in the appendix.
docs.title: Part 6: One page, or three to five slides

docs.text: Questions are not attacks; they are the audience testing whether to trust you . Prepare for the predictable ones. Question What a good answer contains "How do you know?" The definition, the check you ran and the data version: "on-time due shipments ÷ all due shipments; populations reconcile; operations-v1, cutoff 31 December" "What would change your mind?" Specific evidence: "If next month's ParcelOne rate returned to its earlier level with the same volume, the problem was a one-off" "Compared with what?" The baseline and why you chose it "Is this the cause?" Honest scope: "This shows where and when; to show why, we need..." "What happens if we wait?" The cost of delay, with its uncertainty "Why not option X instead?" The trade-off table and the weight-sensitivity result A question you cannot answer "I don't know. I can find out by [specific analysis] by [date]." Never guess a number The best preparation is an appendix of ready answers : small tables that answer the predictable follow-ups. For example, "Is it just one carrier?": due [ "period" ] = np . where ( due [ "promised_month" ] >= "2025-11-01" , "Nov-Dec" , "Jan-Oct" ) answer = due . groupby ([ "carrier" , "period" ])[ "on_time" ] . agg ( due = "size" , rate = "mean" ) . unstack ( "period" ) answer . columns = [ f " { measure } { period } " for measure , period in answer . columns ] answer [[ "due Jan-Oct" , "rate Jan-Oct" , "due Nov-Dec" , "rate Nov-Dec" ]] . assign ( ** { c : lambda t , c = c : t [ c ] . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) for c in [ "rate Jan-Oct" , "rate Nov-Dec" ]}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } due Jan-Oct rate Jan-Oct due Nov-Dec rate Nov-Dec carrier ParcelOne 1546 84% 513 44% Regional Express 947 89% 312 73% SwiftRoute 1832 90% 592 77% The table above lets you answer in one breath: every carrier's rate fell in the peak, but one fell much further. That is a more honest answer than either "yes, it is one carrier" or "no, it is everyone". Check your understanding 5 An executive says: "Your numbers are wrong; our December was fine." Describe, in three steps, how you would respond without becoming defensive.
docs.title: Part 7: Handling questions and challenge

docs.text: Failure What it looks like Fix Burying the lead The recommendation appears on the last slide Recommendation in the first sentence Data dump Twelve charts "for completeness" One summary figure; the rest in the appendix Naked numbers "60%" with no denominator, period or comparison Number + denominator + period + comparison False precision "61.8421%" Round for speech; exact figures in the appendix Hidden uncertainty A single number presented as certain A range and the main assumptions Causal overreach "X caused Y" from descriptive data or co-movement Say what the data show, and what would show causes False links Findings from separate datasets presented as one story Keep each finding in its own context Defensive answers Arguing with the questioner Acknowledge, show the evidence, offer a follow-up No ask Ends with "any questions?" End with the decision you need and the next step
docs.title: Part 8: Common failure modes

docs.text: Briefings and capstones are reviewed with a rubric of criteria and four levels. This working rubric is for feedback , so you know what strong work looks like; it is not an official grade. It includes a criterion for statistical reasoning : whether uncertainty, correlation versus causation and the choice of summaries are handled well. Criterion 4: strong 3: sound 2: developing 1: limited Decision framing and metric contracts Decision bounded; every metric's grain, period, filters and missing-value rule explicit Clear decision; minor gaps in definitions Broad decision or one important definition missing No actionable decision; definitions missing Preparation and analytical correctness Grain and joins preserved; calculations reproducible Core results correct; small non-critical issues A join, date or denominator issue affects a result Core results cannot be trusted Validation and reproducibility Versions, reconciliations, hand checks and corrected bugs complete Critical checks done; minor gaps Checks mostly visual or incomplete Little usable validation Statistical reasoning Uncertainty quantified and explained; association kept separate from causation; right summary for each distribution Uncertainty and causation handled with small gaps Uncertainty ignored or one causal overclaim Repeated overclaims; misleading summaries Visual communication One clear summary figure; so-what titles; labelled units; accessible colours Clear figures with small labelling issues A misleading encoding or missing context Charts misrepresent the evidence Recommendation, synthesis and limitations Prioritised action with owner and monitoring; trade-offs and limits explicit; three or more domains without false links Feasible action; synthesis and limits present Action weakly linked to evidence; superficial synthesis Unsupported recommendation; major overclaim Executive briefing Recommendation first; numbers in context; answers challenge with evidence Clear briefing; competent answers Overlong or unclear; weak answers Cannot explain key results or assumptions The cell below turns the rubric into a scoring table. Each criterion has a weight; a criterion scores weight × level ÷ 4 , so all level-4 scores give 100. The weights are a teaching proposal to show how a rubric combines criteria; your facilitator will tell you how feedback is used in your course. rubric = pd . DataFrame ({ "weight" : [ 15 , 20 , 15 , 15 , 10 , 15 , 10 ], }, index = [ "Decision framing and metric contracts" , "Preparation and analytical correctness" , "Validation and reproducibility" , "Statistical reasoning" , "Visual communication" , "Recommendation, synthesis and limitations" , "Executive briefing" ]) assert rubric [ "weight" ] . sum () == 100 example_levels = [ 3 , 4 , 3 , 2 , 3 , 3 , 4 ] # an illustrative peer's levels, 1-4 scored = rubric . assign ( level = example_levels , points = lambda t : t [ "weight" ] * t [ "level" ] / 4 ) print ( f "Total: { scored [ 'points' ] . sum () : .1f } of 100. Lowest-level criterion: { scored [ 'level' ] . idxmin () } " ) scored Total: 78.8 of 100. Lowest-level criterion: Statistical reasoning .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weight level points Decision framing and metric contracts 15 3 11.25 Preparation and analytical correctness 20 4 20.00 Validation and reproducibility 15 3 11.25 Statistical reasoning 15 2 7.50 Visual communication 10 3 7.50 Recommendation, synthesis and limitations 15 3 11.25 Executive briefing 10 4 10.00 Read the scored table above the way a reviewer would: the total matters less than the lowest criterion , because that is where the next revision should start. A materially wrong critical number is never "averaged away": it must be corrected before the recommendation can be treated as verified.
docs.title: Part 9: The feedback rubric

docs.text: Over the Python sessions you have moved through the whole analytics workflow: Stage What you can now do Question Turn a request into a decision, population, period and measure Data Check grain, keys, types and missing values; clean and log changes Measure Define metrics with contracts; use ratios of sums; avoid the classic traps Describe and relate Summarise distributions, trends and relationships, and know what correlation cannot show Quantify uncertainty Build confidence intervals and read an A/B test honestly Apply Analyse retail, finance, operations, marketing and HR cases under their contracts Communicate Build dashboards, write so-what titles, brief executives and handle challenge What comes next: the Tableau section. The course continues by rebuilding key analyses in Tableau, using the same datasets and the same metric contracts. Everything in this lecture carries over: a Tableau dashboard needs the same so-what titles, context and honesty about uncertainty. See the course roadmap .
docs.title: Part 10: Reflection and next steps

docs.text: Answer these for yourself; your lab's course reflection builds on them. Which one trap from the course (for example, the mean of rates, the current-headcount denominator, dropped pending shipments, a false join) are you most likely to meet at work? How will you spot it? Which check will you now run on every analysis before you share it? Think of a decision at your own workplace. What would its evidence register contain, and which domain would be hardest to measure? What would you do differently if you started your capstone again?
docs.title: Reflection

docs.text: Question Tool Trap to avoid What do I say first? The recommendation, as an action Opening with data and method How do I organise the argument? Pyramid: message → reasons → evidence A chronological story of the work What goes in a title? A so-what sentence built from the data A topic label How do I state a number? Denominator, period, comparison, unit, rounding Naked numbers; false precision How sure am I? A range or interval, plus assumptions, in plain words Hiding uncertainty; "95% probability" wording How do I handle challenge? Prepared appendix answers; "what would change my mind" Guessing, arguing, or causal overreach How is a briefing judged? A rubric with levels, including statistical reasoning Treating a total as more important than the weakest criterion

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 1: From decision to evidence ¶ Turn a vague business request into a clear question, open your first dataset in Tableau, and build a first chart you can explain. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 2 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. Your facilitator will confirm them in class. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first." This is not yet a question you can answer with data. Today you will turn it into one, and then take a first look at the evidence. About the data We use a fictitious retail sample published by Tableau (the "Superstore" sample), prepared for this course. It is not a real company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units; the currency is not stated, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Write a business question that names a decision, a population and a time period. Connect Tableau to a CSV file and recognise dimensions and measures. Build a simple bar chart and add a filter. Explain the difference between one row and one order in this file. Save your workbook on your computer and reopen it. Evidence you keep: your written question, a saved first chart and a one-sentence explanation of what a row means. Before you start ¶ Read the Foundations pages. They explain why the habits in this lesson matter. Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition (see Setup and practice ). Complete the smoke test: open a CSV, create a sum, save, close and reopen. Get the course file order_lines.csv (release superstore-retail-v1 ) from your facilitator. Save it in a folder you can find again, for example Documents/DataAnalytics/data . If Tableau will not install or open Tell your facilitator before the session. You can follow the demonstration, pair with a classmate and still write your question and notes. You will build your own chart later. Part 1: From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course file Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment Putting it together: "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn Rewrite the head's request as your own question. Use the four parts in the table. Keep it to one sentence. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will connect to the file and build a first chart while you watch. Before each step, predict what you think will happen. Things to notice: How Tableau reads each column (text, number or date). Which fields appear as dimensions (things you group by) and which as measures (numbers you add up). What happens to a number when you drag it into the view. Part 3: Guided practice ¶ Follow along step by step. Connect to the file ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition. In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , choose Text file . Find and open order_lines.csv . Tableau opens the Data Source page with a preview of the rows. Check the column types ¶ Look at the small icon above each column in the preview: Icon Meaning Examples in this file Abc Text order_id, segment, region # Number sales, profit, quantity Calendar Date order_date, ship_date Check the IDs order_id and row_id are identifiers, not amounts. Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field. Build a first chart ¶ Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) . Add a filter ¶ Drag Region to the Filters card. Tick one region and click OK . Watch how the bars change. Then clear the filter so all regions are included again. Write it down Every time you filter, record it. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later. Save and reopen ¶ Choose File → Save As and save the workbook in your course folder, for example class01_first_view . Close Tableau, open it again and open your saved workbook. Check that the chart and your filter settings are still there. Part 4: Rows versus orders ¶ Open the Data Source page again and look at a few rows that share the same order_id . One row in this file is one order line : one product within an order. One order can have several lines. So the number of rows is not the number of orders. Quick check In the Data pane, Tableau lists a field named after the file with (Count) at the end. Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Lesson 2 . Part 5: Independent work ¶ On a new sheet, build one more simple view on your own: Choose a different grouping: Region or Category . Show Sales for each group. Add a title that says what the chart shows and for which period. Write one sentence describing what the chart shows. Do not explain why yet. Part 6: Challenge ¶ A colleague says: "The biggest bar is the best segment, so we should invest there." In two or three sentences, explain why a bigger Sales bar alone does not tell us where to invest. What else would you want to see? Exit ticket ¶ Before you finish, write: Your one-sentence business question. What one row in order_lines.csv represents. One thing you are still unsure about. After the lesson ¶ Fix anything that did not work during setup. Read the Analytical workflow page. Start your evidence log (see Setup and practice ) with today's question, file name and filters.

Column What it is Can you add it up? row_id Unique number for each order line No, it is an identifier order_id Order identifier; repeats across that order's lines No, count it distinctly order_date , ship_date Calendar dates No order_month First day of the order's month, for monthly grouping No ship_mode Shipping service chosen No customer_id Fictitious customer identifier No segment Customer group: Consumer, Corporate or Home Office No, use it to group country_region , region Location labels No, use them to group category , sub_category Product groups No, use them to group product_id , product_name Product identifier and name No sales Sales reported for the line, in the file's own monetary units Yes quantity Number of items on the line Yes , but it counts items, not orders profit Profit reported for the line (can be negative) Yes discount Discount value as given in the source No, its exact definition is not documented returned_order_flag 1 if the order appears on the source's returns list, otherwise 0 Not on line rows (see Part 4) order_to_ship_days Days between order date and ship date No, not without care customer_analysis_eligible , customer_order_conflict Flags for a small data issue with customer IDs Used only for customer analysis later Scope of this file The file contains orders placed from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025 . Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ.
