docs.text: Tableau Lesson 3: Which segment deserves a closer look? ¶ Compare the three customer segments using five measures, calculate each one correctly, check that the numbers add up, and make a careful recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 5 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. Today you build a fair comparison. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Define five measures precisely: Sales, Orders, Average order value, Profit and Profit ratio. Build them in Tableau as calculated fields. Calculate ratios from totals , not by averaging other ratios. Check that segment results reconcile with the overall total. Explain how a filter changes every measure. Write a short, evidence-based recommendation with one limitation. Evidence you keep: a segment KPI table, your metric definitions, a validation checklist and a five-sentence recommendation. Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 2 , with the Orders calculated field. Have your grain statement and evidence log ready. Re-read the averages and percentages traps in Foundations. Part 1: Agree the measures ¶ Every measure uses the same rows : all order lines in the file, unless you deliberately apply a filter. Measure What it means How to calculate it Sales Total reported Sales Add up sales Orders Number of different orders Count distinct order_id Average order value (AOV) Typical Sales per order Sales ÷ Orders Profit Total reported Profit (can be negative) Add up profit Profit ratio Profit earned per unit of Sales Profit ÷ Sales About the money Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units. The currency is not stated, so do not add a currency symbol. The source does not explain exactly how Profit is calculated, so call it profit ratio , not "gross margin". Totals first, then divide AOV and Profit ratio must be calculated from the totals for whatever you are looking at. Never average the ratios of individual rows or of segments. You will see why in Part 6. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator builds the five measures for the whole file and shows them as a small table. Before each number appears, predict : Will AOV be larger or smaller than Sales divided by the number of rows ? Why? Can Profit ratio be negative? When? Part 3: Guided practice — build the calculations ¶ Create each calculated field ( Analysis → Create Calculated Field ). Type the name and formula exactly. Sales SUM([Sales]) Orders (from Lesson 2) COUNTD([Order Id]) AOV IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN SUM([Sales]) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Profit SUM([Profit]) Profit ratio IF SUM([Sales]) <> 0 THEN SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) END Why the IF? If a filter leaves no orders or no Sales, dividing would be undefined. The IF makes Tableau show a blank instead of an error or a misleading zero. A blank here means "not available" , never 0%. Format the results: Sales, Profit and AOV: number with two decimal places, no currency symbol. Profit ratio: percentage with one decimal place. Part 4: Guided practice — the segment table ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Segment to Rows . Drag Measure Names to Columns and Measure Values to the table area. Keep only your five measures. Turn on totals: Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Give the sheet a clear title, for example "Segment comparison, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units)" . Check that it reconciles ¶ Tick each check in your evidence log: The three segment Sales add up to the grand total. The three segment Profit values add up to the grand total. The three segment Orders add up to the grand total. (They should, because every order belongs to exactly one segment.) The grand total AOV equals total Sales ÷ total Orders. It is not the average of the three segment AOVs. The grand total Profit ratio equals total Profit ÷ total Sales. It is not the average of the three segment ratios. If a total looks wrong Check that every measure uses the same filters, and that the grand total is recalculated, not summed. Right-click the measure and check which aggregation the total uses. Part 5: Independent work ¶ A. Filter by region ¶ Duplicate your segment sheet. Add Region to Filters and choose one region. Record all five measures for each segment in that region. Write two sentences: does the ranking of segments change inside this region? B. Look at a category ¶ Duplicate the sheet again and filter to one Category . Notice that AOV now means "Sales of this category's lines per order that contains this category" , not full basket value. Rename the column to say so. Remove the filter and put Category on Rows instead of Segment. Do the category Orders add up to the overall total? Explain why not, in one sentence. Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends you this summary: "Our overall profit ratio is the average of the three segment ratios. And our average order value is total Sales divided by the number of rows." Calculate the colleague's two numbers from your own table. Compare them with your correct grand totals. Explain each mistake in one sentence. Which segment has the most influence on the correct overall profit ratio, and why? Think about weights A segment with much more Sales should pull the overall ratio more strongly than a small segment. Does a simple average of the three ratios allow that? Part 7: Make a recommendation ¶ Write five sentences to the retail head: Recommendation: which segment to investigate first. Evidence 1: one measure, with its value and how it compares. Evidence 2: a second, different measure. Limitation: one thing this data cannot tell you. For example, it shows which segment looks different; it does not show why , and it does not prove a discount or promotion caused anything. Next check: one specific piece of evidence to request before changing promotions. Association, not cause If a segment with more discounts has a lower profit ratio, that is a pattern worth investigating. It is not proof that the discounts caused it. Other differences between segments, such as product mix, could explain it. Validation checklist ¶ Before submitting, confirm: Every measure uses the same filters and date scope. Orders are counted distinctly, not as rows. AOV and Profit ratio are calculated from totals. Segment Sales, Profit and Orders reconcile with the grand totals. Money is labelled "source monetary units", with no currency symbol. The recommendation names a limitation and a next check. Exit ticket ¶ Why is the average of three segment ratios not the overall ratio? What does a blank AOV or Profit ratio mean? One question you would want answered before acting on your recommendation. After the lesson ¶ Finish the region and category work from Part 5. Correct the colleague's summary in Part 6 and add it to your evidence log. Keep your workbook for Lesson 4 , where we look at monthly trends and the returns list, and build a dashboard.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 4: Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ¶ Add time to your segment comparison, read growth figures without being fooled by seasons, use the returns list carefully, and bring it all together in one dashboard with a recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 7 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Build a monthly Sales trend and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Combine views into a dashboard with one shared filter. Write a recommendation for a test, with an honest limitation. Evidence you keep: a retail dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, and a short recommendation. This dashboard is your retail portfolio checkpoint . Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 3 with the segment KPI table. Re-read cherry-picked time windows and storytelling with data . Part 1: The monthly trend ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Order Month to Columns . Right-click it and choose the continuous Month option (green pill), so every month from January 2023 to December 2025 appears in order. Drag your Sales measure to Rows . You now have a line chart. Add Segment to Color to see one line per segment. Then remove it again for the overall view. What do you notice? Write down three observations. Look at the same months in different years. Are some months always high? Are January and February always low? Use the month field order_month is the first day of each order's month. Using it keeps every order in the right calendar month and makes year-on-year comparisons simple. Part 2: Two kinds of growth ¶ Month-on-month growth ¶ Compares each month with the previous month. IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) END Year-on-year growth ¶ Compares each month with the same month one year earlier . IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) END To use them: Create both as calculated fields and format them as percentages with one decimal place. Put Order Month (continuous month) on Columns and one growth measure on Rows. Right-click the growth measure, choose Compute Using , and select Order Month . Blank is correct sometimes January 2023 has no previous month in this file, so its month-on-month growth is blank. All of 2023 has no year-earlier month, so its year-on-year growth is blank. Blank means "no comparison available" , never 0%. Filters can remove the comparison LOOKUP compares with the previous month shown in the view . If you filter the view to only 2025, January 2025 can no longer see December 2024 and becomes blank. Keep all months in the view and highlight the period you care about instead of filtering it away. Which one is fair? ¶ Growth type Good for Can mislead when Month-on-month Spotting sudden changes The business is seasonal: January after a busy December always looks like a crash Year-on-year Comparing like with like across seasons A one-off event happened in the same month last year Part 3: The returns list ¶ From Lesson 2, you know the returns flag marks orders that appear on the source's returns list . Create two measures: Orders on returns list COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) Share of orders on returns list IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Add the share to your segment table. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it. A separate synthetic exercise will cover refund amounts later. Part 4: Guided practice — build the dashboard ¶ Create a new dashboard ( Dashboard → New Dashboard ). Drag in three sheets: your segment KPI table from Lesson 3, with the returns share added the monthly Sales trend the year-on-year growth chart Add a Region filter. Click its menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source , so every view responds together. Give each sheet a message title that says what to notice, for example in the form "[Segment] sales [rose / fell] most in [period]" , filled in with what your chart actually shows. Add one short text box stating the scope: "Orders placed 2023–2025. Source monetary units. Fictitious sample data." Design checks ¶ Use what you learned in Designing clear visuals : The most important view is at the top left. Colour is used only where it means something, and each segment keeps the same colour everywhere. Every chart has labelled axes with units. Nothing can be understood only by colour; labels or a table are available too. When you change the Region filter, all views change together and the totals still reconcile. Part 5: Independent work ¶ Choose one segment . Using your dashboard, describe its trend over the three years in three sentences. Compare the same quarter across years for that segment. Is it growing, flat or falling? Add one annotation to the trend chart marking something a manager should notice ( right-click a point → Annotate → Mark ). Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague posts this in a team chat: "Disaster! Sales fell about 75% in January 2025. And I filtered the dashboard to 2025 to check, but now January's growth is blank. Something is broken." Is January's fall a real problem, or a seasonal pattern? Which growth measure would you show instead, and what does it say? Why did January's month-on-month growth become blank after filtering to 2025? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate. Part 7: Recommend a test ¶ Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison period you would use to judge the test, such as year-on-year Sales and profit ratio for the same months. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works. Validation checklist ¶ The trend shows all 36 months with no gaps. Growth measures compute along Order Month, and blanks appear only where no comparison exists. Returns are counted as distinct orders, not lines. The dashboard filter changes every view, and segment totals still reconcile with the overall total. Titles state messages; scope and units are written on the dashboard. Exit ticket ¶ Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What is one thing the returns list cannot tell you? What would you measure to judge whether your proposed test worked? After the lesson ¶ Finish your dashboard and recommendation. Together they form your retail portfolio checkpoint . docs.text: The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year.
docs.title: The business decision

docs.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Build a monthly Sales trend and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Combine views into a dashboard with one shared filter. Write a recommendation for a test, with an honest limitation. Evidence you keep: a retail dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, and a short recommendation. This dashboard is your retail portfolio checkpoint .
docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: Open your workbook from Lesson 3 with the segment KPI table. Re-read cherry-picked time windows and storytelling with data .
docs.title: Before you start

docs.text: Start a new sheet. Drag Order Month to Columns . Right-click it and choose the continuous Month option (green pill), so every month from January 2023 to December 2025 appears in order. Drag your Sales measure to Rows . You now have a line chart. Add Segment to Color to see one line per segment. Then remove it again for the overall view. What do you notice? Write down three observations. Look at the same months in different years. Are some months always high? Are January and February always low? Use the month field order_month is the first day of each order's month. Using it keeps every order in the right calendar month and makes year-on-year comparisons simple.
docs.title: Part 1: The monthly trend

docs.text: Compares each month with the previous month. IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) END
docs.title: Month-on-month growth

docs.text: Compares each month with the same month one year earlier . IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) END To use them: Create both as calculated fields and format them as percentages with one decimal place. Put Order Month (continuous month) on Columns and one growth measure on Rows. Right-click the growth measure, choose Compute Using , and select Order Month . Blank is correct sometimes January 2023 has no previous month in this file, so its month-on-month growth is blank. All of 2023 has no year-earlier month, so its year-on-year growth is blank. Blank means "no comparison available" , never 0%. Filters can remove the comparison LOOKUP compares with the previous month shown in the view . If you filter the view to only 2025, January 2025 can no longer see December 2024 and becomes blank. Keep all months in the view and highlight the period you care about instead of filtering it away.
docs.title: Year-on-year growth

docs.text: Growth type Good for Can mislead when Month-on-month Spotting sudden changes The business is seasonal: January after a busy December always looks like a crash Year-on-year Comparing like with like across seasons A one-off event happened in the same month last year
docs.title: Which one is fair?

docs.text: From Lesson 2, you know the returns flag marks orders that appear on the source's returns list . Create two measures: Orders on returns list COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) Share of orders on returns list IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Add the share to your segment table. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it. A separate synthetic exercise will cover refund amounts later.
docs.title: Part 3: The returns list

docs.text: Create a new dashboard ( Dashboard → New Dashboard ). Drag in three sheets: your segment KPI table from Lesson 3, with the returns share added the monthly Sales trend the year-on-year growth chart Add a Region filter. Click its menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source , so every view responds together. Give each sheet a message title that says what to notice, for example in the form "[Segment] sales [rose / fell] most in [period]" , filled in with what your chart actually shows. Add one short text box stating the scope: "Orders placed 2023–2025. Source monetary units. Fictitious sample data."
docs.title: Part 4: Guided practice — build the dashboard

docs.text: Use what you learned in Designing clear visuals : The most important view is at the top left. Colour is used only where it means something, and each segment keeps the same colour everywhere. Every chart has labelled axes with units. Nothing can be understood only by colour; labels or a table are available too. When you change the Region filter, all views change together and the totals still reconcile.

docs.text: Choose one segment . Using your dashboard, describe its trend over the three years in three sentences. Compare the same quarter across years for that segment. Is it growing, flat or falling? Add one annotation to the trend chart marking something a manager should notice ( right-click a point → Annotate → Mark ).
